-odd component in VBF Higgs production channels.

Quantum entanglement in
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{V}}}\mathup{{{V}}}

The precision with which Higgs production at an
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
collider will be accessible opens also the way to studies of the quantum properties of 4 fermion final states arising from the
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{V}}}_{1}\mathup{{{V}}}_{2}
decays.

The angular momentum in the Higgs boson decay into two weak bosons (which we consider as distinguishable) is fully determined by the tripartite density operator
\rho_{LS_{1}S_{2}}
involving the orbital angular momentum and the spins of the two bosons. In particular, this operator can be used to determine the entanglement between any two parties of the
LS_{1}S_{2}
system. The SM predicts a large entanglement in most cases. Using as entanglement measure an observable
N

[
423
]
called negativity, which takes values between 0 and 1, with 1 indicating largest possible entanglement. For
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{Z}}}\mathup{{{Z}}}
decays one predicts

\displaystyle L-(S_{1}S_{2}):\quad N=0.757\,,

\displaystyle L-S_{1}:\quad N=0.105\,,

\displaystyle S_{1}-(LS_{2}):\quad N=0.998\,,

\displaystyle L-S_{2}:\quad N=0.105\,,

\displaystyle S_{2}-(LS_{1}):\quad N=0.998\,,

\displaystyle S_{1}-S_{2}:\quad N=0.843\,,

(17)

with similar values for
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{W}}}\mathup{{{W}}}

[
424
]
. The numbers on the left side quantify the entanglement between one subsystem and the rest; with all of them being non-zero, the system is said to have genuine tripartite entanglement. The numbers on the right side correspond to the entanglement between two parties when the degrees of freedom of the third one are integrated out. The level of entanglement of the tripartite state, as well as possible violation of Bell inequalities, can be reconstructed from angular distributions of the decay products.

Angular distributions in the decay
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{V}}}_{1}\mathup{{{V}}}_{2}
can be parametrised either using a fixed reference system
(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})
, or a moving one
(\hat{r},\hat{n},\hat{k})
, where
\hat{k}
is taken in the direction of one of the decay products in the Higgs rest frame. The former, referred to as “canonical basis”, is the convenient one to express
\rho_{LS_{1}S_{2}}
. The latter, also known as “helicity basis”, is very useful for measurements, because the orbital angular momentum component in the direction of motion vanishes, which greatly simplifies the description. For example, there are 18 non-zero decay amplitudes in the canonical basis, while in the helicity basis the number is reduced to only three quantities
a_{\lambda_{1}\lambda_{2}}
, with
(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2})=(1,1)
,
(-1,-1)
or
(0,0)
. These amplitudes in general depend on the off-shell boson mass
m_{V^{*}}
.

In the helicity basis the four-dimensional angular distribution is
[
425
,
426
]

\frac{1}{\sigma}\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega_{1}d\Omega_{2}}=\frac{1}{(4\pi)^{2}}\left[1+a_{lm}^{1}Y_{l}^{m}(\theta_{1},\phi_{1})+a_{lm}^{2}Y_{l}^{m}(\theta_{2},\phi_{2})+c_{l_{1}m_{1}l_{2}m_{2}}Y_{l_{1}}^{m_{1}}(\theta_{1},\phi_{1})Y_{l_{2}}^{m_{2}}(\theta_{2},\phi_{2})\right]\,,

(18)

where
\Omega_{1}=(\theta_{1},\phi_{1})
,
\Omega_{2}=(\theta_{2},\phi_{2})
are the angles that determine the orientation of the spin analysers
\mathup{{{f}}}_{1}
,
\mathup{{{f}}}_{2}
for the two bosons
\mathup{{{V}}}_{1}
,
\mathup{{{V}}}_{2}
in their respective rest frame, and
Y_{l}^{m}
are the usual spherical harmonics.
This angular distribution can be considered either differentially as a function of
m_{V^{*}}
, or integrated over this variable. In either case, its determination requires a full reconstruction of the final state, because the momenta of
\mathup{{{f}}}_{1,2}
have to be boosted to the rest frame of the decaying bosons.

At the tree level, the coefficients
a_{lm}^{1,2}
and
c_{l_{1}m_{1}l_{2}m_{2}}
are related to the elements of the spin-density operator
\rho_{S_{1}S_{2}}
in the helicity basis, which can be expanded in a basis of irreducible tensor operators
T^{l}_{m}
as

\displaystyle\rho_{S_{1}S_{2}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{9}\left[\mathbf{1}_{3}\otimes\mathbf{1}_{3}+A^{1}_{lm}\,T^{l}_{m}\otimes\mathbf{1}_{3}+A^{2}_{lm}\,\mathbf{1}_{3}\otimes T^{l}_{m}+C_{l_{1}m_{1}l_{2}m_{2}}\,T^{l_{1}}_{m_{1}}\otimes T^{l_{2}}_{m_{2}}\right]\,.

(19)

The relation is
a_{lm}^{1}=A_{lm}^{1}B_{l}^{1}
,
a_{lm}^{2}=A_{lm}^{2}B_{l}^{2}
,
c_{l_{1}m_{1}l_{2}m_{2}}=B_{l_{1}}^{1}B_{l_{2}}^{2}C_{l_{1}m_{1}l_{2}m_{2}}
, with constants
B_{l}^{i}
that represent the spin analysing power of the fermions
\mathup{{{f}}}_{i}
,
i=1,2
. For decay into charged leptons one has
B_{1}=-\sqrt{2\pi}\eta_{\ell}
,
B_{2}=\sqrt{2\pi/5}
, with
\eta_{\ell}=\pm 1
for
\mathup{{{W}}}^{\mp}
(taking as spin analyser the charged lepton) and
\eta_{\ell}\simeq 0.13
for
\mathup{{{Z}}}
(taking as spin analyser the negative lepton). Next-to-leading order (NLO) effects have been studied for
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{Z}}}\mathup{{{Z}}}

[
427
]
. For terms with
l=2
the corrections with respect to the leading order are quite small, whereas for spin correlation terms
c_{1m_{1}1m_{2}}
, which are suppressed by a small
\eta_{\ell}^{2}\simeq 0.01
factor, NLO corrections are larger.

The statistics of Higgs bosons expected at a future
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
collider is one order of magnitude smaller than at LHC Run 3, and two orders of magnitude smaller than at the HL-LHC. Still, lepton colliders can explore decay modes that have large backgrounds in hadron collisions. Among them, the semileptonic decay modes

•

\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{W}}}\mathup{{{W}}}\to\mathup{{{l}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}

•

\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{Z}}}\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}

are especially promising. The discrimination between quarks and anti-quarks, necessary for the direct measurement of the parameters of the distribution (
18
), may be circumvented by assuming
C\!P
conservation in the decay. In such a scenario, the three helicity amplitudes for
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{V}}}_{1}\mathup{{{V}}}_{2}
(which depend on
m_{V^{*}}
) can be determined from a binned measurement of the parameters
a_{20}^{1,2}
in Eq. (
18
), namely

a_{11}=a_{-1-1}=\left[\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\frac{a_{20}^{i}}{B_{2}^{i}}\right]^{1/2}\qquad a_{00}=-\left[\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\frac{a_{20}^{i}}{B_{2}^{i}}\right]^{1/2}\,.

(20)

The parameters
a_{20}^{i}
multiply spherical harmonics
Y_{2}^{0}(\theta,\phi)
that are even in
\cos\theta
, therefore their experimental determination does not rely on the identification of quarks versus anti-quarks. Once the helicity amplitudes are measured, the density operator
\rho_{LS_{1}S_{2}}
can be determined in a model-independent fashion. A study for the
\mathup{{{Z}}}\mathup{{{Z}}}\to 4\mathup{{{l}}}
channel has shown that even despite the need of a (coarse) binning on
m_{V^{*}}
, there is a great statistical gain when determining the parameters of the density operators by using this method
[
424
]
.

Concerning the rest of decay modes, the fully-hadronic ones seem difficult due to the combinatorics required to properly identify the quarks resulting from each boson decay. The fully-leptonic final state
\mathup{{{W}}}^{+}\mathup{{{W}}}^{-}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\,\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}
is more favourable than in hadron collisions
[
428
]
but still the number of kinematical constraints (five, for the missing energy and on-shell conditions for
\mathup{{{H}}}
and one
\mathup{{{W}}}
boson) is smaller then the number of unknowns (six, for the two neutrino momenta) and the final state cannot be uniquely reconstructed. The possibility of a kinematical reconstruction via a likelihood fit or a multivariate method remains to be explored.

In conclusion,
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
colliders will provide a unique opportunity to study quantum correlations in H to vector bosons decays.

4.1.4
\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
coupling

In this section we focus on the extraction of the properties, in particular strength and CP-parity, of the
\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
coupling from studying rates and distributions in the
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
decay. We consider first a study performed in the context of the FCC-ee on the strength of the coupling and then on the CP properties. Then we report a phenomenological study on the CP properties and finally an exploration of the quantum properties of the spins of the
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
leptons.

In general, in an effective field theory at dimension 6 one can consider the modifications induced in the
\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
coupling, by operators of the form
\frac{c_{\tau\Phi}(\Phi^{\dagger}\Phi)}{\Lambda^{2}}\bar{L}\Phi\tau_{R}+h.c.
. This type of operator gives rise to possibly (P-violating/C-violating) CP-violating (yet flavour-diagonal) interactions of the Higgs boson with fermions that in the EW broken phase can be parametrised as

{\cal L}^{h\tau\tau}_{\text{CPV}}=-\bar{\kappa}_{\tau}m_{\tau}\frac{h}{v}\bar{\psi}_{\tau}(\cos\delta+i\gamma_{5}\sin\delta)\psi_{\tau}\,,

(21)

where the angle
\delta
parametrises the departure from the CP-even case. Another, equivalent parametrisation employs
\kappa_{\tau}=\bar{\kappa}_{\tau}\cos\delta
and
\tilde{\kappa}_{\tau}=\bar{\kappa}_{\tau}\sin\delta
, where
\kappa_{\tau}=1+\delta y_{\tau}
in the notation used for the CP conserving cases in the
\kappa
-framework (with
\kappa>0
). The pure scalar coupling corresponds to
\delta=0
(
\tilde{\kappa}_{\tau}=0
), a pure pseudoscalar coupling to
\delta=90^{\circ}
(
\kappa_{\tau}=0
), while CP violation occurs in all other intermediate cases.

In the literature, the
\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}

C\!P
phase measurement at ILC using different tau decay modes
have also been explored
[
429
,
430
]
.
The studies in Refs.
[
431
,
432
]

exploit the
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}^{\pm}\to\rho^{\pm}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}
channel
and suggest that the sensitivity can reach
\sim 4^{\circ}
,
5
5

5

Note, however, that these analyses do not include the effect of energy mismeasurement.

which is in line with the expectations of first theoretical studies, i.e.,
2.8^{\circ}

[
433
]
, including also other decay modes, e.g.
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}^{\pm}\to a^{\pm}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}
and
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}^{\pm}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{\pm}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}}
.
A recent study
[
434
]
using a likelihood analysis based on the Matrix-Element
claims that the
C\!P
-phase can be measured in the accuracy of
2.9^{\circ}
at the ILC.

At HL-LHC, the resolution of the
\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}

C\!P
-phase measurement is expected to reach

\sim 11^{\circ}
using the tau decay modes

\mathup{{{\uptau}}}^{\pm}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uppi}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{\pm}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}

[
435
]

and
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}^{\pm}\to\rho^{\pm}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}

[
431
]
.
Combining comprehensive decay modes with the Matrix-Element likelihood method, the resolution may reach

5.2^{\circ}

[

]
.
On the other hand, however, Ref.
[
437
]

claims that the detector effect severely impacts on
the performance of
C\!P
measurements at HL-LHC
and the
C\!P
phase hypothesis
\delta=0
can be distinguished from
\delta=90^{\circ}
only at 95 % CL with
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}^{\pm}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uppi}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{\pm}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}
channel.

\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
coupling sensitivity

The large Higgs boson statistics together with the clean environment at an
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
collider can bring spectacular gains in our knowledge of the
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
interaction.
In this study we explore the prospective sensitivity of the
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{Z}}}
,
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
cross section measurement at FCC-ee.

Both signal and background processes have been simulated in the Monte Carlo event generator
Whizard
v3.0.3
[
42
,
43
]
including a parametrisation of initial state radiation. Subsequently,
Pythia6

[
46
]
was used to handle showering and hadronisation as well as tau decays.
Delphes
v3.5.1pre05
[
404
]
simulated the response of IDEA detector
[
438
]
.
We tested two jet algorithms: the
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
inclusive generalized
k_{\text{T}}
algorithm with the jet-radius parameter equal to
R=0.5
and a cut on the merging scale of
p_{\mathrm{T},j}>
2\text{\,}\mathrm{GeV}
, and the
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
exclusive Durham algorithm with
n_{\textrm{jets}}
equal to the expected number of jets.

To reconstruct hadronic tau decays, we have compared two methods based on the initial reconstruction of jets in the events. In the explicit reconstruction method, the four-vector of the taus, the charge and mass, are based on the jet constituents spatially close to the leading charged pion for jets not containing leptons. Reconstructed taus need to have a mass smaller than
3\text{\,}\mathrm{GeV}
. The number of charged pions and photons in the candidates is then used to infer the decay mode. The second method is based on applying a ParticleNet tagger, trained on di-jet Higgs events for FCC-ee
[
384
]
, where the taus are defined by a tau score above 0.5, while quark jets are defined as jets that did not meet this criterion. Leptonic taus decays are identified by looking directly at the isolated leptons in the event. The visible part of the four-momentum of the Higgs boson can then be reconstructed from the taus’ four-momenta.

We organise our analysis based on the decays of the
\mathup{{{Z}}}
(
\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{l}}}\mathup{{{l}}}
with
\mathup{{{l}}}=\mathup{{{e}}},\mathup{{{\upmu}}}
,
\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{{q}}}
with
\mathup{{{q}}}=\mathup{{{u}}},\mathup{{{d}}},\mathup{{{s}}},\mathup{{{c}}},\mathup{{{b}}}
, and
\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}
) and Higgs boson (
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{\uptau}}}_{\mathup{{{l}}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}_{\mathup{{{l}}}}
,
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{\uptau}}}_{\mathup{{{l}}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}_{h}
, and
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{\uptau}}}_{h}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}_{h}
where
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}_{\mathup{{{l}}}}
and
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}_{h}
denote leptonic and hadronic tau decays). After the basic event selection to define the categories, we have optimised cuts on the reconstructed objects and event observables in each category to enhance the signal-to-background ratio, separately for each category of
\mathup{{{Z}}}
decay mode (leptonic, hadronic, neutrino). These include requirements on the reconstructed
\mathup{{{Z}}}
mass, collinear mass, and recoil mass (for leptonic and hadronic
\mathup{{{Z}}}
decays) and on the missing energy (for
\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}
). In all cases the
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
candidates are required to be separated via
\Delta R_{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}>2,\cos\theta_{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}<0
(where
\theta_{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}
is the angle between the two
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
momenta), and
|\cos{\theta^{\text{miss}}}|<0.98
.

Parallel to the cut-based event selection, we have also trained a boosted decision tree (BDT) classifier in each of the categories except for the leptonic
\mathup{{{Z}}}
decays.

(a)

\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{l}}}\mathup{{{l}}}
,
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{\uptau}}}_{\mathup{{{l}}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}_{\mathup{{{l}}}}
.

(b)

\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{l}}}\mathup{{{l}}}
,
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{\uptau}}}_{\mathup{{{l}}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}_{h}
.

(c)

\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{{q}}}
,
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{\uptau}}}_{h}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}_{h}
.

:

:

\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{{q}}}

\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{\uptau}}}_{h}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}_{h}
. Both plots correspond to ParticleNet tau reconstruction with exclusive jet clustering.

The cross section measurement has been extracted with the CMS Combine tool
[
439
]
using binned maximum-likelihood fits.
With the cut-based analysis, the recoil mass distribution for the
\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{l}}}\mathup{{{l}}}
and
\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{{q}}}
categories are used in the fit, while for the
\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}
category the visible mass was fitted.
In categories where the BDT training is available, an alternative fit is also performed directly on the BDT outputs instead of the mass variables.
Combining all categories of
\mathup{{{Z}}}
and Higgs decays with the cut-based strategy, the relative uncertainty on
\sigma_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{Z}}}}\times\mathcal{B}
(
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
) is found to be 0.95% by using the ParticleNet tau reconstruction on inclusively clustered jets. This result is further improved with the BDT selection, where the best performance is found by applying the ParticleNet tau reconstruction on exclusively clustered jets, with the combined relative uncertainty of the cross-section measurement equal to 0.74%.

In conclusion, the relative uncertainty expected at FCC-ee for
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
in
\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{Z}}}
events,
\sqrt{s}=

240\text{\,}\mathrm{GeV}
with
\mathcal{L}_{int}=

10.8\text{\,}{\mathrm{ab}}^{-1}
, is 0.74%.

Quantum entanglement in
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}

The prospects of quantum information measurement with
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}
at future lepton colliders have been studied in Refs.
[
440
,
441
,
442
]
.
Quantum measurements can detect classes of spin correlations that cannot be realised in classical theories.
These include quantum entanglement and Bell non-locality.
When two particles are entangled, the property of one particle cannot be described independently of the other particle within quantum mechanics.
On the other hand, if a particle pair is in a Bell non-local state, there exists a set of measurements about these particles whose data cannot be described by Local Real Hidden Variable (LRHV) theories.
This class of theories demands that any physical property of a local object, say a particle, is fully described without referring to the information about space-like separated regions (locality) and predetermined prior to the act of measurement (reality).
Generally, the measurement outcomes of such theories can be described by a set of unknown (hidden) variables,
\lambda
, with the occurrence
P(\lambda)
.
Let us suppose a pair of particles,
A
and
B
, have interacted locally in the past and then separated far apart.
Alice measures the spin
a
-component of particle
A
, and Bob measures the spin
b
-component of particle
B
.
Their outcomes are denoted by
x
for Alice and
y
for Bob with
x,y\in\{+1,-1\}
.
In LRHV theories, the probability distribution of the event can be written as

P(x,y|a,b)=\int d\lambda P(\lambda)P_{A}(x|a,\lambda)P_{B}(y|b,\lambda)\,.

(22)

On the right-hand side, the probability distributions of Alice (
P_{A}(a|x,\lambda)
) and Bob (
P_{B}(b|y,\lambda)
) are factorised.
Equation (
22
) is often considered to be the defining equation of LRHV theories.

As we will see below, quantum measurements can also detect a type of spin correlation that cannot be attained within quantum theories.
If the observation of such a correlation is confirmed, quantum mechanics is falsified.
Since quantum mechanics may be modified at a short distance scale (for example, to be reconciled with gravity), a high-energy test of quantum mechanics is a valuable experimental programme.

In this section, we briefly describe the analysis and results presented in Ref.
[
440
]
.

The spin state of the two tau leptons produced from the Higgs decay,
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}
, is given by the maximally entangled 2-qubit
[
440
,
443
]

|\Psi_{H\to\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}(\delta)\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(|+,-\rangle+e^{i2\delta}|-,+\rangle\right)\,,

(23)

where
\delta
is the
C\!P
-phase in the
\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
interaction.
The spin correlation matrix is then given by

C_{ij}\equiv\langle\hat{s}^{-}_{i}\hat{s}^{+}_{j}\rangle,\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ C=\begin{pmatrix}\cos 2\delta&\sin 2\delta&0\\
-\sin 2\delta&\cos 2\delta&0\\
0&0&-1\\
\end{pmatrix}\,.

(24)

In this expression,
\hat{s}^{\mp}_{i}
is the
i
-th component of the
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}^{\mp}
spin.
The
i=1,2,3
component corresponds to the
directions of the normalised vectors (
\mathbf{r}
,
\mathbf{n}
,
\mathbf{k}
) in the helicity basis.

Using the definitions in Eq. (
23
) and
in Eq. (
24
), the
concurrence

[
444
,
445
]
, a measure of entanglement, is given by

{\cal C}[\rho]=\text{max}\left[0,\,\frac{D_{+}+C_{kk}-1}{2},\,\frac{D_{-}-C_{kk}-1}{2}\right]\,,

(25)

with
D_{\pm}\equiv\sqrt{(C_{rn}\pm C_{nr})^{2}+(C_{rr}\mp C_{nn})^{2}}
.
The concurrence is a non-negative function of the spin density operator,
\rho
, and vanishes for all separable (nonentangled) states.

{\cal C}[\rho]
takes the maximum value 1 for maximally entangled states.
In fact, for the spin state of the tau pair in
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}
, we have
{\cal C}[\rho]=1
.

Another metric connected to entanglement (but not equivalent in case of mixed states) is related to the so-called CHSH inequality
[
446
]
, one of the Bell inequalities.
This is a statement about the combination of spin correlations defined by

\langle R_{\text{CHSH}}\rangle=\frac{1}{2}\langle\big[\hat{s}^{A}_{a}(\hat{s}^{B}_{b}+\hat{s}^{B}_{b^{\prime}})+\hat{s}^{A}_{a^{\prime}}(\hat{s}^{B}_{b}-\hat{s}^{B}_{b^{\prime}})\big]\rangle\,,

(26)

where
\hat{s}^{I}_{i}
(
I=A,B
,
i=a,b
) is the spin
i
-component of particle
I
.
Alice, the observer of particle
A
, has two possible spin measurement axes,
a
and
a^{\prime}
, while Bob, the observer of particle
B
, has measurement axes
b
and
b^{\prime}
.
The spins are normalised (rescaled) so that the outcomes of Alice and Bob are either
+1
or
-1
.
In LRHV theories, the spin components of
A
and
B
are predetermined prior to the act of measurement.
In that case, one of
(\hat{s}^{B}_{b}+\hat{s}^{B}_{b^{\prime}})
and
(\hat{s}^{B}_{b}-\hat{s}^{B}_{b^{\prime}})
must vanish and the other takes value two.
Therefore,
\langle\rvert R_{\mathrm{C}HSH}\lvert\rangle
cannot exceed 1 in LRHV theories.
In quantum mechanics, on the other hand, we can write
R^{2}_{\mathrm{C}HSH}=1-\frac{1}{4}[\hat{s}^{A}_{a},\hat{s}^{A}_{a^{\prime}}][\hat{s}^{B}_{b},\hat{s}^{B}_{b^{\prime}}]
.
Since the commutator
[\hat{s}^{A}_{a},\hat{s}^{A}_{a^{\prime}}]
cannot have eigenvalues larger than 2 (c.f.
[\sigma_{i},\sigma_{j}]=2\epsilon_{ij}\sigma_{k}
), quantum mechanics cannot give
\langle\rvert R_{\mathrm{C}HSH}\lvert\rangle
larger than
\sqrt{2}
:

R_{\text{CHSH}}\leq\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}1&(\mathrm{HLV}\text{\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{Clauser:1969ny}{}{}]}})\\
\sqrt{2}&(\mathrm{QM}\text{\penalty\ \cite[cite]{[\@@bibref{}{Tsirelson}{}{}]}})\end{array}\right.

(27)

for all sets of measurement axes
a,a^{\prime},b
and
b^{\prime}
.
Observation of
R_{\text{CHSH}}>1
(
\sqrt{2}
) would, therefore, falsify Hidden Local Variable theories (Quantum Mechanical theories).
The tau pair from
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}
saturates the quantum bound:
R_{\text{CHSH}}^{\text{max}}=\sqrt{2}
, where the maximum is taken over all sets of measurement axes.

Suppose that in the rest frame of the
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
the tau spin is polarised into
\mathbf{s}
direction (
|\mathbf{s}|=1
).
The
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
decays into a decay mode,
f
, producing a detectable particle
d
.
The conditional probability that the particle
d
takes the direction
\mathbf{u}
(
|\mathbf{u}|=1
) when the
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
spin is polarised in
\mathbf{s}
direction is given by
[
448
]

P(\mathbf{u}|\mathbf{s})\,=\,1+\alpha_{f,d}\,\mathbf{s}\cdot\mathbf{u}\,,

(28)

with the normalisation
\int\frac{d\Omega}{4\pi}P(\mathbf{u}|\mathbf{s})=1
,
where
\alpha_{f,d}\in[-1,1]
is called the spin analysing power.
For the CP counterpart,
(f,d)\xleftrightarrow{\text{CP}}(\bar{f},\bar{d})
,
\alpha_{\bar{f},\bar{d}}=-\alpha_{f,d}
.

We denote the
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}
polarisation by
\mathbf{\bar{s}}
(
|\mathbf{\bar{s}}|=1
).
The direction of its decay product,
d^{\prime}
, measured at the rest frame of the
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}
, is represented by a unit vector
\mathbf{\bar{u}}
.
We want to relate the spin correlation
\langle\rvert\mathbf{s}\otimes\mathbf{\bar{s}}\lvert\rangle

with the angular correlation
\langle\rvert\mathbf{u}\otimes\mathbf{\bar{u}}\lvert\rangle
since the latter is measurable.
Using the probability distribution (
28
), one can derive
[
440
]

C_{ab}\,=\,\langle\rvert s_{a}\bar{s}_{b}\lvert\rangle\,=\,\frac{9}{\alpha_{f,d}\alpha_{f^{\prime},d^{\prime}}}\langle\rvert u_{a}\bar{u}_{b}\lvert\rangle\,,

(29)

where
u_{a}\equiv\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{a}
,
\bar{s}_{b}\equiv\mathbf{\bar{s}}\cdot\mathbf{b}
, etc. are the components with respect to arbitrary unit vectors
\mathbf{a}
and
\mathbf{b}
.
Using this relation, one can compute both the concurrence
{\cal C}[\rho]
(Eq. (
25
)) and the CHSH variable
R_{\text{CHSH}}
(Eq. (
26
)) from the angular correlation observables
\langle\rvert u_{a}\bar{u}_{b}\lvert\rangle
. In
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}
, the set of four measurement axes (
\mathbf{a}_{*}
,
\mathbf{a^{\prime}}_{*}
,
\mathbf{b}_{*}
,
\mathbf{b^{\prime}}_{*}
) that maximises
R_{\text{CHSH}}
can be easily obtained
[
440
]
.
We study the quantum information measurement in
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}
at future lepton colliders, assuming two collider settings, ILC and FCC-ee, listed in Table
16
in
Section

4.1
.
In the analysis we focus on the
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{\pm}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uppi}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{\pm}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}
channel, where the spin analysing power is maximum,
\alpha_{f,d}=1
for
f=\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uppi}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}
and
d=\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uppi}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
.
At lepton colliders, the Higgs is produced via the associated production
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to\mathup{{{Z}}}\mathup{{{H}}}
.
From the total initial momentum,
P_{\text{in}}^{\mu}=(\sqrt{s},0,0,0)
and the reconstructed
\mathup{{{Z}}}
momentum,
p_{\mathup{{{Z}}}}^{\mu}
,
the Higgs momentum four-vector,
p_{\mathup{{{H}}}}^{\mu}
, can be obtained as
p_{\mathup{{{H}}}}^{\mu}=P_{\text{in}}^{\mu}-p_{\mathup{{{Z}}}}^{\mu}
.
The distribution of the recoil mass,
m_{\text{recoil}}=\sqrt{(P_{\text{in}}-p_{\mathup{{{Z}}}})^{2}}
,
therefore sharply peaks at the Higgs mass in the signal.
By selecting events that fall within a narrow window,
|m_{\text{recoil}}-m_{\mathup{{{H}}}}|<5
GeV, one can achieve background/signal
\sim 0.05
with a signal efficiency of
93\%
and
96\%
for the ILC and FCC-ee, respectively.

We generate signal and background events with
MadGraph5_aMC@NLO

[
38
]
at leading order in the Standard Model, i.e.
(\kappa,\delta)=(1,0)
and we employ the
TauDecay
package for
\tau
decays
[
449
]
.

On the right-hand-side of Eq. (
29
),
the direction
u_{a}
(
\bar{u}_{b}
) is measured in the rest frame of the respective mother tau lepton
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
(
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}
).
This means that in order to measure the spin correlation, it is crucial to reconstruct the
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
and
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}
rest frames accurately.
This requires the precise reconstruction of two neutrino momenta.
For six unknown neutrino momentum components, there are two mass-shell constraints:
m_{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}^{2}=(p_{\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upnu}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{\!\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}}}+p_{\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uppi}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}})^{2}
and
m_{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}^{2}=(p_{\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{\upnu}}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{\!\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}}}+p_{\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uppi}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}})^{2}
,
and four conditions from the energy-momentum conservation:

(P_{\text{in}}-p_{\mathup{{{Z}}}})^{\mu}=(p_{\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upnu}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{\!\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}}}+p_{\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uppi}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}}+p_{\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{\upnu}}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{\!\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}}}+p_{\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uppi}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}})^{\mu}
.
By solving those six constraints for the six unknowns, an event can be fully reconstructed up to twofold solutions:
i_{s}=1,2
.
The best solution can be selected by constructing and minimising the log-likelihood function incorporating the impact parameter information of the charged pion tracks from the tau decays.
The exact method has been developed in Ref.
[
440
]
by adopting the formalism outlined in Refs.
[
450
,
451
,
452
]
.

To take into account the energy mismeasurement,
we smear the energies of all visible particles in the final state as

E^{\text{true}}\,\to\,E^{\text{obs}}=(1+\sigma_{E}\cdot\omega)\cdot E^{\text{true}}

with the energy resolution
\sigma_{E}=0.03

[
9
,
65
]

for both ILC and FCC-ee,
where
\omega
is a random number drawn from the normal distribution.

The biggest experimental challenge in the
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}
channel is that
{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}
s are heavily boosted because
m_{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}\ll m_{\mathup{{{H}}}}
.
This means that going back to the rest frame of
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
and
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}
, one has to apply large boosts.
Small reconstruction errors in the lab frame are amplified by the large boosts in the tau rest frame, which often spoil the measurement.
In fact, it has been demonstrated that entanglement and CHSH violation cannot be observed in the simple kinematical method described above
[
440
]
.

To overcome this problem and refine the accuracy of the reconstruction, we include the impact parameter information.
Since tau leptons are marginally long-lived,
c\tau=87.11

\mu
m
[
453
]
, and highly boosted, one can observe a mismatch between the interaction point and the origin of the
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uppi}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{\pm}}}
in
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{\pm}}}\to\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uppi}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{\pm}}}
.
The impact parameter
\vec{b}_{\pm}
is the minimal displacement of the extrapolated
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uppi}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{\pm}}}
trajectory from the interaction point.
The magnitude of the impact parameter
|\vec{b}_{\pm}|
follows an exponentially falling distribution with the mean
|\vec{b}_{\pm}|\sim$100\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$
for
E_{\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{\pm}}}}\sim m_{\mathup{{{H}}}}/2
,
which is significantly larger than the experimental resolutions
[
65
]
.
In our numerical simulation,
we take constant values

\sigma_{b_{T}}=$2\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$
(transverse)
and
\sigma_{b_{z}}=$5\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$
(longitudinal)
for the impact parameter resolutions,
although the actual resolutions are
functions of the track momentum and
the polar angle
\theta^{*}
from the beam direction.
The above modeling with the constant parameters gives a reasonable approximation for
the track momentum
\sim 100
GeV
and
\theta^{*}\gtrsim 20^{\circ}

as can be seen in Figure II-3.10 in Ref.
[
65
]
.

If all quantities are accurately measured, the impact parameter,
{\vec{b}_{\pm}}
, from the
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{\pm}}}\to\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uppi}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{\pm}}}
decay,
is related to the directions of
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}
and
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uppi}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}

and their angle
\Theta_{\pm}

[
435
]
.
We use this information to curb the effects of energy mismeasurement. The details of this procedure are reported in Ref.
[
440
]
.

,

In Table

we show the result of our quantum information measurements.
We see that for both ILC and FCC-ee the components of the
C
-matrix are correctly measured.
The concurrence
{\cal C}[\rho]

is also measured with good accuracy.
and the formation of entanglement is observed at
more than 5
\sigma
.
Observation of CSHS violation is the most challenging one since it is the strongest quantum correlation.
As can be seen in the last line in Table
15
,
the violation of the CHSH inequality is confirmed at the FCC-ee at
\sim 3\,\sigma
level,
while
R^{*}_{\text{CHSH}}>1
is not observed at the ILC beyond the statistical uncertainty.
The superior performance of FCC-ee is attributed to the fact that the beam energy resolution of FCC-ee is much better than ILC.
The precise knowledge of the initial state momentum is crucial to reconstruct the rest frame of
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{\pm}}}
accurately.

C\!P
studies in
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}

If the
C
-matrix is measured with good accuracy, one can use it to constrain the
C\!P
-phase
\delta
.
From Eq. (
24
) we see that
only the
rn
part (i.e. the upper-left
2\times 2
part) of the
C
-matrix is sensitive to
\delta
. By comparing the measured
C
-matrix entries in the
rn
part and the prediction in Eq. (
24
), we construct the
\chi^{2}
function as
[
440
]

\chi^{2}(\delta)=\frac{\left(C_{rr}-\cos 2\delta\right)^{2}}{\sigma^{2}_{rr}}+\frac{\left(C_{rn}-\sin 2\delta\right)^{2}}{\sigma^{2}_{rn}}\,+\,\frac{\left(C_{nn}-\cos 2\delta\right)^{2}}{\sigma^{2}_{nn}}+\frac{\left(C_{nr}+\sin 2\delta\right)^{2}}{\sigma^{2}_{nr}}\,,

(30)

where
C_{ij}
and
\sigma_{ij}
are the central value and the standard deviation, respectively, obtained from the result of the quantum information measurement with the
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}^{\pm}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uppi}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{\pm}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}
channel summarised in
Table

15
in the previous section.
The goodness of fits is
\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{min}}(\mathrm{ILC})/\mathrm{d.o.f.}=0.93/3

and

\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{min}}
(FCC-ee)/d.o.f. = 0.86/3,
where we used the benchmark collider parameters listed in
Table
16
.

, is considered, where
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
are produced from off-shell
\mathup{{{Z}}}/\gamma
. The numbers of signal and background reported here include the decay branching ratios and the efficiency of the event selection,
|m_{\mathrm{recoil}}-m_{\mathup{{{H}}}}|<5
GeV.

The analysis is based on
\Delta\chi^{2}(\delta)\equiv\chi^{2}(\delta)-\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{min}}
, whose values around
\delta=0
are plotted in Fig.

.
We note that the allowed windows are asymmetric. This is due to the statistical uncertainty of the 100 pseudo-experiments.

We see that the resolution of
\delta
obtained from this analysis is roughly
\sim 7.5^{\circ}
(ILC) and
\sim 5^{\circ}
(FCC-ee) at 1

These results should be compared with the resolutions
obtained in the standard approach for the
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}},\mathup{{{\uptau}}}^{\pm}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uppi}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{\pm}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}
channel,
which exploits the angle
\varphi^{\star}

[
455
,

]

defined between the two planes, each spanned by the pair of momentum 3-vectors
(\vec{p}_{\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uppi}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}},\vec{p}_{\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}})
and

(\vec{p}_{\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uppi}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}},\vec{p}_{\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}})
in the Higgs rest frame.
Using the same analysis described in the previous section
and the statistical method based on 100 pseudo-experiments,
we find the resolution of the
C\!P
-phase
with the
\varphi^{\star}
method
is
6.4^{\circ}
for FCC-ee.
This shows that the proposed method based on Eq. (
30
) is at least as good as the standard method with
\varphi^{\star}
.

Under the
C\!P
conjugation, the
C
-matrix transforms as

C\xrightarrow{C\!P}C^{T}
.
This fact can be used for a model-independent test for
C\!P
violation.
To measure the asymmetry in the
C
-matrix,
we define
[
440
]

A=(C_{rn}-C_{nr})^{2}+(C_{nk}-C_{kn})^{2}+(C_{kr}-C_{rk})^{2}\geq 0\,.

(31)

An experimental verification of
A\neq 0
immediately confirms the violation of
C\!P
.

From the result summarised in
Table

15
,
A
is obtained as

A\,=\,\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}0.168\pm 0.131&\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \mathrm{(ILC)}\\
0.081\pm 0.060&\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ (\mathrm{FCC}\text{-}\mathrm{ee})\end{array}\right.

(32)

Here, the error corresponds to a 1
\sigma
statistical uncertainty obtained from 100 pseudo-experiments.
The result is consistent with
the Standard Model (i.e. absence of
C\!P
violation)
at
\sim 1\,\sigma
level.

In the explicit model leading to (
24
),
we obtain
A=4\sin^{2}(2\delta)
.
One can interpret the above model-independent result
within this model and derive bounds on
\delta
.
In the domain around
\delta=0
, the following limits are obtained at
1\,\sigma

[
440
]

|\delta|<\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}7.9^{\circ}\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \mathrm{(ILC)}\\
5.4^{\circ}\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ (\mathrm{FCC}\text{-}\mathrm{ee})\end{array}\right.\,,

(33)

consistent with the limits obtained in the
\chi^{2}
analysis (see Table
17
).

4.1.5
Higgs hadronic couplings

Fully hadronic final states are produced in the vast
majority of Higgs boson decays in the SM:
61% of Higgs boson decays produce quark-antiquark pairs,
8% yield gluon-gluon pairs, and about 14% lead to hadrons
via intermediate production of
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{W}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{W}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
,
\mathup{{{Z}}}\mathup{{{Z}}}
or
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
.
Reconstructing and precisely measuring the branching fraction for
these decays is crucial for measuring the Yukawa couplings
of the Higgs boson to quarks, the effective coupling to
gluons, and potentially can also provide additional constraints
on the couplings to gauge weak bosons and to the
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
lepton.

The sensitivity of the measurement of the signal strengths
of Higgs bosons decaying to hadronic final states
has previously been studied for ILC, CLIC, and CEPC
[
457
,
6
,
394
,
458
]
.
In this section, a recent study performed in the context of FCC-ee is reported.
A much deeper discussion of the strange-quark coupling is given in
Section

4.2
.

The event selection targets
\mathup{{{Z}}}\mathup{{{H}}}
events with
\mathup{{{Z}}}
bosons decaying either
to
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}},\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}},\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}}
, or
\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}
. The contribution from vector-boson fusion is small after the selection
and considered as part of the signal.

The
Whizard
generator
[
42
,
43
]
has been used to produce signal events, where a Higgs
boson is produced together with a
\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{e}}}
,
\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}}
,
\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}}
, or
\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}
pair.
The same generator has also been used to produce background samples such as

\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{e}}}

\to

\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{e}}}
, ee
\to

\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}}
, and ee
\to

\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upnu}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{\!\mathup{{{e}}}}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{\upnu}}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{\!\mathup{{{e}}}}}}

\mathup{{{Z}}}
.
The
Pythia8
generator
[
47
]
has been used for the production of the other background event samples (inclusive
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{W}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{W}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
,
\mathup{{{Z}}}\mathup{{{Z}}}
, ee
\to

\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}
production).
Samples are generated for centre-of-mass energies of 240 and 365
G
eV

, assuming
integrated luminosities of
10.8\text{\,}{\mathrm{ab}}^{-1}
and
3.0\text{\,}{\mathrm{ab}}^{-1}
, respectively.

The generated events are passed through a parametric simulation of the detector
response implemented in
Delphes

[
404
]
.
The reconstruction efficiencies and resolutions for various particle hypotheses
are those expected for the IDEA detector with a crystal electromagnetic
calorimeter upstream of a dual-readout fibre calorimeter.
Lepton misidentification is assumed to be negligible.
The kinematic properties of the jets are assumed to be determined from those
of the constituents via a particle-flow algorithm.
Jet flavour tagging is performed by a dedicated algorithm
[
384
]
based on a graph
neural network exploiting several low-level features of the input constituents.
The network provides seven output scores, corresponding to the probabilities
that a jet originates from the hadronisation of a b, c, s, u, d
quark or a gluon, or from the hadronic decay of a
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
lepton.

Three analyses are performed in parallel, targeting three different final states:
a
leptonic
analysis targeting
\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
(
\mathup{{{l}}}
=
\mathup{{{e}}}
,
\mathup{{{\upmu}}}
) decays;
a
invisible
analysis targeting
\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}}
decays; and
a
hadronic
analysis targeting
\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}
decays.
The leptonic analysis selects events with an opposite-sign, same-flavour lepton
pair with invariant mass close to that of the
\mathup{{{Z}}}
boson, vetoing events with additional
high-momentum leptons. The other two analyses apply a veto on the presence of
high-momentum leptons, yielding datasets orthogonal to the first one.
The invisible (hadronic) analysis requires (vetoes) events with a large “missing” mass,
calculated as the invariant mass of the system recoiling against all reconstructed
objects.

All the analyses cluster the reconstructed particles (excluding the
two
\mathup{{{Z}}}
boson decay products in the leptonic analysis) into jets.
The exclusive
k_{\text{T}}

Durham
algorithm
[
405
,
378
]
is used. The particles are
clustered into two (four) jets in the leptonic and invisible (hadronic) analyses.
In the leptonic and invisible analysis, the two jets are assumed to originate from
the decays of the Higgs boson; in the hadronic analysis, the pairing of the four
jets and the association to either a
\mathup{{{Z}}}
or Higgs boson decay is performed
based on the output scores of the jet flavour tagger for each jet and on the
invariant masses of the jet pairs.
A few additional requirements suppress the main backgrounds, while maintaining
a large efficiency for the signal.
Loose preselections are applied to the quantities that are used for
signal-vs-background discrimination in maximum-likelihood fits to the
selected candidates: the mass of the system recoiling against the
two leptons in the leptonic analysis; the missing mass and the invariant
mass of the dijet pair in the invisible analysis;
the invariant mass of the dijet pair from the Higgs boson decay and
the invariant mass of the system recoiling against it in the hadronic analysis.
The kinematic selection criteria are different at 240 and 365
G
eV

to take into
account the different Lorentz boost of the Higgs and
\mathup{{{Z}}}
bosons in the two
scenarios.

At
\sqrt{s}=240

G
eV

, the typical signal selection efficiencies of the
three analyses for events with Higgs bosons decaying to quarks
or gluon pairs are: 60% for the leptonic analysis, 80% for the
invisible analysis, and 85% for the hadronic analysis.
The expected signal yield for
\mathup{{{H}}}\rightarrow\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{b}}}}}}}
events is about 50k/230k/690k
for the leptonic/invisible/hadronic analyses;
for other decays it scales approximately with the ratios of branching
fractions. For
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{s}}}}}}}
, the expected yield is 23/100/300 for the three analyses.
At
\sqrt{s}=365

G
eV

, the efficiencies are around 45%/65%/70% for the
three channels, about 15–20% relatively smaller than at
\sqrt{s}=240

G
eV

;
combined with the 70% lower integrated luminosity and the 40% lower
\mathup{{{Z}}}\mathup{{{H}}}
production cross-section, they lead to expected signal yields which are almost
an order of magnitude smaller than at 240
G
eV

.

After the event selection, events are classified in orthogonal categories enriched
in dijet pairs of a given flavour or in events from a given Higgs boson decay.
The leptonic and invisible analyses use a multi-output neural network to classify events
in
\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{b}}}}}}}
,
\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{c}}}}}}}
, gg,
\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{s}}}}}}}
,
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{W}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{W}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
,
\mathup{{{Z}}}\mathup{{{Z}}}
,
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
-enriched categories. The network uses as inputs the seven
output scores of the flavour tagger for each of the two jets
and the minimum distance between the particles that are
clustered together by the jet clustering algorithm in the
4\to 3
and
3\to 2

clustering steps (2, 3 and 4 indicate the number of jets and particle candidates
in the event at a given step).
An alternative version of the invisible analysis and the hadronic analysis uses the
highest sum of the output scores of the taggers for a given flavour hypothesis
for the jet candidates from the Higgs boson decay to classify the events in

\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{b}}}}}}}
,
\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{c}}}}}}}
, gg,
\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{s}}}}}}}
,
\mathup{{{u}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{u}}}}}}}
,
\mathup{{{d}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{d}}}}}}}
,
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
-like categories.
All the analyses further split the event classes into two or three subcategories with
different signal-to-background ratio to enhance the sensitivity of the measurement.

The results for each analysis are determined by a binned, maximum-likelihood fit to the
distribution of one or two quantities that discriminate between the signals and
the background. These are the recoil mass in the leptonic analysis, the visible
mass and the recoil mass in the invisible one, and the invariant mass of the dijet
candidate from the Higgs boson decay and the invariant mass of the system
recoiling against it in the hadronic analysis.
Templates for the various signal and background processes are determined
from the simulation. The normalisation of the signal processes is floating,
expressed as the product of a signal strength
\mu_{i}
(
i
=
\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{b}}}}}}}
,
\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{c}}}}}}}
, …)
times the SM expected yield for the corresponding Higgs boson decay in
the targeted
\mathup{{{Z}}}
boson decay channel. The background normalisations are
constrained to the expectations within a 5% uncertainty. Statistical
uncertainties in the templates from the limited amount of simulated events
are included.

The results for a given centre-of-mass energy are combined
by performing a simultaneous fit to the categories of the three different final states, correlating the signal
strengths and the normalisation parameters of the same background processes across the categories. For
the analysis of
\sqrt{s}=365

G
eV

simulations in the
\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{{H}}}
final state, different templates are used
for
\mathup{{{Z}}}\mathup{{{H}}}
,
\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}
, and for the W-boson fusion (WBF).
The systematic uncertainties on the background normalisations are constrained from the sidebands,
and as such scale with the integrated luminosity. The results of the analysis at
\sqrt{s}=240

G
eV

are given in
Table

18
, and
the preliminary results of the analysis at
\sqrt{s}=240

G
eV

are given in
Table

19
.
For the
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{W}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{W}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
fully hadronic final state we obtain with the 240
G
eV

dataset a precision on the signal strength of 1.1%
that requires to be combined at a later stage with dedicated analyses targeting the semi- and fully-leptonic final states.

In summary, with an integrated luminosity of 10.8
\text{ab}^{-1}
at
\sqrt{s}=240

G
eV

, the signal strength of Higgs bosons decaying to

\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{b}}}}}}}
, gg, and
\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{c}}}}}}}
could be measured with precisions close to 0.2%, 0.8%, and 1.6%, respectively, and
a precision close to 1% could also be obtained for the
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{W}}}\mathup{{{W}}}
fully-hadronic decay;
while data collected at
\sqrt{s}=365

G
eV

could provide measurements with uncertainties around 2–3 times larger.
A deeper discussion of the
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{s}}}}}}}
is given in the next section.

4.2
Focus Topic:

\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{s}}}}}}}

4.2.1
Introduction

One of the crucial aspects of the physics program at future Higgs factories is the precise measurement of the Higgs boson couplings to fermions. This has been studied thoroughly within the last European Strategy Update
[
406
,
459
,
460
]
and more recently in the context of the 2021 Snowmass community exercise
[
461
,
462
]
.
The study of the couplings of the Higgs boson to the light quarks (i.e., up, down, and strange quarks) was considered nearly impossible due to the small branching ratio when assuming SM couplings as well as the difficulty in identifying the flavour of quark-initiated jets (flavour tagging). Nevertheless, the exploration of the Higgs coupling to the strange quark
y_{s}
has emerged with increasing interest, given also its tight connections with detector technologies and layout optimisation. Enabling sensitivity to inclusive
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{s}}}}}}}
production would allow for a complete exploration of the second-generation Yukawa couplings, and go beyond the current LHC’s limited reach for
y_{s}
via
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\upvarphi\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}
decays
[
463
,
464
]
.

At the LHC, in addition to the small branching fraction, the rare
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{s}}}}}}}
decay mode is inaccessible with the current detector capabilities. In fact, one of the most powerful handles to identify a strange-quark-initiated jet (strange-tagging) is the possibility to distinguish between kaons and pions up to tens of GeV in momentum. This relies on dedicated detector subsystems which are not included in the LHC multi-purpose detectors, as will be detailed in
Section

4.2.6
. Furthermore, the overwhelming multi-jet production rate at the LHC inhibits the study of strange, up, and down quark couplings with inclusive
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}
decays, in addition to the dominant
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{b}}}}}}}
decay mode. Therefore, future Higgs factories present a unique opportunity to probe new physics frontiers with the strange quark, but this requires the design of detectors and algorithms that enable such studies. Along with the SM scenario, this signature provides the possibility of testing several BSM theories that allow for extended Higgs sectors, as discussed in
Section

4.2.2
.

In the past years, preliminary proof-of-concept investigations at future colliders have been performed. Some of them
[
384
]
focus primarily on strange-tagging algorithms and some others
[
465
,
466
]
include also their application to
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{s}}}}}}}
searches, interpretations in BSM frameworks, and potential detector designs. The assumptions and the detector concepts used in these studies differ, as summarised in
Section

4.2.5
. All the results show promising avenues and motivate more in-depth explorations and future harmonisation. However, modelling the fragmentation of strange quarks is a complex matter. While this was not specifically addressed in the above studies, a discussion is now presented in
Section

4.2.4
of this document, highlighting the synergies and complementarity between the Higgs and SM measurement programs at future Higgs factories.

Analyses developed since Snowmass 2021 are summarized in
Section

4.2.5
.
Target detector performance aspects relating to strangeness tagging, and current tagging performance are described in
Section

4.2.6
.
Algorithmic developments for strangeness-tagging specifically in the context of
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{s}}}}}}}
are reviewed in
Section

4.2.7
.
Finally,
Section

4.2.8
presents exciting opportunities for new studies to be carried out in the future.

4.2.2
Theoretical motivation and phenomenological landscape

The current measurements of the Higgs coupling to
\mathup{{{b}}}
and
\mathup{{{t}}}
quarks confirm the SM predictions of
y_{\mathup{{{b}}},\mathup{{{t}}}}\propto m_{\mathup{{{b}}},\mathup{{{t}}}}

[
467
,
468
,
469
,
470
,
471
,
472
,
473
]
.
Therefore, one can conclude that the mass of the heavy quarks is dominated by the SM Higgs mechanism and then constrain deviations from the SM prediction, for example, in the form of dimension-six operator
\bar{q}qHH^{\dagger}H
.
The
c
-quark Yukawa is probed via inclusive
[
474
,
475
,
476
,
477
,
471
]
and exclusive rates to Higgs and a vector meson
[
478
,
479
,
480
,
481
,
482
]
and kinematical effects
[
483
,
484
,
485
]
, where the tightest bound is
\sim 10
times its SM value
[
476
,
471
]
.
Moreover, the non-universality of the Higgs Yukawa couplings was established both in the lepton and quark sectors
[
475
]
.
However, the situation is different for light quarks,
\mathup{{{u}}}
,
\mathup{{{d}}}
, and
\mathup{{{s}}}
, which are very challenging to probe due to the tiny expected rates and the large QCD backgrounds.
Currently, these can be searched for via exclusive decays
[
463
,
486
,
487
,
488
]
, or indirectly via global fits
[
463
]
or kinematical effects
[
489
,
490
,
491
]
, resulting in rather weak bounds.
However, correlated observables in models can extend this reach further
[
492
]
.

Probing the Higgs-strange Yukawa coupling is motivated for a number of reasons.
First, it will shed light on how the strange quark receives its mass: is it from the SM Higgs, or from another mechanism related to the first two generations (see e.g. Refs.
[
493
,
494
]
)?
Second, it can be utilised to probe BSM models and in particular flavour models (see Ref.
[
495
]
and Refs.
[
459
,
460
]
and references within as well as more recent work in Refs.
[
496
,
492
,
497
,
498
,
499
]
).
Finally, there would be particularly strong motivation to probe the Higgs–strange coupling directly, if there were to be a sign of BSM physics in the Higgs couplings that could be attributed to the light quark Yukawa couplings or the gluon.

A summary of models that can modify the Higgs couplings to fermions including the
\mathup{{{s}}}
Yukawa can be found in Refs.
[
459
,
460
]
.
Assuming that the new physics is associated with a heavy scale,
\Lambda
, the modification for the Yukawa coupling can be captured by the following irrelevant operator

\displaystyle\frac{1}{\Lambda^{2}}\bar{s}_{L}s_{R}HH^{\dagger}H\,.

(34)

The resulting deviation from the SM can be written as

\displaystyle\kappa_{\mathup{{{s}}}}\equiv\frac{y_{\mathup{{{s}}}}}{y_{\mathup{{{s}}}}^{\mathrm{SM}}}=1+\frac{1}{y_{\mathup{{{s}}}}^{\mathrm{SM}}}\frac{v^{2}}{\Lambda^{2}}\,.

(35)

It is translated to the following scale

\displaystyle\Lambda\approx\frac{14\,{\mathrm{TeV}}}{\sqrt{|\kappa_{\mathup{{{s}}}}-1|}}\approx\frac{2\,\mathrm{TeV}}{\sqrt{\kappa_{\mathup{{{s}}}}/40}}\,.

(36)

where the last step is inspired by the bound on
\kappa_{\mathup{{{s}}}}<40
from the global fit of the Higgs data
[
463
,
475
]
.

Nevertheless, it is important to note that while an EFT description can be used to parametrise the effects at low energy, unless there is a power counting that explains why this is the leading effect while also suppressing flavour-changing neutral currents (FCNC), it is not particularly insightful.
In particular, to generate a large enough effect in Eq. (
34
) that it is relevant for measurements requires a large tree-level coupling between new physics states that couple to both the strange quark and the Higgs.
This can be accomplished in one of two ways: either through a new scalar two-Higgs-doublet model (2HDM) state or vector-like quarks (VLQ).
However, in either case that means there are also correlated observables that are not understood from the bottom up EFT perspective.
Recently there has been work that tries to analyse these cases for a 2HDM where a symmetry can be implemented to be consistent with flavour data
[
496
,
492
]
and for VLQ where FCNC suppression is put in by hand
[
499
]
.
As can be seen in Figure
25
, in the case of a 2HDM strange flavour tagging at a future Higgs factory as discussed here can extend beyond the LHC reach when comparing with correlated observables.

Figure 25
:
95% CL bounds on the CP-even Higgs-strange Yukawa coupling,
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{s}}}}}}}}
, as well as on
125\text{\,}\mathrm{G}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}
SM Higgs-strange Yukawa coupling,
\kappa_{\mathup{{{s}}}}\equiv\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{s}}}}}}}}/\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{s}}}}}}}}^{\textrm{SM}}
, for the 2HDM model described in Refs.
[
496
,
492
]
. See Ref.
[
466
]
for more information.

4.2.3
Interpretation as Higgs-strange Yukawa coupling

Since the Higgs couplings to the third generation fermions have been
measured at the 10 % level at the LHC
[
500
,
501
]
and will be pinned down to the per-cent or sub-per-cent level at future
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
colliders
[
462
]
, the
next step will be to obtain information about the Higgs couplings to the second generation.
A starting point is provided by the sensitivity to the muon and charm Yukawa couplings at the LHC, but more accurate measurements are expected at
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
colliders.
In this context a relevant question arising is related to the Yukawa coupling to strange quarks.
First studies for FCC-ee are quite promising.
However, the sophisticated treatment of signal and background processes is of high relevance.
This section contributes to the present state of the art on the theoretical side.

Figure 26
:
Typical diagrams contributing to (a)
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{s}}}}}}}

\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{s}}}}}}}\mathup{{{g}}}
and (c)
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{s}}}}}}}\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}
.

Higgs decays into strange quarks are induced by the strange Yukawa

[

]
), if the strange Yukawa coupling is

\overline{MS}

\overline{m}_{\mathup{{{s}}}}(M_{\mathup{{{H}}}})
at the scale of the Higgs mass
M_{\mathup{{{H}}}}
. The
inclusive strange Yukawa-induced branching ratio of
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{s}}}}}}}
amounts to
0.022\%
, thus being very small and below the per-mille level. This immediately poses the question of competing Higgs decays with strange quarks in the final state that are not induced by the strange Yukawa coupling. The leading processes of this kind are the loop-induced strong and weak Dalitz decays of the Higgs boson,
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{s}}}}}}}+\mathup{{{g}}}/\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}
, see

Figure

more than an order of magnitude larger than the strange-Yukawa-induced branching ratio of
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{s}}}}}}}
. However, in order to clear up the situation of the measurement of the strange-Yukawa coupling, the corresponding distributions need to be investigated in more detail, since appropriate cuts on the invariant mass of the
\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{s}}}}}}}
pair in the final state will affect the loop-induced and Yukawa-induced contributions in different ways.

\mathup{{{Z}}}
