]
.
Hence, future colliders
together with HL-LHC can observe
such a sizable deviation DEV(
\mathup{{{g}}}
) at high significance while they can not
observe such a moderate deviation DEV(
\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}
) significantly.

In summary, we have found that the deviations of these MSSM decay
widths from the SM values can be quite sizable in the MSSM with general
QFV, in strong contrast to the usual studies in the MSSM with MFV.
Here, we remark that SUSY QFV parameters (such as
T_{U23}
,
T_{U32}
)
can have an important impact on
not only
QFV observables
(such as
\text{B}(\mathup{{{\mathup{{{h}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{{s}}})
), but also quark flavour conserving (QFC)
observables (such as DEV(c) and DEV(b)).
Future lepton colliders such as ILC, CLIC, FCC-ee, CEPC and the muon collider
can observe such sizable deviations from the SM at high signal significance
even after the potential non-discovery of SUSY particles at the HL-LHC.
In case the deviation pattern shown here is really observed at the lepton
colliders, then it would strongly suggest the discovery of QFV SUSY (the
MSSM with general QFV).

Projected sensitivity

The SM predicts the branching ratio of
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{{s}}},\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{{d}}},\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{u}}}
to be strongly suppressed by the GIM mechanism, while the
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}},\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}},\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}}
processes are strictly forbidden. These decay channels are thus very sensitive to possible New Physics contributions. The effective FCNC couplings of quarks to the Higgs boson can be parametrised as

\mathcal{L}\supset\,y_{ij}(\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}_{i,L}\mathup{{{q}}}_{j,R})\mathup{{{H}}}+y_{ji}(\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}_{j,L}\mathup{{{q}}}_{i,R})\mathup{{{H}}}+\mathrm{h.c.}\,,

(44)

where
ij=\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{{s}}},\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{{d}}},\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{u}}}
, and similarly for leptons by replacing
\mathup{{{q}}}\to\mathup{{{l}}}
. This Lagrangian can be obtained as the low energy realization of various extensions of the SM, e.g., the addition of vector-like quarks
[
642
,
643
]
, or in the Two-Higgs-Doublet Model (2HDM)
[
644
,
645

.

At future lepton colliders, such as FCC-ee and CEPC, about
10^{6}

\mathup{{{H}}}
will be produced on-shell at the
\mathup{{{Z}}}\mathup{{{H}}}
threshold run,
\sqrt{s}=$240\text{\,}\mathrm{GeV}$
. Due to the smallness of the SM flavour changing branching ratios, reported below, for these relatively small statistics the expected sensitivity is well above the SM values, and we can only set upper bounds on the decay branching ratios.

Quarks:

Updated computations of
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{q}}}_{i}\mathup{{{q}}}_{j}
yield
[

,
647
,
588
]

{\cal B}(\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{{s}}})=\left(8.9\pm 1.5\right)\times 10^{-8}\,,\quad{\cal B}(\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{{d}}})=\left(3.8\pm 0.6\right)\times 10^{-9}\,,\quad{\cal B}(\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{u}}})=\left(2.7\pm 0.5\right)\times 10^{-20}\,,

(45)

where
{\cal B}(\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{q}}}_{i}\mathup{{{q}}}_{j})={\cal B}(\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}_{i}\mathup{{{q}}}_{j})+{\cal B}(\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{q}}}_{i}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}_{j})
. The reported uncertainties contain both the theoretical uncertainties from numerical inputs and the leading two-loop corrections to the amplitudes.

Present direct bounds on flavour changing Higgs boson decays come from searches for decays to undetermined final states,
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\text{undet.}
, at LHC. The ATLAS and CMS analyses lead to the rather poor limit
{\cal B}(\mathup{{{H}}}\to\text{undet.})<16\%

[
648
,
649
]
, which translates to
|y_{ij},y_{ji}|\lesssim 7\times 10^{-3}
.

Indirect bounds on flavour changing Higgs couplings can be extracted from measurements of meson mixing parameters, e.g. the mass splitting of
B_{s}-\bar{B}_{s}
. Assuming no large cancellations in the effective couplings, these bounds are

{\cal B}(\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{{s}}})<2\times 10^{-3}\,,\quad{\cal B}(\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{{d}}})<10^{-3}\,,\quad{\cal B}(\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{u}}})<2\times 10^{-2}\,,

(46)

which translate to
|y_{ij},y_{ji}|\lesssim 10^{-3}
. Additional bounds can be extracted by Higgs decays to a photon and flavourful vector mesons,
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}+VM^{0}

[
576
,
650
,
487
]
; these exclusive channels are either poorly or not at all constrained, thus provide much weaker bounds.

For the FCC-ee, the total detector acceptance for
\mathup{{{H}}}
hadronic decays is expected to be
\sim 70\%
. In order to reduce the background and enhance the signal, it is convenient to select events where the
\mathup{{{Z}}}
boson decays to charged leptons even at the expense of further reduction in statistics. In that case, the main background arises from
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{{q}}}
decays
[
588
]
, which mimics the signal when one of the jets is mistagged.

To project the sensitivity of future colliders, we exploit the method described in Refs.
[
477
,
651
,
652
,
588
]
, leveraging jet-flavour taggers to create when possible a binned two-dimensional distribution from which to extract the signal. As a working case, we choose the Particle-Net tagger performances reported for the FCC-ee, utilizing the IDEA detector concept
[
384
,
653
]
. Indicating by
\epsilon_{\beta}^{q}
the efficiency of the
q
-tagger to tag the
\beta
-flavoured jet, with
\beta=\{g,\mathup{{{s}}},\mathup{{{c}}},\mathup{{{b}}}\}
, we have

\begin{split}\epsilon_{\beta}^{\mathup{{{b}}}}&=\{0.02,\,0.001,\,0.02,\,0.90\}\,,\\
\epsilon_{\beta}^{\mathup{{{s}}}}&=\{0.09,\,0.80,\,0.06,\,0.004\}\,,\\
\epsilon_{\beta}^{\mathup{{{c}}}}&=\{0.02,\,0.008,\,0.80,\,0.02\}\,.\end{split}

(47)

We do not consider
\mathup{{{d}}}
and
\mathup{{{u}}}
taggers, given that they are still currently in development. Because of this, we consider two taggers for the
\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{{s}}}
channel and only one tagger for the
\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{{d}}}
and
\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{u}}}
channels. Notice that, thanks to the excellent capabilities of state-of-the-art flavour taggers, backgrounds that require two mistagged jets are greatly suppressed, e.g.
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{c}}}
backgrounds for searches of
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{{s}}}
. Systematic uncertainties on the tagger efficiencies are expected to be at or even below the
1\%
level; however the reach on
\mathup{{{H}}}
flavour changing decays will be limited by the low statistics.

The expected reaches are

{\cal B}(\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{{s}}})<9.6\times 10^{-4}\,,\quad{\cal B}(\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{u}}})<2.5\times 10^{-3}\,,

(48)

which translate to the bounds
|y_{\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{{s}}}},y_{\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{{b}}}}|\lesssim 5\times 10^{-4}
and
|y_{\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{u}}}},y_{\mathup{{{u}}}\mathup{{{c}}}}|\lesssim 8\times 10^{-4}
, respectively. The
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{{d}}}
suffers from a lower statistics and the absence of a
\mathup{{{d}}}
tagger, leading to the weaker constraint
{\cal B}(\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{{d}}})<5\times 10^{-3}
.

Thus, future colliders can improve the strongest indirect constraints on flavour-changing Higgs couplings by a factor of a few for
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{{s}}}
and
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{u}}}
, and in general exclude regions where the New Physics signals could be hidden by large cancellations between coupling.

Leptons:

Lepton flavour changing decays of the Higgs are forbidden in the SM, thus any signal would be a smoking gun for New Physics. Presently, direct bounds have been obtained by exclusive searches at LHC from both ATLAS and CMS
[
654
,
655
,
656
]
, leading to

{\cal B}(\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}})<2.0\times 10^{-3}\,,\quad{\cal B}(\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}})<1.5\times 10^{-3}\,,\quad{\cal B}(\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}})<4.4\times 10^{-5}\,.

(49)

Flavour violating decays of charged leptons will lead to indirect bounds on Higgs off-diagonal couplings
[
657
]
. While
\mathup{{{H}}}
decays involving the
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
are poorly constrained, with
{\cal B}(\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}/\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}})\lesssim 0.1
, flavour changing decays of the muon, as
\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\to 3\mathup{{{e}}}
and
\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\to\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}
, lead to limits as strong as
{\cal B}(\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}})\lesssim 10^{-9}
.

Oppositely to the previous case, here we can select
\mathup{{{Z}}}
boson hadronic decays; the total width of the latter channel is
\Gamma(\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\text{had.})\simeq 67\%
, with a detector acceptance of nearly
100\%

[
658
]
. The main suppression in the signal acceptance will thus come from reconstruction and identification of the final state leptons. In particular, decays involving the
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
will suffer from low signal efficiency, as the
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
has to be reconstructed either from the decay to a
\mathup{{{\upmu}}}
and missing energy from neutrinos,
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\to\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}}
, or from the “3-prong" decay to pions,
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\to 3\mathup{{{\uppi}}}+\mathup{{{\upnu}}}
. Following the detailed analysis of Ref.
[
659
]
, the efficiency for the
\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}}
channel is
\sim 40\%
, while it reduces to
\sim 5\%
for the
\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
and
\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
cases.

The projected bounds on branching ratios at future circular lepton colliders are

{\cal B}(\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}})\lesssim 1.6\times 10^{-4}\,,\quad{\cal B}(\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}})\lesssim 1.4\times 10^{-4}\,,\quad{\cal B}(\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}})\lesssim 1.2\times 10^{-5}\,,

(50)

which translate to the limits on the respective couplings

|y_{\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}},y_{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\mathup{{{e}}}}|\lesssim 3.6\times 10^{-4}\,,\quad|y_{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}},y_{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}|\lesssim 3.4\times 10^{-4}\,,\quad|y_{\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}}},y_{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{e}}}}|\lesssim 1.0\times 10^{-4}\,.

(51)

Apart from the
\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}}
case, these bounds show a significant improvement over present limits.

4.4
Focus Topic:
Higgs self-coupling

4.4.1
Introduction

Many open questions of particle physics are related to the Higgs sector and, in particular, to the Higgs potential.
In the SM, the form of the potential follows directly from the symmetries of the theory and the requirement of renormalisability,

V_{\mathrm{S}M}(\phi)=-\mu^{2}\phi^{\dagger}\phi+\lambda(\phi^{\dagger}\phi)^{2}=\frac{1}{2}m_{\mathup{{{H}}}}^{2}\mathup{{{H}}}^{2}+\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}\mathup{{{H}}}^{3}+\frac{1}{4}\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}\mathup{{{H}}}^{4}+\ldots\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ (\mu^{2},\penalty\ \lambda>0).

(52)

However, its key structural properties, determined by the signs of the quartic and quadratic terms, are decided ad-hoc to trigger Electroweak Symmetry Breaking (EWSB) and to have a potential that is bounded from below, respectively.
This leaves open the question of whether there is underlying new physics that explains the origin and true dynamics of EWSB.
The Higgs potential also plays a role in determining how
the electroweak phase transition (EWPT) in the early universe took place, and could be linked to possible explanations of the observed asymmetry between matter and anti-matter in the universe in terms of electroweak baryogenesis.

After the Higgs boson discovery at the LHC, the values of all the terms in
Equation

52
are unambiguously predicted in the SM in terms of the vacuum expectation value,
v
, (or, alternatively, the Fermi constant) and the Higgs boson mass:

\mu^{2}=\frac{1}{2}m_{\mathup{{{H}}}}^{2},\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \lambda=\frac{\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}}{v}=\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}=\frac{m_{\mathup{{{H}}}}^{2}}{2v^{2}}.

(53)

As for any other SM prediction, e.g. all the other Higgs couplings and EW observables, the observation of a modification of the Higgs boson self-interactions with respect to these predictions
would give evidence of the presence of new physics.

The actual form of the Higgs potential that is realised in nature and its physical origin are, however, largely unknown up to now.
While the bilinear term proportional to
\mathup{{{H}}}^{2}
is related to the measured value of
m_{\mathup{{{H}}}}
, and tells us about the potential around the electroweak (EW) minimum,
understanding the shape of the potential away from that point requires an experimental determination of the
Higgs boson three- and four- (and possibly higher) point self-couplings.
The observable effects of these interactions have only been loosely constrained experimentally so far.
In this regard, it is important to clarify that the Higgs boson self-coupling(s), like any other coupling, are not themselves physical observables, hence their determination is tied to the interpretation of an observable (e.g. the single Higgs boson or Higgs pair production cross sections) within a given theory framework. Therefore, a fully model-independent measurement of a Higgs coupling is not possible as a matter of principle at any collider, and the choice of both an appropriate theory framework and the observables to be interpreted play a role in the sensitivity to the strength of the Higgs (self-)interactions.
In this section, we focus our attention on the challenges surrounding the experimental determination, and theory interpretation, of the Higgs trilinear coupling
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
, proportional to
\mathup{{{H}}}^{3}
, whose measurement will provide the next step in understanding the shape of the Higgs potential. The main probes
used currently in LHC experiments as well as those possible at future
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
colliders are briefly described in what follows, with the progress made in the latter being the core focus of the section.

The existing constraints on
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
from the LHC have mainly been obtained from the searches for the Higgs pair production process, dominated by the gluon-fusion channel.
Assuming that all other Higgs boson couplings besides
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
are fixed to their SM values, the current bounds on the di-Higgs production cross section from ATLAS and CMS can be translated into limits on the Higgs self-coupling,
-1\lesssim\kappa_{\lambda}\lesssim 7
at 95
\%
C.L., with
\kappa_{\lambda}\equiv\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}/\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}^{\textrm{SM}}

[
660
,
649
]
.
These results will be significantly improved with the high-luminosity upgrade of the LHC. Assuming the SM value of
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
is realised in nature, current HL-LHC projections
[
661
]
give an expected 68
\%
C.L. uncertainty for
\kappa_{\lambda}
of
1^{+0.29}_{-0.26}
(see also
Figure

14(b)
). Further improvements are expected when all (single- and double-Higgs) production and decay channels are included, and when the extended acceptance of the HL-LHC detectors is taken into account.
It should be noted that, in the gluon fusion channel, the leading-order one-loop diagram containing
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
and the top Yukawa coupling
y_{\mathup{{{t}}}}
enters together with a box diagram involving the coupling factor
y_{\mathup{{{t}}}}^{2}
, see
Figure

39
. Because of the destructive interference between the contributions from these two diagrams, the total cross section for di-Higgs production changes very substantially, if
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
is varied around the SM value. This is illustrated in the top-left panel of
Figure

40
, where the Higgs pair production cross section is shown as a function of
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
for the different production modes. In this regard, it should also be noted that
a change in
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
would not only affect the total cross section, but also the kinematic properties of the Higgs pairs, e.g. their invariant mass, and hence the signal acceptance and efficiency. Both the modified kinematic properties and the single Higgs production (which benefits from a constructive interference) at the HL-LHC can be harnessed to mitigate the loss in statistical sensitivity due to the smaller cross section for moderately large values of
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
, around the minimum in
Figure

40
.

While the existing bounds on
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
are rather weak,
they can still probe so-far untested parameter regions of physics beyond the SM (BSM), in those scenarios where corrections to

\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
are much larger than those to the interactions between

\mathup{{{H}}}
and the gauge bosons and fermions (noting that the interaction between the Higgs boson and gauge bosons and fermions, and EW observables, can be measured much more precisely).
Power counting arguments, both from an effective field theory perspective
[

and in particular classes of models
[

,

,

,

suggest that such a hierarchy of corrections can indeed be generated by new physics at the tree,

This is discussed and illustrated with some examples in
Section

4.4.2
.
Furthermore, an
\mathcal{O}(1)
upward shift in
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
is also motivated in many scenarios giving rise to a strong first-order EWPT which is for instance required for electroweak baryogenesis
[
670
]
. (A large value of
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
could therefore also have cosmological consequences, detectable as a gravitational wave stochastic background at the future space-based observatory LISA
[
671
,
672
]
.)
A first-order electroweak phase transition can occur in many BSM theories proposed for several decades. These include singlet scalar extensions, triplet scalar extensions, two-Higgs doublet models, supersymmetric models, left-right symmetric models, Pati-Salam model, Georgi–Machacek model, Zee–Babu model, extended composite Higgs models, neutrino mass models and hidden sector models involving scalars, and others (see the extended list of references compiled in Ref.
[
673
]
).
For a recent example in the case of the 2HDM see e.g. Ref.
[
674
]
, where the parameter region featuring a strong first-order EWPT and a potentially detectable gravitational wave signal at the future space-based observatory LISA is correlated with an enhancement of
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
compared to the SM value by about a factor of 2.
On the other hand, it is also important to note that large
\mathcal{O}(1)
corrections to
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
are not expected to be obtained in the more natural models explaining electroweak symmetry breaking, like the minimal supersymmetry or composite Higgs models, without some tuning, and some special dynamical features are needed (discussed in
Section

4.4.2
) to generate large deviations of
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
and to remain compatible with all other experimental constraints (e.g. single-Higgs measurements or electroweak precision data).

At future colliders, information about
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
could be obtained in different and complementary ways.
At
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}

Starting with Higgs pair-production: at
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
colliders a CM energy of at least 500 GeV would be needed to measure the

Related to the possibility of measuring the Higgs pair production process and, aside from detecting possible enhancements in the value of

Below the threshold for Higgs pair production processes, future
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
Higgs factories
are also sensitive to the effects of the Higgs self-coupling via its virtual loop effects in precision observables. Specifically, single Higgs observables, like the production cross section and branching ratios, receive one-loop contributions that depend on
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
, while in the predictions for the electroweak precision observables at the Z pole and for the W-boson mass
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
enters at the two-loop level. In particular, special attention has been paid to the determination
of the Higgs self-coupling from measurements of single-Higgs processes, where sub-percent precision would bring sensitivity to quantum effects of
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}

[
675
]
.
As will be discussed in
Section

4.4.4
, FCC-ee would obtain a determination of
\kappa_{\lambda}=1\pm 0.27
(27%) or
\kappa_{\lambda}=2\pm 0.28
(14%) using this approach
[
306
]
. In combination with HL-LHC the precision obtainable would be 18% for
\kappa_{\lambda}=1
and 11.5% for
\kappa_{\lambda}=2
.
Thus,
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
precision single-Higgs measurements open the possibility of testing
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
in a way that is complementary to Higgs pair production.
For example, in single-Higgs processes
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
enters in diagrams with two off-shell and one on-shell Higgses,
while in pair production, both at hadron and lepton colliders,
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
contributes in a diagram
where the situation is reversed, with one off-shell and two on-shell Higgses.
In general, the loop contributions involving
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
compete with larger lowest-order contributions, and with other loop contributions (e.g. a top-quark loop). The sensitivity to
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
via loop effects may also be more affected by the theoretical uncertainties induced by unknown higher-order contributions and by the experimental errors of the SM input parameters.
The latter, however, are known or will be measured with a precision that suggests these parametric uncertainties are under control
[
676
]
, as will be discussed in
Section

4.4.4
.

For the study of sensitivity to
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
in single Higgs processes, the possible deviations in the Higgs self-coupling with respect to the SM have been typically parametrised within the so-called SMEFT formalism, see
Section

7.1
, truncated to dimension six.
8
8

8

This includes only effects of
{\cal O}(1/\Lambda^{2})
with
\Lambda
the heavy scale acting as cutoff of the EFT. As is also shown in the results in
Section

7.1
, the inclusion of effects of
{\cal O}(1/\Lambda^{4})
with the precision achievable at future colliders would seem to have only a small impact on the dimension-six results, suggesting the EFT expansion is well behaved.

The studies presented in Ref.
[
406
]
(see Figure 11 in that reference) reported the sensitivity to
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
for different future colliders, assuming the SM value is realized in nature, i.e.
\kappa_{\lambda}=1
. Although these studies take into account the effect of projected SM theory uncertainties mentioned above and also illustrate some illuminating points about the interplay of different EFT contributions, they were restricted to the EFT calculations available at that time and, as we discuss below, recent EFT calculations of additional NLO effects could affect the
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
interpretation.
For instance, in
an EFT analysis including only the 1-loop contributions from
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
as well as any possible contribution at leading-order, measurements at a single centre-of-mass energy show an approximate degeneracy, which can efficiently be lifted by performing measurements at a second
\sqrt{s}

[
677
]
.
With runs at
240\text{\,}
and
365\text{\,}\mathrm{GeV}
, the FCC-ee would achieve the sensitivity pictured in
Figure

42
.
However, without any extra model assumptions, a consistent analysis in the EFT approach at next-to-leading order (NLO) requires the introduction of contributions from
all the operators that are relevant at that order.
This introduces
a large number of additional EFT contributions, in particular from
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\mathup{{{t}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{t}}}}}}}
operators, which are currently poorly constrained. This opens the possibility of testing also these new effects, though at the expense of potentially reducing the precision in
\kappa_{\lambda}
.
For the main production process,
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to\mathup{{{Z}}}\mathup{{{H}}}
, such NLO contributions have only been recently identified in Refs.
[
678
,
679
]
.
Details on this calculation and its implications are discussed in
Section

4.4.5
.
The study of the effect of these contributions in the determination of
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
and of the observables needed to constrain them
will be the topic of future work.

Figure 42
:
1\sigma
sensitivity achievable on the trilinear self-coupling of the Higgs boson (
\delta\kappa_{\lambda}=\kappa_{\lambda}-1
, shown on the
x
axis) with 240 and
365\text{\,}\mathrm{GeV}
runs at the FCC-ee.
Aside from the single Higgs coupling to the Z boson (
\delta c_{\mathup{{{Z}}}}
, shown on the
y
axis),
26 additional Higgs and EW coupling modifications have been marginalised over to obtained the ellipses shown.

While the previous paragraphs and the different parts of this chapter focus on introducing/discussing aspects of the use of single- and double-Higgs measurements as probes of the Higgs boson self-coupling separately, it is important to remember that these are not to be considered as alternative probes but, as mentioned above, rather complementary ones. Indeed, since single- and double-Higgs processes are affected differently by new physics,
a disagreement between a determination of
\kappa_{\lambda}
from both methods with similar precision would evidence the presence of additional new effects, making clear the synergetic aspects of the two approaches. Therefore, as in any other of situation where a sign of new physics may be discovered in the data,
having as many different types of observables as possible where one can test the new effect would help in characterising its origin.
It should also be remembered that a future hadron collider FCChh could reach 3% or better precision on
\kappa_{\lambda}
.

4.4.2
Generating large corrections to the Higgs self-coupling in new physics models

As mentioned above, the dynamics and nature of the EWPT are closely connected to the Higgs self-coupling value.
For instance, if a strong first-order phase transition is needed to explain the observed matter/anti-matter asymmetry, this is something that cannot be realised in the SM but can be obtained in many BSM theories, typically in correlation with a large (order one) deviation of
\lambda_{\mathup{{{h}}}\mathup{{{h}}}\mathup{{{h}}}}
from its SM value
[
680
,
681
,
682
,
683
,
684
]
.

Given the already tight constraints on the Higgs couplings to gauge bosons and heavy fermions, and their foreseen improvements at the (HL-)LHC, one can wonder if there is still room for possible large deviations in the Higgs self-couplings.
In generic models of heavy decoupling new physics, the deviations in all Higgs couplings are expected to be roughly of the same order. For instance, in models that follow the
Strongly-Interacting Light Higgs
(SILH) power counting
[
685
]
, like composite Higgs or decoupling supersymmetric models, we expect

\delta\kappa_{\lambda}\sim\delta\kappa_{V}\sim\frac{v^{2}}{f^{2}},

(54)

where the
f
parameter is related to the typical coupling
g_{\star}
and mass scale
m_{\star}
of the new dynamics by
f\sim m_{\star}/g_{\star}
. (Similarly to
\kappa_{\lambda}
, we have introduced
\kappa_{V}
as the Higgs coupling to vector bosons, normalised to the SM value.)
There are two main ways to depart from this relation:

1.

enforcing a particular structure of the heavy new physics;

2.

having non-decoupling/relatively light particles.

Even in the first class, the relation in
Equation

54
can be avoided in many ways and perturbativity arguments only give an upper bound on the ratio of the Higgs coupling deviations
[
666
]
:

\left|\frac{\delta\kappa_{\lambda}}{\delta\kappa_{V}}\right|\lesssim\mathrm{min}\left(\left(\frac{4\pi v}{m_{\mathup{{{H}}}}}\right)^{2},\frac{m_{\star}^{2}}{m_{\mathup{{{H}}}}^{2}}\right).

(55)

However, among UV models with single particle extensions
[
589
]
, only the one with a custodial electroweak quadruplet explicitly realises a parametric enhancement of the Higgs self-coupling deviation and gets close to saturate the bound in
Equation

55
, see
Figure

43
(left).
Another way to get parametrically large
\delta\kappa_{\lambda}
is to rely on Goldstone bosons resulting from large charged spurion symmetry breaking, as in the Gegenbauer’s Twin models
[
686
,
666
]
, as illustrated in the right panel of
Figure

43
. Other dynamics that lead to large
\delta\kappa_{\lambda}
include (i) scenarios in which the Higgs is a generic bound state of a strongly coupled dynamics (i.e. not a Goldstone boson), (ii) bosonic technicolour scenarios, (iii) Higgs-portal models.

Figure 43
:
(Left) Single-Higgs coupling and self-coupling deviations expected for a custodial electroweak quadruplet model, as a function of the heavy state coupling,
\lambda
, and mass,
M
. From Ref.
[
666
]
.
In the grey region, vacuum stability requires sizeable contributions from potential terms not included in the analysis.
(Right) Ratio of self-coupling to
HVV
corrections in the Gegenbauer’s Twin model for several values of the charge of global symmetry breaking spurion. In the empty upper-left corner of the figure, the SM vacuum is no longer the global minimum of the potential and therefore becomes unstable. From Ref.
[
666
]
.
In both figures,
\delta_{h^{3}}
and
\delta_{VV}
correspond to the quantities
\delta\kappa_{\lambda}
and
\delta\kappa_{V}
used in this report, respectively.

Examples of the second class of models are models with extended scalar sectors because of large higher-order radiative corrections from the additional BSM scalars (which we generically denote
\Phi
)
[
667
,
687
,
688
,
689
,
690
,
691
,
692
,
693
,
694
,
695
,
695
,
696
,
697
,
698
,
699
,
700
,
701
,
702
,
703
,
704
,
668
,
705
,
669
,
706
,
707
]
.
These corrections are controlled by couplings of the general form
g_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\Phi\Phi}\propto(m_{\Phi}^{2}-\mathcal{M}^{2})/v^{2}
, where
m_{\Phi}
is the physical mass of the scalar
\Phi
,
\mathcal{M}
is some mass scale controlling the decoupling of the BSM states, and
v
is the SM vacuum expectation value. In scenarios where a splitting occurs between
\mathcal{M}
and
m_{\Phi}
, the
g_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\Phi\Phi}
couplings can grow rapidly and produce large BSM contributions to
\kappa_{\lambda}
. It should be emphasised that these loop effects involving BSM scalars and
g_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\Phi\Phi}
couplings are not a perturbation of the tree-level trilinear Higgs coupling, but rather a new class of contributions only entering at the loop level. They can therefore become larger than the tree-level contribution, without being associated with a violation of perturbativity (this situation is analogous to that of loop-induced processes like e.g.
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}
or
\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}\mathup{{{Z}}}
).

Figure 44
:
(Left) One- and two-loop predictions for
\kappa_{\lambda}

\mathup{{{h}}}
to refer to the SM-like Higgs boson, to distinguish it from the other possible heavy Higgs bosons that appear, e.g. in 2HDM models, for which the notation
\mathup{{{H}}},\mathup{{{H}}}^{\pm}
is used.)
For the scenario considered here,
9

with

[

at the LHC allows excluding significant parts of the otherwise unconstrained parameter space of the model. For instance, in this specific scenario, the mass range

to be larger than 7.2

Additionally, the mass range

of this scenario would be probed at the HL-LHC, as indicated in purple in the left panel of

.
Importantly, the mass-splitting effects shown in that same figure and the exclusions obtained with current LHC data, or expected with future colliders, are not restricted to the 2HDM, but have been found to occur in various BSM theories with additional scalars – as can now be studied with the public tool anyH3
[
669
]
.

The occurrence of large radiative corrections in
\lambda_{\mathup{{{h}}}\mathup{{{h}}}\mathup{{{h}}}}
raises the questions of how sizeable higher-order corrections to other Higgs properties involving
g_{\mathup{{{h}}}\mathup{{{h}}}\Phi\Phi}
couplings can become, and where one would first observe a deviation from the SM predictions in these types of scenarios. Power counting arguments
[
710
]
show that, in the limit of large
g_{\mathup{{{h}}}\mathup{{{h}}}\Phi\Phi}
couplings, the leading one-loop BSM contributions to the trilinear Higgs coupling are of
\mathcal{O}(g_{\mathup{{{h}}}\mathup{{{h}}}\Phi\Phi}^{2})
, while those in single-Higgs couplings grow at most linearly with
g_{\mathup{{{h}}}\mathup{{{h}}}\Phi\Phi}
.

As a simple but illustrative example, we consider the
Z_{2}
-SSM,
10
10

10

We refer the reader to e.g. Ref.
[
704
]
for an overview of the notations and conventions we employ in this work (we consider here the
N=1
case of the
O(N)
-symmetric SSM of Ref.
[
704
]
).
i.e. a real-singlet extension of the SM with an unbroken global
Z_{2}
symmetry. Due to this symmetry, the BSM scalar
S
does not mix with the detected Higgs boson at 125 GeV. Its mass takes the form
m_{S}^{2}=\mu_{S}^{2}+\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\Phi}v^{2}
where
\mu_{S}
is the singlet Lagrangian mass term and
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\Phi}
the portal quartic coupling between the singlet and the (SM-like) doublet. The coupling
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\Phi}
plays in the
Z_{2}
-SSM the exact role of the generic
g_{\mathup{{{h}}}\mathup{{{h}}}\Phi\Phi}
coupling in the discussion above. In this model, single-Higgs couplings
g_{\mathup{{{h}}}XX}
, where
X
can be a gauge boson or fermion, only receive BSM contributions via external-leg corrections — there are no mixing effects at the tree level, and moreover vertex-type corrections do not appear because of the singlet nature of the BSM scalar and the unbroken
Z_{2}
symmetry.
This allows obtaining compact expressions for the single-Higgs coupling modifier
c_{\text{eff}}\equiv g_{\mathup{{{h}}}XX}/g_{\mathup{{{h}}}XX}^{\text{SM}}
at one and two loops
[
710
]
.
In the right panel of

, we present contour lines for

(red) as well as the quantity

(blue), both computed at the two-loop order, in the
\{\mu_{S},m_{S}\}
parameter plane of the
Z_{2}
-SSM. As a conservative choice, we fix
\lambda_{S}=0
in the plane; this cancels the effects from two-loop terms involving
\lambda_{S}
in
\kappa_{\lambda}
and
c_{\text{eff}}
(we note that for these contributions, like for those involving only
g_{\mathup{{{h}}}\mathup{{{h}}}\Phi\Phi}

have a higher scaling in powers of

than those in

). We implemented the expected levels of accuracy on single-Higgs couplings at the HL-LHC as “measurements” (assuming SM-like central values) in HiggsSignals
[

]
, and orange lines in the left panel of
Figure

44
correspond respectively to the
1\sigma
(solid) and
2\sigma
(dashed) exclusion ranges from HL-LHC measurements.
The values indicated in each contour line for
\kappa_{\lambda}
(
c_{\text{eff}}
) indicate the maximum (minimum) value of the parameter
predicted in the region below the line.
Therefore, these lines provide information about the regions of the
Z_{2}
-SSM parameter space for which large corrections to
\kappa_{\lambda}
can be obtained while those to
c_{\text{eff}}
are small.
As can be observed, comparing for instance the uppermost red and blue contour lines in the right panel of

44
, values of
\kappa_{\lambda}
up to 1.5 could be obtained while corrections
to

are kept below
0.5\%
.

Other examples where this hierarchy of corrections can be obtained from large radiative corrections include, for instance, the Inert Doublet Model (IDM), a variant of the 2HDM in which the second doublet is charged under an unbroken
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
symmetry, see e.g. Refs.
[

]
for an overview of the model.
As in the above example for the
Z_{2}
-SSM, using the two-loop predictions for
\kappa_{\lambda}
(from Refs.
[
700
,
701
,
714
]
) and the one-loop BSM deviation in the

corrections of
\kappa_{\lambda}
are predicted, while keeping the modifications of the Higgs couplings to vector bosons well below
1\%
.

Of course, future Higgs/electroweak/top factories will be making precise measurements of
c_{\text{eff}}
and
\kappa_{\lambda}
that will increasingly constrain the available parameter space.

As we discuss next, the large values of
\lambda_{\mathup{{{h}}}\mathup{{{h}}}\mathup{{{h}}}}
discussed in this section
could be probed via double-Higgs production
at future
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
colliders operating at CM energies around 500 GeV.
Similarly, while corrections to single Higgs coupling can remain small in these models,
deviations at the level of a few tens of percent in the value of
\kappa_{\lambda}
would also
induce effects at one-loop level in single-Higgs observables that could be tested
at future
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
Higgs factories operating at more than one centre-of-mass energy such as FCC-ee, as is explained in
Section

4.4.4
.

4.4.3
Progress in Higgs-pair production at
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}

In combination with the
\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\rightarrow\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{b}}}}}}}\mathup{{{W}}}\mathup{{{W}}}^{*}
channel, the precision on the cross-section improves from the

\mathup{{{Z}}}\rightarrow\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}

\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\rightarrow\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{b}}}}}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}

cross-section improves further to
11.2\text{\,}\%
, corresponding to a precision on a SM-like self-coupling value
\uplambda_{\mathrm{SM}}
of
18.1\text{\,}\%
.
This sensitivity of 18% on
\uplambda_{\mathrm{SM}}
corresponds to
4\text{\,}{\mathrm{ab}}^{-1}
collected at

G
eV

One of the main limiting factors not yet addressed by novel algorithms is the jet clustering. Assuming that future developments, e.g. based on ML, will improve the di-jet mass resolution, we estimate that
\uplambda_{\mathrm{SM}}
could be determined with a precision of
15\text{\,}\%
from
\mathup{{{Z}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}

The analysis of the
\mathup{{{W}}}\mathup{{{W}}}

[

717

at a centre-of-mass energy of
1\text{\,}\mathrm{T}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}

500\text{\,}\mathrm{G}\mathrm{e}\mathrm{V}

\mathup{{{W}}}\mathup{{{W}}}

from the

\mathup{{{Z}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}

\uplambda_{\mathrm{SM}}
to a precision of
17\text{\,}\%
with current tools and
14\text{\,}\%
when assuming improved jet clustering.

The results summarised above have been extrapolated to other centre-of-mass energies. In particular, partial MC productions have been performed in full, Geant4-based simulation of ILD as well as using SGV

and centre-of-mass energies of

4.4.4
Probing the Higgs self-coupling via single-Higgs processes

The measurements of single-Higgs processes that could be taken at any
of the future
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
Higgs factories, namely the inclusive cross section and rates for different decay channels of the Higgs boson,
are typically interpreted in terms of single-Higgs couplings to the SM fermions and vector bosons, quantities that in the SM contribute
to these processes at tree level. But, clearly, owing to the quantum nature of these observables, such interpretation needs to
be improved beyond this leading order approximation, as what these experiments measure are not single-Higgs couplings, but
combinations of such couplings and all the other interactions that enter in the process at the quantum level.

In the SM, the 1-loop corrections coming from the Higgs self-coupling to, e.g. the
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to\mathup{{{Z}}}\mathup{{{H}}}
cross section at 240 GeV,
are relatively small, increasing the LO cross section by
\sim 1.5\%
. In the full set of NLO electroweak contributions, bosonic and fermionic corrections
partially cancel, so the total NLO correction amount to
\sim 3\%
.
Furthermore, the NNLO from fermion loops are currently known to increase only the NLO result by
0.7\%

[
723
]
, and the uncertainty from missing bosonic electroweak corrections has been estimated to be less than
0.3\%

[
723
]
. Therefore, it is reasonable to expect
that, with some moderate progress in the SM calculations, by the time of a future Higgs factory the SM uncertainty due to higher-order corrections will be further reduced and become much smaller than the leading
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
effects. Similarly, benefiting from future EW and Higgs measurements, parametric uncertainties from the EW input parameters are also expected to be very small, well below the experimental precision.
11
11

11

An estimate using the SM part of the calculation of
[
679
]
gives an expected parametric uncertainty at FCC-ee well below
0.1\%
.
It is of particular relevance to improve the precision of the Higgs boson mass to around or below 20 MeV. See Ref.
[
676
]
for estimates on the corresponding SM uncertainties on Higgs decay rates.

Thus, with an experimental precision at the per mille level in
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to\mathup{{{Z}}}\mathup{{{H}}}
, it is clear that a future
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
Higgs factory would provide a clean test of the SM prediction for
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
.
The precision of such test, or the one on the determination of
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
if everything but this parameter is assumed to be SM-like, could be obtained parametrising the modifications of single-Higgs observables in terms of the following contribution to the Higgs potential

\Delta V(\mathup{{{H}}})=(\kappa_{\lambda}-1)\frac{1}{2}\frac{m_{\mathup{{{H}}}}^{2}}{v}\mathup{{{H}}}^{3}.

(56)

In general, however,
estimating the actual precision of the determination of
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
that would be possible from this (or any other)
type of measurements is not something that can be addressed in a completely model-independent way. For instance,
different new particles could be exchanged virtually, e.g. in the EW loops, opening the possibility of testing
many other new physics effects, but also requiring a commensurate number of other observables to identify the
origin of a possible non-SM effect in the data. As mentioned in the previous section, this can be addressed in a fairly general way for the case of decoupling new physics.
The use of additional observables needed to constrain all the possible additional loop effects and extract
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
in this case is briefly discussed at the end of this chapter and is part of future work.

Equation

56
could be used to extend the simplest Lagrangian description of
the scenarios of the so-called
\kappa
framework
[
724
]

considering only modifications of SM-like interactions to include corrections to the Higgs self-coupling,

\Delta{\cal L}=\Delta V(\mathup{{{H}}})+2m_{Z}^{2}\kappa_{V}\frac{\mathup{{{H}}}}{v}Z_{\mu}Z^{\mu}+2m_{W}^{2}\kappa_{V}\frac{\mathup{{{H}}}}{v}W_{\mu}W^{\mu}-\sum_{\psi}m_{\psi}\overline{\psi}_{L}\kappa_{\psi}\frac{\mathup{{{H}}}}{v}\psi_{R}+{\mathrm{h}.c.},

(57)

where we have assumed custodial symmetry.
A simple exercise performing a frequentist fit of
Equation

56
and
Equation

57
to the expected precision of all the single-Higgs measurements at
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
colliders using two centre-of-mass energies, taking as an example FCC-ee at 240 and 365 GeV (from Ref.
[
398
]
, updated to the FCC-ee baseline with 4 interaction points
[
307
]
, see
Table

1
for the actual luminosities), would give the constraints on
\kappa_{\lambda}
shown in
Figure

47
.
The results are obtained including also the information that will be available from the HL-LHC
studies of Higgs pair production.
In the figure we consider not only the possibility of
\kappa_{\lambda}=1
but also use Asimov datasets generated with
Equation

56

for different values of
\kappa_{\lambda}
. We use the theoretical expressions of Refs.
[
725
,
677
]
to describe the one-loop dependence of
\kappa_{\lambda}
, while the effects of the modifications of other Higgs couplings are kept at leading order.
One thing to note is that, with
\kappa_{\lambda}
entering at the loop level in single-Higgs observables, for moderate deviations from the SM value
the change in the single Higgs cross sections is rather small and the absolute precision on
\kappa_{\lambda}
at
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
does not change substantially.
This leads to a determination of
\kappa_{\lambda}=1\pm 0.27
(27%) or
\kappa_{\lambda}=2\pm 0.28
(14%) for FCC-ee. In combination with HL-LHC the precision obtainable would be 18% for
\kappa_{\lambda}=1
and 11% for
\kappa_{\lambda}=2
.
It is important to note that a disagreement between FCC-ee and HL-LHC on a similar-precision
\kappa_{\lambda}
extraction would be a sign of new physics in the
\mathup{{{Z}}}\mathup{{{H}}}
loops, making the measurement from single-Higgs production very much synergistic with that of pair-production at HL-LHC.

Figure 47
:
1\sigma
sensitivity on the trilinear self-coupling of the Higgs boson
achievable with the single-Higgs measurements at 240 and 365 GeV from FCC-ee,
in combination with the HL-LHC results from double-Higgs production.
The results are obtained assuming different values of
\kappa_{\lambda}
are realized in nature, and presented under two assumptions in the Lagrangian in
Equation

57
: (orange) all parameters are set to their SM values except for
\kappa_{\lambda}
; (blue) all couplings are considered as floating parameters and marginalized over to obtain the sensitivity to
\kappa_{\lambda}
. The lower panel shows the relative uncertainty.

To give precise meaning to the modifications in
Equation

57
, this must be embedded in a concrete model or in
a well-defined effective field theory.
The projections available for
\kappa_{\lambda}
from single-Higgs measurements in Refs.
[
677
,
406
]
were prepared in the so-called Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT).
We refer to
Section

7
for a small description of the assumptions defining this framework
to describe the low-energy effects of decoupling new physics.
Following the power-counting of the SMEFT, at the leading order in the EFT expansion — a power series in
1/\Lambda
, with
\Lambda
the cut-off of the EFT — there are many more types of possible sources of BSM effects than those in
Equation

57
, including not only modifications of the SM Higgs properties, but also of the EW interactions and types of operators absent in the SM.
While the large number of BSM effects provides a more general description of new physics scenarios, global analyses including different types of observables are required if one wants to individually constrain all the different directions in the EFT parameter space.
This is particularly relevant when going beyond tree level in the description of new physics effects,
as needed for the determination of
\kappa_{\lambda}
from single-Higgs couplings,
as this increases the number of SMEFT operators that can enter in the analysis via their loop contributions.
The status of the NLO calculations required for this and steps needed to extend the results in Refs.
[
677
,
406
]
are described in the next section.

It is important to note that, while these global analyses of the sensitivity to
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
in single-Higgs measurements performed within the EFT formalism depend on a large number of parameters that need to be constrained from data, a consequence of this is that the resulting
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
-sensitivity is expected to be a conservative estimate of that which would be possible in actual models described by the EFT.
Indeed, interpretations within specific models, which match into lower-dimensional slices of the EFT parameter space, add extra theory correlations between the different operators, reducing the uncertainty that would be present should all these operators be independent degrees of freedom in the study. For a trivial example, a model predicting only a deviation of the Higgs self-coupling would match into the results of a SMEFT fit with only one operator to dimension six,
(\phi^{\dagger}\phi)^{3}
. For our purposes, this is equivalent to considering only the effect given by
Equation

56
. As illustrated in the example in
Figure

47
with the improvement in the
\kappa_{\lambda}
determination when this is the only degree of freedom in the fit (compare the orange band with the blue one, obtained including additional parameters), this model would be better constrained than in
Figure

42
, where one marginalizes over many other SMEFT parameters that would be zero in this particular scenario.
Finally, as in any other theory calculation, the level of agreement of the EFT fit results when matched to a model and that in the particular scenario will depend on the precision of the EFT theory calculations, both in the computation of observables as well as in the matching.
12
12

12

For example, it is well known that in some types of scenarios with extra scalar doublets it is important to include terms of dimension eight in the EFT expansion
[
726
]
. See also
[
727
]
for a more general discussion on the assessment of accuracy in the interpretation of the EFT description.

Continuing the effort of improving these interpretations to higher orders both in the EFT expansion as well as in perturbation theory, like the calculation described next, is therefore important to extend the range of applicability of current EFT results.
Conversely, this also highlights the need to, in the meantime, augment these interpretations with studies directly in terms of well-motivated models in those cases where they may not be described accurately in terms of current SMEFT calculations.

4.4.5
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to\mathup{{{Z}}}\mathup{{{H}}}
at NLO in the SMEFT

We conclude this section discussing the progress on the theory side regarding the determination of
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
from single Higgs measurements, where the sensitivity to the Higgs self-coupling in single Higgs processes comes from one-loop level contributions, in the context of the SMEFT.
Within the SMEFT framework, the full set of NLO contributions from dimension-six operators to
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to\mathup{{{Z}}}\mathup{{{H}}}
has recently been computed, first for operators involving the top quark
[
678
]
and then to the whole dimension-six basis
[
679
]
. A sample of such contributions is shown in
Figure

49
. From the point of view of the
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
SMEFT interpretation,
these calculations open the possibility of extending previous studies in the direction of a model-independent interpretation within the assumptions of this EFT, see
Section

7.1
.
13
13

13

To achieve this, calculations of the NLO effects in other processes relevant for Higgs physics at
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
are still missing, e.g.
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to\nu\bar{\nu}\mathup{{{H}}}
(via
W
boson fusion).

Aside from the operators entering at LO, there are a total of 6 bosonic (4 of them CP violating), 9 two-fermion and 14 four-fermion dimension-six operators that contribute to
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to\mathup{{{Z}}}\mathup{{{H}}}
at NLO.
Of particular importance are the contributions of the top-quark operator mentioned before, e.g.
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\mathup{{{t}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{t}}}}}}}

.

The large number of different interactions entering at NLO would suggest that in the single-Higgs analysis at NLO there will be a considerable amount of degeneracy.
With more operators simultaneously included, more observables need to be combined to constrain all directions
in a global fit
and single out the potential new contributions to
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
.
In Higgsstrahlung production itself, angular distributions and radiative return to lower effective centre-of-mass energies could for instance be considered
[
728
]
.
Outside Higgs physics, the above-mentioned top interactions could be tested at the tree level in
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to\mathup{{{t}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{t}}}}}}}
at
350\text{\,}\mathrm{-}
365\text{\,}\mathrm{GeV}
. Finally, some of the same top operators enter in Z-pole observables also at the loop-level, and a combined analysis exploiting the extreme high precision of the Tera-Z run could also help in a global analysis.
The determination
of
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
thus relies on having precision measurements of a large enough number of observables to constrain any possible BSM effects in other contributions that enter in the calculations of the observables to the same order in perturbation theory as the leading contributions of
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
.

There is currently an ongoing effort to extend the
\lambda_{\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}\mathup{{{H}}}}
EFT determination from single-Higgs measurements, including these recent NLO effects, and other aspects related to this EFT interpretation.

5
Developments in Electroweak Physics & QCD

The various centre-of-mass energy stages proposed by future
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
collider projects provide opportunities for a wealth of measurements in the electroweak and QCD sectors. Prospects for a precision
\mathup{{{W}}}
-boson mass measurement and
\mathup{{{W}}}
-boson couplings are discussed in
Section

5.1
and
Section

5.2
. The electroweak precision measurements achievable from the very large statistics of two-fermion final states both at and above the
\mathup{{{Z}}}
-pole are discussed in
Section

5.3
. Other
\mathup{{{Z}}}
-boson and neutrino measurements are addressed in
Section

5.4
.
Section

5.5
presents new results on the sensitivity to triple-gauge couplings that could be achieved through differential
\mathup{{{W}}}\mathup{{{W}}}
measurements.
Section

5.6
addresses fragmentation and hadronisation, both in terms of what could be learned from future
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
colliders, and where this could be a limiting factor on other measurements. Finally
Section

5.7
briefly considers other SM parameters that enter the interpretation of electroweak precision measurements.

5.1
Focus Topic:
W boson mass measurement

The mass of the
\mathup{{{W}}}
boson (
m_{\mathup{{{W}}}}
) is a fundamental parameter of the standard model (SM).
A precise experimental
m_{\mathup{{{W}}}}
determination is highly desirable to test the SM consistency and as a means to reveal possible new physics effects
[
729
]
.
The level of precision to which
m_{\mathup{{{W}}}}
could be determined at a future
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
collider with a scan of cross sections at the pair-production threshold, and from measurements of decay kinematics is greatly superior to current measurements
[
453
]
, and expected to by far exceed measurements at the LHC which yield uncertainties around 10 MeV
[
730
,
731
]
.

To obtain an estimate of the achievable theory and experimental systematic uncertainties at am
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
Higgs factory, the potential of analysis, calibration and event reconstruction methods, currently in development, should be assessed. Several complementary methods will be used to measure
m_{\mathup{{{W}}}}
. Ideally their systematic uncertainty should match or be better than the statistical precision of the data.
While
\mathup{{{W}}}
-pair threshold cross section scans are expected to be less impacted by systematic uncertainties, detector performance will play a crucial role in
m_{\mathup{{{W}}}}
measurements that make use of kinematic information obtained from event reconstruction.
In the following we outline the main methods envisaged.

\mathup{{{W}}}
-pair production at threshold

The rapid rise of the
\mathup{{{W}}}
-pair production cross section near its kinematic threshold can be exploited to obtain a precise and direct determination of the
\mathup{{{W}}}
boson mass.
The threshold method is clean and simple as it just involves classifying and counting events.
A small amount of LEP
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
collision data taken in 1996 at a single energy point near 161 GeV allowed the
\mathup{{{W}}}
mass to be determined with a precision of 200 MeV
[
732
,
733
,
734
,
735
]
.

Collecting over 1 ab
-1
of integrated luminosity at threshold energies will enable a determination of the
\mathup{{{W}}}
mass with a statistical uncertainty below 1 MeV
[
736
]
.
Measuring the threshold cross section at more than one energy point will allow measurement of both the
\mathup{{{W}}}
mass and width, with similar precision
[
264
,
265
]
.
Polarised collisions can enhance or suppress
t
-channel signal production, enabling further control of the background
[
737
,
738
]
.

\mathup{{{W}}}
-pair decay kinematics

The primary method to measure the
\mathup{{{W}}}
mass and width at LEP2 was with the kinematic reconstruction of semileptonic (
\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}\ell\nu
) and fully hadronic (
\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}
)

\mathup{{{W}}}
-pair decays
[
739
,
740
,
741
,
742
,
743
]
.
These results were obtained by imposing the constraint that the total four-momentum in the event should be equal to the known initial centre-of-mass energy and zero momentum.

It is foreseen that performing similar measurements with future collider data would yield a statistical precision of a few MeV or less
[
738
,
265
]
,
but the impact of systematic uncertainties is more difficult to predict; in particular, those arising from the modelling of non-perturbative QCD effects in the
\mathup{{{W}}}
-boson hadronic decays, that stood out in the LEP2 measurements
[
743
]
.

In the standard (LEP2-style)
\mathup{{{W}}}
-mass kinematic reconstruction, non-perturbative QCD uncertainties arise on two fronts.
The first is from overall uncertainties on the modelling of core jet properties, in particular on
the jets boost (
\beta_{\text{jet}}=p_{\text{jet}}/E_{\text{jet}}
) that is a key ingredient of the kinematic fit.
Uncertainties on
\beta_{\text{jet}}
will affect similarly both the
\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}\ell\nu
and
\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}
channels.
The second source is from colour reconnection (CR) effects, that can
lead to an important impact and uncertainty on
m_{\mathup{{{W}}}}
, but only in the
\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}
channel.

The energy spectrum endpoints in leptonic decays, that are free from QCD uncertainties, can also be used to measure the
\mathup{{{W}}}
mass
[
738
]
.
In the case of fully leptonic decays, a pseudomass
[
742
]
can be computed and employed for a
\mathup{{{W}}}
-mass measurement.
Using only the lepton decay kinematics degrades the statistical sensitivity of the measurement, that
is finally expected to achieve a precision
of 3–5 MeV with this approach
[
738
]
.

All the above methods to determine the W mass, including the threshold lineshape, necessitate a precise knowledge of the collision energy
as the beam energy uncertainty propagates directly to the
W -ass systematic uncertainties with

\Delta m_{\mathup{{{W}}}}(E_{\text{beam}})\simeq\Delta E_{\text{beam}}
.
A future circular collider would provide a calibration of the beam energy by resonant depolarisation with a precision well below 1 MeV, up to the W-pair threshold
[
736
]
.
Finally a direct measurement of the hadronic mass, without kinematic constraints, can be performed
[
744
]
where the uncertainties will be dominated by the hadronic energy scale calibration.

Theoretical and phenomenological targets and challenges

Precise predictions of total and differential
\mathup{{{W}}}
-pair production

Accounting for the high experimental precision in the
m_{\mathup{{{W}}}}
determination
at
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
colliders in predictions
requires a proper inclusion of radiative corrections
to the
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to
4f processes with intermediate
\mathup{{{W}}}
pairs.
Depending on the
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
CM energy
E_{\text{CM}}
,
different physical effects and corrections
dominate, and the target precisions are not the same.
Customised treatments are required for CM energies near the
W-pair threshold (
|E_{\text{CM}}-2m_{\mathup{{{W}}}}|<n\Gamma_{\mathup{{{W}}}}
,
n\sim 2{-}3
),
at intermediate energies of a typical future circular collider
(
2m_{\mathup{{{W}}}}+n\Gamma_{\mathup{{{W}}}}<E_{\text{CM}}<
250 GeV),
or at higher energies.

“Improved-Born approximations”
based on leading universal corrections (initial-state radiation,
Coulomb singularity, effective couplings)
can be formulated uniformly for the whole energy range, but
are good only to
\sim 2\%
for integrated cross sections
up to intermediate energies (and deliver only
\sim 10\%

accuracy for
E_{\text{CM}}\sim
1 TeV).
For intermediate energies, a pair of on-shell
\mathup{{{W}}}
bosons
dominates the cross section, so that NLO corrections can be included
in the “double-pole approximation (DPA)”
[
218
,
59
]
, which is based on
the leading term of an expansion of amplitudes about the
\mathup{{{W}}}
resonance poles.
The quality of the DPA was estimated to
0.5{-}1\%
for integrated
cross sections and later confirmed in a comparison
to NLO predictions for the full
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to 4\text{f}
cross sections
[
279
]
which should be good within
a few
0.1\%
even in the
\mathup{{{W}}}
-pair threshold region, where the DPA breaks down
(see Section 6.5.5 of Ref.
[
303
]
for more details and
original references).
At threshold, the currently best calculation is based on complete
NLO results for
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to
4f
[
279
]

and partial higher-order effects
for the total cross section from an effective field theory (EFT) framework
[
215
,
151
]
, suggesting a theory uncertainty on
m_{\mathup{{{W}}}}
of about 3 MeV for
m_{\mathup{{{W}}}}
extracted from a threshold measurement
[
151
]
, excluding the uncertainty from QED initial-state radiation.

The quality of differential predictions in dominant phase-space regions
widely follows the precision estimates for integrated cross sections,
but the precision significantly deteriorates in regions where
resonant
\mathup{{{W}}}
-pair production becomes less dominant, e.g. in the
backward direction of
\mathup{{{W}}}
production or at very large CM energies
(see also Section 8 of Ref.
[
169
]
).

To account for the leap in precision from LEP to a future
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
collider,
predictions for
\mathup{{{W}}}
-pair production have to be improved considerably,
most notably the treatment of initial-state radiation
[
745
,
746
]
.
At threshold, NNLO corrections to the “hard”
\mathup{{{W}}}
-pair production and
\mathup{{{W}}}
decay
processes as well as leading corrections beyond NNLO can be calculated within
the EFT approach, and a precision of 0.5 MeV in
m_{\mathup{{{W}}}}
from an
energy scan near threshold seems feasible
[
676
]
.
For intermediate and high energies, a full NNLO calculation for
\mathup{{{W}}}
-pair
production in DPA would be most desirable, a task that should be
achievable in the next decade, anticipating further progress at
the frontier of loop calculations.

Estimates and control of QCD effects

Accurate jet evolution and prediction of radiation patterns are important ingredients for the
\mathup{{{W}}}
-mass measurement.

Hadronisation models might impact jet properties such as the boost, as well as the energy scale due to differences in the baryon ratios. For the jet energy calibrations from
\mathup{{{Z}}}
-peak events, beam energy, jet mass and jet momentum are affected by baryon and strange ratios.
Hadronisation models can also affect the measured jet energy, resolution and jet mass via the charged/neutral ratio fraction of very low and high
p_{\text{T}}
tracks and the shower shape.
\mathup{{{Z}}}
-peak events have a different flavour composition from
\mathup{{{W}}}
-boson events. Studies of
\mathup{{{b}}}
and
\mathup{{{c}}}
tags exist but
\mathup{{{s}}}
quarks must also be considered.

Colour reconnection (CR) in all-hadronic events affects particles with large
\Delta R
to the jet (parton) direction by pulling them towards or away from the jet, since they change the colour topology underpinning the hadronisation process. These have a large lever arm on the jet direction. At LEP2, the effect was reduced with cuts on
\Delta R
or cuts on soft particles or weights. Theoretically well-behaved algorithms, e.g. Cambridge/Aachen with freeze-out, are needed to address this issue. Experimentally, CR can be accessed using particle flow in the region between jets. Different models with similar measured flow can have significantly different effects on the reconstructed jet direction, and thus the
\mathup{{{W}}}
mass. All “realistic” CR models should be considered to estimate the possible impact in lack of further constraints. Constraints on CR can be obtained from change of jet direction (or
\mathup{{{W}}}
mass) by changing parameters of jet algorithms (e.g. jet freeze out). Jet algorithms that do not include soft particles with large
\Delta R
in the jet associated with the partons from the
\mathup{{{W}}}
-boson decay might have larger modelling uncertainties.
\mathup{{{Z}}}
-boson peak events with two jets can be used to calibrate the direction resolution.

Newly developed colour reconnection and hadronisation models
[
529
,
747
,
748
,
749
]
should be considered to put further constraints on the predictivity for such final states.

Detector performance and analysis methods

Detector and analysis performances are particularly relevant for measurements with the reconstruction of the
\mathup{{{W}}}
-boson decay kinematics.
In the case of the reconstruction of fully leptonic or semileptonic
\mathup{{{W}}}
-pair decays, the determination of lepton energy scale is a key ingredient.
Previous studies concluded that the evaluation of
\mathup{{{J\mspace{-2mu}/\mspace{-2mu}\uppsi}}}\to\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}}
events could provide the most precise constraints of the track momenta, as the
\mathup{{{J\mspace{-2mu}/\mspace{-2mu}\uppsi}}}
mass is currently known to the level of 1.9 ppm, corresponding to about 6 keV
[
453
]
. However, at
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
colliders the production of
\mathup{{{J\mspace{-2mu}/\mspace{-2mu}\uppsi}}}
is expected to be statistics limited. More recent studies reported in the ECFA workshop
[
750
]
, based on Refs.
[
751
,
752
]
, have explored how a combination of mass information from several well measured particles, in particular
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{K}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{S}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uppi}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uppi}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
and
\mathup{{{\Uplambda}}}\to\mathup{{{p}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uppi}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
can be used an absolute calibration of track momenta at a future high-energy
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
collider. With sufficient statistics it is estimated that a centre-of-mass energy uncertainty of
2\times 10^{-6}
could be achieved, competitive with the uncertainty in the centre-of-mass energy expected at FCC-ee.

In contrast, the jet energy scale is not expected to be known better than the level of
10^{-4}
, with dominant uncertainties arising from modelling uncertainties such as flavour dependence, hadronisation, colour reconnection, as outlined above.
Nevertheless, measurements of the
\mathup{{{W}}}
-boson mass in the hadronic channel, without kinematic constraints, will provide complementary results with uncorrelated uncertainties, useful for cross-checking and combination with the measurements in other channels.

Particle reconstruction and flavour identification in jets are important for the event selection and to calibrate and control flavour-dependent effects. In current experiments, novel machine-learning techniques have proven to facilitate unprecedented performance in signal-to-background separation and flavour identification.

If external information about the beam energy is used in the reconstruction of hadronic (
\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}
) or semileptonic (
\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}\ell\\
PGn
)
\mathup{{{W}}}
-pair decays, the hadronic jet energy scale can be constrained by the four momentum conservation in the event, removing the importance of the experimental jet energy determinations.
Still, a precise modelling and control of the hadronic jets boost (
\beta=p/E
) will be essential for precise
m_{\mathup{{{W}}}}
measurements from
\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}
and
\mbox{$\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}$}\ell\\
PGn
events.

In view of the need for extreme precision on jet internal properties such as the boost, it will be highly desirable for detector capabilities to be highly efficient and precise in identifying and measuring all particles inside hadronic jets.
Excellent particle reconstruction capabilities should extend to low momentum particles away from the jet axis, and in the inter-jet regions, where colour reconnection (CR) effects in the
\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}
channel can be determined and constrained
in situ
.

An ultimate aim should be to fit simultaneously
\mathup{{{W}}}\mathup{{{W}}}
,
\mathup{{{Z}}}\mathup{{{Z}}}
and
\mathup{{{Z}}}\gamma
leptonic and hadronic decay modes, in order to extract a determination of the
m_{\mathup{{{W}}}}/m_{\mathup{{{Z}}}}
ratio with potentially large cancellations of most systematic uncertainties, from theory, experiment, and beam energy.

5.2
Precision W-boson coupling measurements

In a future
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
physics program a total of 40-150
10^{6}
W-pair events can be produced, mostly at
\sqrt{s}
= 240–250 GeV and at
\sqrt{s}
= 162 GeV energies.

As the LEP2 program has demonstrated, a very large fraction of the produced W-pair events
can be collected (85-95% efficiency), with low background levels (90–95% purity),
in all decay final states, including fully hadronic
\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}
, semi-leptonic
\mathup{{{l}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}
,
and fully leptonic
\mathup{{{l}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{{l}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}
channels, with
\mathup{{{l}}}=\mathup{{{e}}}
,
\mathup{{{\upmu}}}
and
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
.

The event yields in the
\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}
channel, the three
\mathup{{{l}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}
qq channels, and the six

\mathup{{{l}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{{l}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}
channels can be combined, taking into account their cross-contaminations and correlations, in order to fit the W decay branching ratios, and the total W-pair cross sections.
A fit that does not assume W-lepton coupling universality can be performed to extract the leptonic decay couplings
B_{\mathup{{{e}}}}
,
B_{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}
and
B_{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}
, while a fit that assumes lepton universality can be performed to extract the
hadronic decay coupling
B_{\mathup{{{q}}}}
. In both fits the sum of leptonic and hadronic branching fractions is constrained to unity.
