5.4
Other Z-boson and neutrino interactions

5.4.1
Electron couplings from transversely polarised beams

The investigation of electroweak dipole moments is essential for exploring the internal structure of particles.
These moments can be effectively described by a subset of dimension-six operators in the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT)
[
832
,
408
]
, characterised by flipping fermion chirality.
This property causes dipole operators to contribute to the cross section either quadratically at
\mathcal{O}(1/\Lambda^{4})
or in association with the fermion mass at
\mathcal{O}(1/\Lambda^{2})
, where
\Lambda
denotes the scale of new physics (NP) beyond the Standard Model (SM).
Consequently, constraining the Wilson coefficients of light-fermion dipole operators has proven extremely challenging in current global SMEFT analyses.
To address this issue, we propose incorporating polarised observables associated with the transverse spin of light fermions into such analyses.
As an interference effect between different helicity states, the transverse spin compensates for the helicity-flipping effect from the dipole operators, allowing them to interfere with SM interactions at
\mathcal{O}(1/\Lambda^{2})
without mass suppression or dependence on additional NP effects.
Therefore, this approach will greatly enhance the sensitivity power.

Although the same approach applies to other generations and can be extended to quark dipole moments
[
833
,
834
,
835
]
, we illustrate this idea for the first-generation leptonic dipole operators in the SMEFT
[
836
]
,

\mathcal{L}_{\text{eff}}=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\bar{\ell}_{L}\sigma^{\mu\nu}\left(g_{1}\Gamma_{B}^{e\lx@paragraphsign}B_{\mu\nu}+g_{2}\Gamma_{W}^{\mathup{{{e}}}}\sigma^{a}W_{\mu\nu}^{a}\right)\frac{H}{v^{2}}e_{R}+{\text{h.c.}}

(66)

where we redefine the electron dipole couplings
\Gamma_{\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}}^{\mathup{{{e}}}}=\Gamma_{W}^{e}-\Gamma_{B}^{\mathup{{{e}}}}
and
\Gamma_{\mathup{{{Z}}}}^{\mathup{{{e}}}}=c_{W}^{2}\Gamma_{W}^{\mathup{{{e}}}}+s_{W}^{\lx@paragraphsign 2}\Gamma_{B}^{\mathup{{{e}}}}
in the mass eigenstate basis.
The imaginary parts of these couplings, if nonzero, violate parity and
CP
symmetries.

The dipole couplings
\Gamma_{\mathup{{{Z}}},\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}}^{\mathup{{{e}}}}
are most suitably probed at an
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}
collider with transversely polarised beams, through measurements of the azimuthal distributions in the production of final state
i=\mathup{{{Z}}}\mathup{{{H}}}
,
\mathup{{{Z}}}\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}
,
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{W}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{W}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
, or
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
.
The transverse spin
\bm{s}_{T}=b_{T}(\cos\phi_{0},\sin\phi_{0})
or
\bar{\bm{s}}_{T}=\bar{b}_{T}(\cos\bar{\phi}_{0},-\sin\bar{\phi}_{0})
of the electron or positron, respectively, enters the cross section through off-diagonal elements of the density matrices,

\Sigma^{i}(\phi,\bm{s},\bar{\bm{s}})=\rho_{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{1}^{\prime}}({\bm{s}})\rho_{\alpha_{2}\alpha_{2}^{\prime}}(\bar{{\bm{s}}})\mathcal{M}^{i}_{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}}(\phi)\mathcal{M}_{\alpha_{1}^{\prime}\alpha_{2}^{\prime}}^{i*}(\phi)=\Sigma^{i}_{UU}+b_{T}\Sigma^{i}_{TU}(\phi)+\bar{b}_{T}\Sigma^{i}_{UT}(\phi)+b_{T}\bar{b}_{T}\Sigma^{i}_{TT}(\phi),

(67)

where
\rho(\bm{s})
is the fermion spin density matrix, and
b_{T}

(\bar{b}_{T})>0
denotes the magnitude of the electron’s (positron’s) transverse spin.

\mathcal{M}^{i}_{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}}(\phi)
is the helicity amplitude of
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}_{\alpha_{1}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}_{\alpha_{2}}\to i
, with the azimuthal angle
\phi
defined for either particle in
i
.
Using rotation symmetry, one has
\mathcal{M}_{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}}(\phi)=e^{i(\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2})\phi}\mathcal{A}_{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}}
, where
\mathcal{A}_{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}}=\mathcal{M}_{\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}}(0)
, independent of
\phi
.
Then the azimuthal dependence of the single-spin quantities
\Sigma_{TU,UT}
is,

\Sigma_{TU}=\frac{1}{2}{\operatorname{Re}}\left[e^{i(\phi-\phi_{0})}\left(\mathcal{A}_{+-}\mathcal{A}_{--}^{*}+\mathcal{A}_{++}\mathcal{A}_{-+}^{*}\right)\right],\qquad\Sigma_{UT}=\frac{1}{2}{\operatorname{Re}}\left[e^{i(\phi-\bar{\phi}_{0})}\left(\mathcal{A}_{+-}\mathcal{A}_{++}^{*}+\mathcal{A}_{--}\mathcal{A}_{-+}^{*}\right)\right],

(68)

both yielding characteristic
\cos\phi
and
\sin\phi
distributions that can be observed to probe the dipole couplings
\Gamma_{\mathup{{{Z}}},\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}}^{\mathup{{{e}}}}
, which govern the chirality-flipping amplitudes
\mathcal{A}_{\pm\pm}
.

For simplicity, we integrate over the polar angle and consider only the
\phi
-dependent differential cross section,

\frac{2\pi\,d\sigma^{i}}{\sigma^{i}\,d\phi}=1+A_{R}^{i}(b_{T},\bar{b}_{T};\operatorname{Re}\Gamma_{\mathup{{{Z}}},\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}}^{\mathup{{{e}}}})\cos\phi+A_{I}^{i}(b_{T},\bar{b}_{T};\operatorname{Im}\Gamma_{\mathup{{{Z}}},\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}}^{\mathup{{{e}}}})\sin\phi+b_{T}\,\bar{b}_{T}\,B^{i}\cos 2\phi+\mathcal{O}(1/\Lambda^{4}),

(69)

where the coefficients
A_{R,I}^{i}
depend linearly on
b_{T}
,
\bar{b}_{T}
and the real (
R
) or imaginary (
I
) parts of the dipole couplings
\Gamma_{\mathup{{{Z}}},\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}}^{\mathup{{{e}}}}
, while
B^{i}
is given only by the SM.
It is convenient to extract them by constructing the azimuthal asymmetry observables, dubbed as single transverse spin asymmetries (SSAs),

A_{LR}^{i}\,=\frac{\sigma^{i}(\cos\phi>0)-\sigma^{i}(\cos\phi<0)}{\sigma^{i}(\cos\phi>0)+\sigma^{i}(\cos\phi<0)}=\frac{2}{\pi}A_{R}^{i},\quad A_{UD}^{i}\,=\frac{\sigma^{i}(\sin\phi>0)-\sigma^{i}(\sin\phi<0)}{\sigma^{i}(\sin\phi>0)+\sigma^{i}(\sin\phi<0)}=\frac{2}{\pi}A_{I}^{i}.

(70)

By measuring these observables for the various channels of
i
, one can constrain both the real and imaginary parts of the dipole couplings with linear sensitivity, respectively, as well as the potential
CP
violation.

Figure 60
:
Expected constraints from the spin asymmetry observables on the electron dipole couplings
\Gamma_{\mathup{{{Z}}},\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}}^{\mathup{{{e}}}}
.

We choose the benchmark centre-of-mass energy at
\sqrt{s}=$250\text{\,}\mathrm{GeV}$
with
(b_{T},\,\bar{b}_{T})=(0.8,\,0.3)
and integrated luminosity of
\mathcal{L}=$5\text{\,}{\mathrm{ab}}^{-1}$
.
The beam spin directions can be optimized to maximize the sensitivity, for which we study two scenarios: the aligned spin setup
(\phi_{0},\bar{\phi}_{0})=(0,0)
and the opposite spin setup
(\phi_{0},\bar{\phi}_{0})=(0,\pi)
.
Assuming the experimental measurements centre around the SM prediction, i.e.,
\langle A_{LR,\,UD}^{i}\rangle=0
, we present in
Figure

60
the expected constraints on the dipole couplings at 68% confidence level.
Combining all the four processes allows
\Gamma_{\mathup{{{Z}}}}^{\mathup{{{e}}}}
and
\Gamma_{\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}}^{\mathup{{{e}}}}
to be separated, and yields the same constraints on their real and imaginary parts, with typical upper limits of
\mathcal{O}(0.01\%)
for
\Gamma_{\mathup{{{Z}}}}^{\mathup{{{e}}}}
and
\mathcal{O}(0.1\%)
for
\Gamma_{\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}}^{\mathup{{{e}}}}
.
These limits are significantly stronger compared to other methods applied in Drell–Yan and
\mathup{{{Z}}}
-pole processes, which usually constrain
|\Gamma_{\mathup{{{Z}}},\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}}^{\mathup{{{e}}}}|
to around
\mathcal{O}(1\%)
even when considering one operator at a time.

5.4.2
Flavour changing
Z-boson decays

The SM predicts the branching ratio of
\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{{s}}},\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{{d}}},\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{u}}}
to be strongly suppressed by the GIM mechanism, while the lepton flavour violating processes,
\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}},\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}},\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
, are forbidden. Precise measurements of these decay channels are then highly sensitive to possible New Physics contributions. We parametrise the latter in terms of effective FCNC couplings to the
\mathup{{{Z}}}
boson,

\mathcal{L}\supset\,g_{ij}^{L}(\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}_{i,L}\gamma_{\mu}\mathup{{{q}}}_{j,L})\mathup{{{Z}}}^{\mu}+g_{ij}^{R}(\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}_{i,R}\gamma_{\mu}\mathup{{{q}}}_{j,R})\mathup{{{Z}}}^{\mu}\,,

(71)

where
ij=\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{{s}}},\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{{d}}},\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{u}}}
, with analogous definitions for lepton flavour-changing couplings. This Lagrangian can be obtained as the low-energy realization of various extensions of the SM, e.g. the addition of vector-like quarks
[
642
,
643
]
.

In their operational phase at the centre-of-mass energy
\sqrt{s}=$91\text{\,}\mathrm{GeV}$
, corresponding to the
\mathup{{{Z}}}
pole mass, both CEPC and FCC-ee are expecteded to produce
N_{\mathup{{{Z}}}}=$5\text{\times}{10}^{12}\text{\,}\,$\mathup{{{Z}}}
bosons. Considering this impressive statistical yield, the reach for quark decays will be mostly limited by the systematic uncertainties on the tagger performances, while for lepton decays it will depend on the particle identification capability of the detector.

Quarks:

Updated computations yield
[
837
,
838
,
839
,
588
]

{\cal B}(\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{{s}}})=\left(4.2\pm 0.7\right)\times 10^{-8}\,,\quad{\cal B}(\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{{d}}})=\left(1.8\pm 0.3\right)\times 10^{-9}\,,\quad{\cal B}(\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{u}}})=\left(1.4\pm 0.2\right)\times 10^{-18}\,,

(72)

where
{\cal B}(\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{q}}}_{i}\mathup{{{q}}}_{j})={\cal B}(\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}_{i}\mathup{{{q}}}_{j})+{\cal B}(\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{q}}}_{i}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}_{j})
. The reported uncertainties contain both the theoretical uncertainties from numerical inputs and the leading two-loop corrections to the amplitudes.

While existing direct limits on the non-standard hadronic decays of the
\mathup{{{Z}}}
follow from the agreement of the measurement and the SM prediction for the
\mathup{{{Z}}}
hadronic width
[
840
]
, giving
\mathcal{B}(\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{{q}}}^{\prime})<2.9\times 10^{-3}
at
95\,\%\,\mathrm{CL}
, the low-energy constraints are much more powerful. The effective couplings in
Equation

71
will contribute to a wide range of observables, as D and B meson mixings, leptonic and semi-leptonic decays. In particular, for
\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{{d}}}
and
\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{{s}}}
, these transitions essentially constrain the New Physics effect in flavour changing processes to be well below the SM value; thus the limit on direct observations of these branching ratios is at the moment the SM value itself, within uncertainties. For the
\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{u}}}\mathup{{{c}}}
decay instead, we obtain
{\cal B}(\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{u}}}\mathup{{{c}}})<4\times 10^{-7}
from the flavour global fit. Additional bounds, although much weaker, can be obtained by rare
\mathup{{{Z}}}
decays to a photon and a vector meson,
\mathrm{\mathup{{{Z}}}\to VM^{0}+\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}}

[
576
,
650
,
487
]
.

At the FCC-ee, the total detector acceptance for hadronic
\mathup{{{Z}}}
decays is estimated to be
\sim 0.994

[
658
]
. Coupled with the accurate mass and energy reconstruction capabilities, this allows most of the background to be removed such that only other SM hadronic decays,
\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{{q}}}
, need to be considered as possible noise signal, where one of the two jets is mistagged. We therefore employ an identical analysis to the case of Higgs flavour-changing decays
[
477
,
651
,
652
,
588
]
, including the same jet-flavour tagger performances (see
Equation

47
and the discussion in
Section

4.3
). Analogously, backgrounds from processes where a double mistag is needed to provide a fake signal can also be safely disregarded.
We find that in order to probe the SM value for
{\cal B}(\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{{s}}})
, we would need very performant taggers with very low systematic uncertainties (<0.1%). Similar results hold for
\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{{d}}}
and
\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{u}}}\mathup{{{c}}}
. For
0.1\%
systematic uncertainties, the expected reaches are

{\cal B}(\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{{s}}})<7.33\times 10^{-6}\,,\quad{\cal B}(\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{u}}})<4.06\times 10^{-4}\,.

(73)

One could in principle apply a similar metholodogy to the
\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{{d}}}
channel. However, there is currently not a reliable
\mathup{{{d}}}
-jet tagger. Employing only a
\mathup{{{b}}}
-tagger we obtain the weaker constraint
{\cal B}(\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{{d}}})<2.45\times 10^{-4}
.

Thus we conclude that, for realistic efficiencies and uncertainties, indirect probes set BSM bounds that are much stronger than the projected FCC-ee reach.

Leptons:

As lepton flavour changing decays of the
\mathup{{{Z}}}
are forbidden in the SM, any clear signal would point to the existence of New Physics.
The current direct constraints have been derived from dedicated searches conducted at the LHC by ATLAS
[
841
,
842
]
, resulting in the following limits at 95 % CL:

{\cal B}(\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}})<$5.0\text{\times}{10}^{-6}\text{\,}\,$,\quad{\cal B}(\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}})<$6.5\text{\times}{10}^{-6}\text{\,}\,$,\quad{\cal B}(\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}})<$2.62\text{\times}{10}^{-7}\text{\,}\,$.

(74)

Low energy probes of charged lepton flavour violation, as muon and tau exotic decays (
\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\to 3\mathup{{{e}}}
,
\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\to\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}
,
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\to\mathup{{{\uprho}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}}
etc.), will pose indirect limits on the
\mathup{{{Z}}}
boson off-diagonal couplings
[
843
]
. For the
\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{e}}}
case, these bounds can reach
{\cal B}(\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}})\lesssim${10}^{-13}$
, while in the
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
sector, we have typically
{\cal B}(\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}}/\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\mathup{{{e}}})\lesssim${10}^{-7}$
.

The projected bounds on branching ratios at future circular lepton colliders are
[
844
]
:

{\cal B}(\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}})\lesssim(${10}^{-8}\text{\,}\mathrm{-}$${10}^{-10}\text{\,}\mathrm{)}$\,,\quad{\cal B}(\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}})\lesssim${10}^{-9}\text{\,}\,$,\quad{\cal B}(\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}})\lesssim${10}^{-9}\text{\,}\,$,

(75)

where the range of values for
\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{e}}}
reflects whether or not particle identification via
\text{d}E/\text{d}x
will be available. As expected, these will improve the limits on decays involving the
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
lepton, while for
\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{e}}}
the low energy bounds dominate.
This would lead to the following projected bounds on the lepton flavour-violating
\mathup{{{Z}}}
couplings (see
Equation

71
):

|g^{L,R}_{\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}|\lesssim$3.2\text{\times}{10}^{-3}\text{\,}\,$,\quad|g^{L,R}_{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}|\lesssim$3.7\text{\times}{10}^{-3}\text{\,}\,$,\quad|g^{L,R}_{\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}|\lesssim$7.3\text{\times}{10}^{-4}\text{\,}\,$,

(76)

assuming only one coupling being turned on at time. More detailed studies are warranted, as the very large samples of
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
decays at FCC-ee will allow for significantly improved tests of LFU
[
845
]
.

5.4.3
Z-boson decays in models with right-handed neutrinos

The see-saw type I model
[
846
,
847
,
848
]
is arguably one of the most appealing explanations for neutrino masses. In its simplest incarnation, it extends the SM with right-handed neutrinos
N
of very large mass
m_{N}
, so that a natural mixing between
N
and the SM neutrinos induces, after EWSB, masses for the latter of order
m_{\nu}\sim v^{2}/m_{N}
, with
v
the Higgs VEV.
However, less simple (and perhaps more realistic) realizations of this model allow
N
to be at the EW scale itself
[
849
,
850
]
, and generally involve further heavier particles
[
851
,
852
]
. If both conditions hold, then the physics at current accessible energies is precisely described by the EFT of the SM extended with
N
, also known as NSMEFT
[
853
,
854
,
855
]
. The corresponding Lagrangian reads:

L_{\text{NSMEFT}}=L_{\text{SM}+N}+\frac{1}{\Lambda^{2}}\sum_{i}O_{i}+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{\Lambda^{3}}\right)\,,

(77)

where
\Lambda
stands for the cut-off of the EFT. The operators
O_{i}
span a basis of dimension-6 interactions; they can be found in Ref.
[
856
]
. This theory is well understood theoretically, including its quantum structure. It has been renormalised at one loop in a series of works
[
857
,
858
,
859
,
860
]
, and the matching on to its low-energy version (in which the top quark, the Higgs and the
Z
and
W
bosons are integrated out) is known to tree level
[
861
]
.

Under some mild assumptions
[
862
]
, it can be argued that, for
1\lesssim m_{N}\lesssim 100

\text{\,}\mathrm{GeV}
, and not too a large cut-off (
\Lambda\lesssim 10

\text{\,}\mathrm{TeV}
),
N
decay mostly via loop operators
14
14

14

These are of the form
O_{NV}=\overline{L}\sigma_{\mu\nu}N\tilde{\Phi}V^{\mu\nu}
with
L
and
\Phi
representing the lepton and Higgs doublets, respectively, and with
V
being either a photon or a
Z
boson.
following
N\to\\
PGn\\
PGg
and, to a lesser extent, via tree-level four-fermion interactions into
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}
or into quarks. The corresponding widths are of the order
10^{-15}m_{N}^{3}/$\text{\,}\mathrm{GeV}$^{2}
and
10^{-20}m_{N}^{5}/$\text{\,}\mathrm{GeV}$^{4}
; respectively.

Several signatures of the production and subsequent decay of
N
have been explored at colliders, including rare top decays
\mathup{{{t}}}\to N\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{{l}}},N\to\nu\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}

[
863
,
862
]
, rare Higgs decays
\mathup{{{H}}}\to N\nu,N\to\nu\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}
as well as a variety of meson decays, long-lived signals, and others
[
864
,
865
,
866
,
867
,
868
,
869
,
870
,
871
]
. We also find rare
\mathup{{{Z}}}
decays of the form
\mathup{{{Z}}}\to N\mathup{{{\upnu}}}
and
\mathup{{{Z}}}\to NN
. Depending on the
N
decay mode, they give rise to a variety of signals:
\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\\
PGn\\
PGn\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}
,
\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}
,
\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
,
\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
as well as channels with quarks; see Fig.
61
for example diagrams. To the best of our knowledge, none of these modes has been studied either phenomenologically or experimentally. In what follows, we elaborate on the tremendous sensitivity that an
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
collider, operating at the Z pole and producing about
5\times 10^{12}
Z bosons, has to these processes. To this aim, we provide rough numbers for the first three cases. In all cases, we have that
\Delta\Gamma(\mathup{{{Z}}})\sim\frac{m_{\mathup{{{Z}}}}^{3}v^{2}}{\pi\Lambda^{4}}
. Assuming
\mathcal{O}(1)
couplings in the EFT and a
\Lambda=1
TeV, we find the expected branching ratio
\Delta\mathcal{B}(\mathup{{{Z}}})\sim 10^{-3}
.

Figure 61
:
Example diagrams of
\mathup{{{Z}}}
rare decays mediated by a neutral lepton
N
.

For the first mode, the current experimental bound on the corresponding branching ratio, ensuing from monophoton events in
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
collisions at the
\mathup{{{Z}}}
pole by the L3 collaboration
[
872
]
, is
\mathcal{B}(\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{{\upgamma}}})<3.2\times 10^{-6}
. Following this reference, and being rather conservative, we assume an event selection efficiency of
\sim 0.2
(compared with
\sim 0.85
in the aforementioned work) and require
10
observed events. This implies an expected bound at a future
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
facility of
\mathcal{B}(\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\\
PGn\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{{\upgamma}}})\lesssim 10^{-11}
, which amounts to testing
\Lambda\sim 100
TeV.

For the second mode, the current experimental bound on the corresponding branching ratio is
\mathcal{B}(\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}\mathup{{{\upgamma}}})<3.1\times 10^{-6}
. It follows from searches in
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
collisions at LEP by the OPAL collaboration in events with
m_{\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}}=(60\pm 5)
GeV
[
873
]
. Following the same reasoning as for the previous channel (in this case though, the event selection efficiency of the original analysis is
\sim 0.56
), we obtain also
\mathcal{B}(\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\\
PGn\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{{\upgamma}}})\lesssim 10^{-11}
and so again
\Lambda\sim 100
TeV. We find no reason to think that different diphoton mass windows could affect the bound significantly.

For the third mode, the current experimental bound on the corresponding branching ratio can be inferred to be
\mathcal{B}(\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}})\lesssim 6\times 10^{-7}
from current measurements of
\mathcal{B}(\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}})=(4.41\pm 0.30)\times 10^{-6}

[
874
]
. (For comparison, the SM prediction is
(4.50\pm 0.01)\times 10^{-6}

[
875
]
.) It is hard to extrapolate from this bound, derived from analysis of events produced in a hadron facility, to a future search at a high-energy lepton collider. Still, since the background can be assumed to be negligible to good approximation, it is not unreasonable to expect the corresponding sensitivity to be as strong as in the previous channels.

5.4.4
Four-fermion interactions with neutrinos

Since the explanation of neutrino oscillations requires the neutrino masses to be nonzero, the observation of neutrino oscillations provides a clear evidence of new physics beyond the Standard Model (SM).
A model-independent way of studying new physics in neutrino experiments was given in the effective field theory framework of nonstandard neutrino interactions (NSI); for reviews see Refs.
[
876
,
877
,
878
]
. In this framework, NSI are typically described by dimension-six four-fermion operators.
The Lagrangian of neutral current (NC) NSI with electrons can be written as,

\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{NSI}}^{\text{N}C,e}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-2\sqrt{2}G_{F}\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}^{eL}(\bar{\nu}_{\alpha}\gamma^{\mu}P_{L}\nu_{\beta})(\bar{e}\gamma_{\mu}P_{L}e)-2\sqrt{2}G_{F}\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}^{eR}(\bar{\nu}_{\alpha}\gamma^{\mu}P_{L}\nu_{\beta})(\bar{e}\gamma_{\mu}P_{R}e)

(78)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle-\sqrt{2}G_{F}\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}^{eV}(\bar{\nu}_{\alpha}\gamma^{\mu}P_{L}\nu_{\beta})(\bar{e}\gamma_{\mu}e)+\sqrt{2}G_{F}\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}^{eA}(\bar{\nu}_{\alpha}\gamma^{\mu}P_{L}\nu_{\beta})(\bar{e}\gamma_{\mu}\gamma^{5}e)\,,

(79)

where

\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}^{eV}\equiv\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}^{eL}+\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}^{eR}\,,\quad\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}^{eA}\equiv\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}^{eL}-\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}^{eR}\,,

(80)

with
\alpha
,
\beta
labeling the lepton flavours (
\mathup{{{e}}},\mathup{{{\upmu}}},\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
), and

\epsilon^{eV}_{\alpha\beta}
(
\epsilon^{eA}_{\alpha\beta}
) describing the
strength of the new vector (axial-vector) interactions between electrons.

NSI with electrons will lead to new contributions to the monophoton process
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}}\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}
at electron colliders. An early study of NSI with electrons using monophoton events at LEP has been given in Ref.
[
879
]
, and constraints on NSI with electrons from neutrino scattering, solar and reactor neutrino experiments are performed in Refs.
[
880
,
881
,
882
]
. A combination of the data from LEP, neutrino scattering, solar and reactor neutrino experiments can be found in Refs.
[
883
,
884
]
.
The
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
collider experiment LEP can help in removing degeneracy in the global analysis of constraints on NSI parameters. Moreover, the current constraints on tau-type NSI with electrons are mainly coming from LEP. However, due to cancellation between the left-handed (vector) and right-handed (axial-vector) NSI parameters, the allowed ranges of NSI with electrons are still large if both the left and right-handed NSI parameters exist. Considering that will provide much more data than LEP, it is necessary to study the constraints on NSI with electrons from the proposed future
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
collider experiments.

Since we simulate the data assuming the SM, the point (0,0) will always be included in the allowed regions. Also, the allowed regions from each running mode will lie between two concentric circles. From Fig. (
62
-
63
), we see that the direction from the SM point (0,0) to the circle centre with
\sqrt{s}=240\ \mathrm{GeV}
is almost parallel to that with
\sqrt{s}=160\ \mathrm{GeV}
, and the allowed regions with
\sqrt{s}=160\ \mathrm{GeV}
can be superseded by
\sqrt{s}=240\ \mathrm{GeV}
in the neighbourhood of the SM point (0,0). For electron-type NSI,
the direction from the SM point (0,0) to the circle centre with
\sqrt{s}=91.2\ \mathrm{GeV}

is approximately perpendicular to that with the other two running modes. Therefore, the allowed parameter space of electron-type NSI is severely constrained by combining the data from three running modes. Even if both
\epsilon_{\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{e}}}}^{eL}
and
\epsilon_{\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{e}}}}^{eR}
are present, the allowed ranges for
|\epsilon_{\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{e}}}}^{eL}|
or
|\epsilon_{\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{e}}}}^{eR}|
can be constrained to be smaller than 0.002.
As for muon-type or tau-type NSI, the direction from the SM point (0,0) to the circle centre with
\sqrt{s}=91.2\ \mathrm{GeV}
is approximately opposite to that with the other two running modes. Hence, the allowed regions will become long ellipses after combining the data from three running modes. If both
\epsilon_{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}},\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}^{eL}
and
\epsilon_{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}},\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}^{eR}
are present, the allowed ranges of muon-type and tau-type NSI are about one order of magnitude weaker than that of electron-type NSI.

In Table

5.4.5
Neutrino anomalous magnetic moment

Experimental evidence from solar and atmospheric neutrino oscillation experiments
[
885
,
886
]
show that at least two neutrino species have mass. If neutrinos are Dirac particles, this observation then allows for the exploration of the magnetic and electric dipole moments of these particles. The corresponding electromagnetic neutrino current
J_{\mu}(x)
projected onto momentum eigenstates gives a matrix element parametrised as

\displaystyle\langle p^{\prime}|J_{\mu}(x=0)|p\rangle=e\penalty\ \bar{\nu}(p^{\prime})\Big(F_{1}(q^{2})\gamma_{\mu}+i\frac{F_{2}(q^{2})}{2m_{\nu}}\sigma_{\mu\nu}q^{\nu}\Big)\nu(p)\,,

(81)

where
e
is the electromagnetic unit charge, and
F_{1}(q^{2})
and
F_{2}(q^{2})
are the electric and magnetic form factors, respectively. These depend on
q^{2}\equiv(p-p^{\prime})^{2}
, with
p
and
p^{\prime}
being the neutrino 4-momenta. The symbol
m_{\nu}
indicates the Dirac neutrino mass and, as usual,
\sigma_{\mu\nu}=i[\gamma_{\mu},\gamma_{\nu}]/2
. Then, in units of the Bohr magneton
\mu_{B}
, the magnetic moment
k
of a neutrino
\nu
is given by

k\mu_{B}=\frac{F_{2}(0)}{2m_{\nu}}\,.

(82)

The present bounds on the magnetic moment of the
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
-neutrino (
k_{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}
) are several order of magnitudes below the corresponding constraints that hold for electron and muon neutrinos
[
595
]
. Experimentally, the neutrino magnetic moment can be directly constrained at collider experiments by analyzing the inclusive production in
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
annihilations of a neutrino pair plus a photon at the
\mathup{{{Z}}}
-boson resonance

\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}}\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}\,.

(83)

For the signal that we seek, the photon (
\gamma
) must be emitted from either of the neutrinos in the final state via the magnetic dipole interaction in
Equation

81
, as shown in the Feynman diagrams (a) and (b) of Fig.
64
.

Figure 64
:
Dominant Feynman diagrams for the processes
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}}\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}
at the
\mathup{{{Z}}}
-boson resonance. The red dots in the diagrams (a) and (b) indicate the vertex induced by the effective neutrino magnetic dipole moment sourced by
Equation

81
.

The differential cross section for the process in
Equation

83
can be approximated as
[
887
]

\displaystyle\frac{\text{d}\sigma}{E_{\gamma}\text{d}E_{\gamma}\text{d}\cos{\theta_{\gamma}}}=\frac{\alpha^{2}k^{2}}{96\pi}\mu_{B}^{2}\penalty\ R(s^{2}_{W})\left(\frac{s-2\sqrt{s}E_{\gamma}+\frac{1}{2}E_{\gamma}^{2}\sin^{2}{\theta_{\gamma}}}{(s-M_{Z}^{2})^{2}+M_{Z}^{2}\Gamma_{Z}^{2}}\right)\,,

(84)

where
\theta_{\gamma}
and
E_{\gamma}
are the scattering angle and energy of the photon in the
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
centre-of-mass (c.o.m.) frame, respectively,
\sqrt{s}
is the c.o.m. energy, and
s_{W}=\sin{\theta_{W}}
, with
\theta_{W}
being the Weinberg angle. The
\mathup{{{Z}}}
-boson mass and width are respectively indicated with
M_{\scriptscriptstyle{Z}}
and
\Gamma_{Z}
, whereas the function
R
is given by

R(x)=\frac{8x^{2}-4x+1}{x^{2}(1-x)^{2}}\,.

(85)

As the flavour of the produced neutrinos cannot be selected, the process is sensitive to the combination
k^{2}\equiv\sum_{\alpha=\mathup{{{e}}},\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}k^{2}_{\alpha}
, where
k_{\mathup{{{e}}},\mathup{{{\upmu}}},\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}
are the magnetic moments of electron, muon, and
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
neutrinos.

By integrating over the scattering angle and using the Breit-Wigner approximation, we obtain the linear dependence of the
\mathup{{{Z}}}
-boson width on the rescaled photon energy, given by

\frac{\text{d}\Gamma}{\text{d}x_{\gamma}}=\frac{\alpha\penalty\ k^{2}M_{Z}^{3}\penalty\ \mu_{B}^{2}}{24\pi^{2}c_{W}^{2}s_{W}^{2}}F(x_{\gamma})\,

(86)

where
c_{W}\equiv\cos{\theta_{W}}
,
x_{\gamma}=E_{\gamma}/M_{Z}
, and
F(x)=x(1-2x+x^{2}/3)
. The distribution
\frac{\text{d}\Gamma}{\text{d}x_{\gamma}}
, shown in Fig.
65
, has a maximum near
E_{\gamma}\simeq 24.4\penalty\ {\textrm{GeV}}
, which is peculiar to the magnetic dipole interactions.

Figure 65
:
The normalised distribution in
Equation

86
as a function of the rescaled energy of the photon
x_{\gamma}=E_{\gamma}/M_{Z}
. Its peculiar shape could allow disentangling the origin of possible excesses measured in the number of mono-photon events.

The process in
Equation

83
consists of a single final-state photon accompanied by missing energy, carried by the neutrinos. The main Standard Model (SM) background for the energy region of interest is given by the Feynman diagrams (c) and (d) in Fig.
64
, in which the emission of a photon is due to the initial
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
states.

The proposal of constraining the magnetic moment of the
\nu_{\tau}

based on single-photon final states was considered in Ref.
[
887
]
, for LEP searches
[
888
,
872
,
889
,
890
]
, and previously in Ref.
[
891
]
in the context of
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
collider experiments at lower energies.

At LEP, the DELPHI
[
888
]
and L3
[
872
]
collaborations analyzed this process at the
\mathup{{{Z}}}
peak to establish one of the most stringent constraints on
k_{\tau}
. More recently, analogous bounds have been investigated in the context of new physics searches at future
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
colliders such as CLIC and ILC
[
892
,
893
,
894
,
895
,
896
,
897
]
.

The L3 analysis
[
872
]
used an integrated luminosity of
{\textrm{L}}_{\textrm{LEP}}=137\penalty\ {\mathrm{p}b}^{-1}
and cuts optimized for a photon energy
E_{\gamma}>15
GeV and scattering angles
20^{\circ}<\theta_{\gamma}<34.5^{\circ}
,
44.5^{\circ}<\theta_{\gamma}<135.5^{\circ}
,
giving a total of 14 events after selections. The result is consistent with the Monte Carlo simulation of the SM expectation due to production of neutrino pairs accompanied by initial-state radiation, radiative Bhabha events and
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}(\mathup{{{\upgamma}}})

[
872
]
, which predicted 14.1 events altogether. Under the assumption of lepton universality in the
Z
decay to neutrinos, this yields the following upper bounds at 90% confidence level (CL) on the magnetic moment of
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
-neutrino
[
872
]

k^{\mathrm{L}EP}_{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}<3.3\times 10^{-6}\penalty\ \penalty\ 90\%\penalty\ {\mathrm{C}L}\,.

We now turn to the prospects for investigating the
\tau
-neutrino magnetic moment through the process in
Equation

83
at the future FCC-ee collider. After running for 4 years at the
\mathup{{{Z}}}
-boson
resonance, the FCC-ee is expected to produce
3\times 10^{12}

\mathup{{{Z}}}
bosons
[
9
,
898
]
, thereby dramatically improving over the statistics limit of the LEP program. The corresponding expected integrated luminosity collected over this period is
{\mathrm{L}}_{\mathrm{F}CC}=150\penalty\ {\mathrm{a}b}^{-1}
.
By using the same kinematic cuts mentioned above that were optimized for L3, the reach of the FCC-ee can be estimated by simply rescaling the LEP bound by the fourth root of the luminosity ratio
({\mathrm{L}}_{\mathrm{L}EP}/{\mathrm{L}}_{\mathrm{F}CC})^{1/4}\simeq 1/31
, giving

k^{\mathrm{F}CC}_{\tau}<1.1\times 10^{-7}\penalty\ \penalty\ 90\%\penalty\ {\mathrm{C}L}\,.

(87)

Presently, the strongest bound on
k_{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}
is given by the DONUT collaboration by analyzing the scattering of
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
-neutrinos on electrons
\nu_{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}\penalty\ \mathup{{{e}}}^{-}\to\mathup{{{\upnu}}}_{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}\penalty\ \mathup{{{e}}}^{-}
, yielding
[
899
,
595
]

k^{\mathrm{D}ONUT}_{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}<3.9\times 10^{-7}\penalty\ \penalty\ 90\%\penalty\ {\mathrm{C}L}\,.

(88)

We stress that the limit in
Equation

88
applies exclusively to
k_{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}
, while the one derived from the process in
Equation

83
includes all the contributions of the three magnetic moments of neutrinos.

In conclusion, after four years of operation at the
\mathup{{{Z}}}
peak, the FCC-ee could offer the possibility of improving the present limit
Equation

88
by a factor of almost 4. This estimate maintains the kinematic cuts used to optimize the L3 analysis at LEP, hence it is plausible that further improvements could be achieved once the FCC-ee detectors and machine will be understood and dedicated kinematic cuts identified.

5.5
Focus Topic:
WW differential measurements

Constraints on gauge boson interactions are essential for global interpretations in both the SMEFT framework and UV-complete models. In scenarios where the electroweak symmetry is linearly realized, new physics contributions to anomalous triple gauge couplings are intrinsically linked to modified Higgs couplings. This connection establishes a profound complementarity between measurements in the gauge and Higgs sectors, enabling a more comprehensive exploration of potential deviations from Standard Model predictions.
In the most general formulation, the vertex between a neutral and two charged electroweak gauge bosons encompasses 14 complex couplings, amounting to 28 real parameters
[
900
]
. Within the SM, only four of these couplings are expected to have values of one, while all remaining parameters are predicted to be zero. Any deviation from this configuration would serve as a precise indicator of physics beyond the SM. Due to the limited constraining power of LEP data on the full set of trilinear gauge couplings (TGCs), the number of parameters traditionally analyzed is substantially reduced by imposing conservation laws such as C, P, and CP invariance, along with electromagnetic gauge invariance and
SU(2)\times U(1)
symmetry. This leaves three independent parameters, commonly taken to be
g_{1,Z}
,
\kappa_{\gamma}
, and
\lambda_{Z}
which are used to define the corresponding Lagrangian

\displaystyle\Delta\mathcal{L}^{\text{aTGC}}=

\displaystyle ie\delta\kappa_{\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}}A^{\mu\nu}W^{+}_{\mu}W^{-}_{\nu}

(89)

\displaystyle+ig\cos\theta_{W}\left[\delta g_{1Z}(W^{+}_{\mu\nu}W^{-\mu}-W^{-}_{\mu\nu}W^{+\mu})Z^{\nu}+(\delta g_{1Z}-\frac{g^{\prime 2}}{g^{2}}\delta\kappa_{\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}})Z^{\mu\nu}W^{+}_{\mu}W^{-}_{\nu}\right]

\displaystyle+\frac{ig\lambda_{\mathup{{{Z}}}}}{m^{2}_{\mathup{{{W}}}}}\left(\sin\theta_{W}W^{+\nu}_{\mu}W^{-\rho}_{\nu}A^{\mu}_{\rho}+\cos\theta_{W}W^{+\nu}_{\mu}W^{-\rho}_{\nu}Z^{\mu}_{\rho}\right).

The sensitivity of the HL-LHC to anomalous triple gauge couplings (aTGC) has been estimated by extrapolating existing differential measurements of the leading lepton transverse momentum in inclusive diboson production
[
901
]
. While the cross-section of inclusive
\mathup{{{W}}}\mathup{{{W}}}
production can be measured with roughly twice the precision compared to
\mathup{{{W}}}\mathup{{{W}}}
electroweak scattering
[
902
]
, both processes provide complementary information. Their combination is a critical input for global EFT fits, enabling a more comprehensive exploration of deviations from Standard Model predictions
[
903
]
.
By taking existing ATLAS and CMS measurements and assuming a 50% reduction in systematic uncertainties, the sensitivity achieved with VBS-only fits at the HL-LHC is projected to surpass current constraints from combined diboson and VBS analyses. For certain EFT operators, improvements of at least a factor of 10 over current bounds are anticipated
[
904
]
.

Numerous studies have examined the potential of future colliders to probe aTGCs. The most comprehensive theoretical analysis —- ignoring effects from detector resolution, backgrounds, or systematic uncertainties -— demonstrates that at a high-energy
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
collider operating at
\sqrt{s}=$500\text{\,}\mathrm{GeV}$
with polarised beams, including transverse polarisation, all 28 real coupling parameters can be disentangled and constrained effectively
[
905
,
906
]
. More recently, the sensitivity to the three couplings of the LEP parametrisation was examined within a SMEFT fit to the Higgs and electroweak sectors, relying on optimal observables at the theory level
[
398
]
. This study projects an improvement in precision exceeding a factor of 100 relative to the HL-LHC. The effects of detector resolution and residual backgrounds on the optimal observable technique were analyzed in Ref.
[
907
]
, showing that while both can introduce significant biases in central values, machine learning techniques can effectively provide the necessary corrections.

Studies incorporating realistic detector simulations have thus far been conducted only for the ILC at
\sqrt{s}=$500\text{\,}\mathrm{GeV}$
and
1\text{\,}\mathrm{TeV}

[
908
,
909
,
910
]
. Due to constraints on
Geant4
-based Monte Carlo simulations at the time, these studies focused exclusively on
\mathup{{{W}}}
-pair production. They analyzed three out of five angular observables within a binned analysis, resulting in highly conservative outcomes. These studies served as inputs for fits conducted in, for example, Ref.
[
911
]
. So far, projections for lower centre-of-mass energies were only derived by interpolating between the
500\text{\,}\mathrm{GeV}
/
1\text{\,}\mathrm{TeV}
projections and actual LEP2 results
[
912
]
, which indicate that at
250\text{\,}\mathrm{GeV}
, sensitivity is expected to degrade by a factor of 4-5 relative to
500\text{\,}\mathrm{GeV}
for the same final states. The inclusion of single-
\mathup{{{W}}}
final states was found to provide a substantial precision gain in the
\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}
channel, with improvements by a factor of 2-3 over analyses limited to
\mathup{{{W}}}
-pair events.

The first comprehensive study addressing experimental uncertainties and their mitigation has been reported in Ref.
[
913
]
. This work demonstrates that by combining data from various 2-fermion and 4-fermion final states, the relevant physics observables (including TGCs as well as forward-backward asymmetries) can be separated from systematic effects—such as those due to luminosity, beam polarisation, energy scale, and detector acceptance—in a combined fit that includes both physics and nuisance parameters. Notably, this approach minimizes the residual impact of systematic uncertainties on the extracted physics observables, particularly when both beams are polarised, thus providing sufficient redundancy across data sets to effectively constrain the fit.

To achieve an improved sensitivity estimate for differential
\mathup{{{W}}}\mathup{{{W}}}
measurements beyond the interpolation approach discussed in Ref.
[
912
]
, dedicated analyses were carried out for ILD at
\sqrt{s}=$250\text{\,}\mathrm{GeV}$
and CLD at
\sqrt{s}=$240\text{\,}\mathrm{GeV}$
. Diboson events were generated using
Whizard

[
42
,
43
]
, processed through
Pythia6

[
46
]
for parton showering, and subsequently passed through the full
Geant4
simulation of the ILD and CLD detectors, respectively.

For the ILC scenario, event samples were obtained from the official mass production campaign
[
914
]
, while for the CLD case, dedicated samples were privately simulated using
DDSim
. Reconstruction for both experiments was performed within the
Marlin
framework, with CLD employing the
Key4hep

Marlin
wrapper
[
915
]
. Event samples were then appropriately mixed and re-weighted to reflect unpolarised data for the FCC-ee case and polarised data for the ILC case.

The analysis examines the sensitivity of five key observables: the production angle of the
\mathup{{{W}}}^{-}
,
\cos\theta_{\mathup{{{W}}}^{-}}
, defined as the angle between the electron beam and the
\mathup{{{W}}}^{-}
, along with the polar and azimuthal angles of the fermion pair in the rest frame of the parent
\mathup{{{W}}}^{-}
or
\mathup{{{W}}}^{+}
. These angular observables are measured in the semi-leptonic decay channel, utilizing the charged lepton and the reconstructed neutrino.

Given the importance of measuring the charged lepton and the increased difficulty in the electron channel thereof, the electron acceptance of the detectors was evaluated in a first step as shown in
Figure

66
.

The extraction of constraints on triple gauge couplings is most effectively performed using optimal observables.
Figure

67
illustrates the expected reconstruction of these optimal observables and compares them to the truth level expectation.
The three observables correspond to the couplings in the LEP parametrisation, which are also used in linear dim-6 SMEFT fits.
As can be seen from the plot, the detector-resolution effects have almost no impact on the size and shape of the ellipses and only introduce a bias to the central values.

The performed studies have successfully set the foundations needed to perform a full optimal observable-based analysis of
\mathup{{{W}}}\mathup{{{W}}}
-pair production. In the signal-only comparison, the optimal observable technique has proven itself to be extremely stable under detector resolution effects. However, we expect additional influence from background contamination in the ongoing full analysis which needs to be quantified before actual projections for further global interpretations will be provided.

5.6
Focus Topic:
Fragmentation and hadronisation

Fragmentation and hadronisation of quarks and gluons are key ingredients for the precision modeling of physics processes.
The issues are entangled, and their systematic uncertainties are expected to be limiting factors in precision Higgs and electroweak measurements at a future Higgs factory. To assess their impact, it is important to review the state of the art, to project how future theory developments could reduce current uncertainties, and to devise ways to constrain fragmentation and hadronisation from measurements at the Higgs factories.

The full QCD description of an event can be split into perturbative and
nonperturbative aspects, although the two are often intertwined.
The former involves matrix elements for the hard process,
parton showers for the subsequent softer emissions, and a consistent
matching and merging of them. Much work is ongoing in extending
matrix elements and showers to higher orders, so improved perturbative
predictions can confidently be foreseen in the years to come, as is
described in
Section

3.2
.

The nonperturbative aspects mainly deal with the hadronisation
of quarks and gluons into primary hadrons, and the subsequent
decays of these primaries into the final-state observable particles.
Hadronisation is typically modelled by string or cluster fragmentation.
A fair amount of studies are ongoing here, not least stimulated by
unexpected LHC observations. This is likely to further our understanding
also for
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
colliders, but in a less easily quantifiable way.
Decays seldom attract much attention, but is not to be dismissed
as trivial. Notably for B hadrons, the lack of measured reasonably
complete decay tables is a problem, exacerbated by the possibility
for a given final state to arise via different interfering intermediate
states.

In the following we will discuss a few of the open questions on the
theory side, along with target observables for experimental exploration.
Notably this includes the target topics of the fragmentation of
\mathup{{{b}}}

quarks into B hadrons and the splitting of gluons into heavy-quark pairs. A related discussion on fragmentation, with special emphasis on strangeness production, can be found in
Section

4.2.4
.

5.6.1
Fragmentation functions

In the high-precision limit, fragmentation functions will not be universal, i.e. they are expected to depend on observables and initial states. It is argued that the factorisation of the perturbative and non-perturbative parts of the problem is not possible without dedicated tuning of free parameters in the required fragmentation model used. There are ongoing developments in disentangling hadronisation and fragmentation, specifically the cross-talk between parton shower and fragmentation. New work is needed for NLL-accurate showers.

There has been a lot of progress recently on the computation of perturbative bottom and charm fragmentation functions (FFs). Heavy quark FFs can be computed
in perturbation theory in QCD, starting from initial conditions at a reference scale
\mu_{0}\sim m_{\text{Q}}
(with
m_{\text{Q}}
the mass of the heavy quark)
and employing the time-like DGLAP evolution equations to evolve them up to any other scale.
Initial conditions for the gluon- and heavy-quark-initiated fragmentation into a
heavy quark are known at order
\alpha_{\mathrm{S}}

[
916
,
917
]
and have been computed at order
\alpha_{\mathrm{S}}^{2}

[
918
,
919
]
.

The time-like DGLAP evolution equation is implemented in public codes such as
QCDnum

[
920
]
,

FFevol

[
921
]
,
APFEL

[
776
]
or
MELA

[
922
]
, up to NNLL logarithmic accuracy.
In Ref.
[
923
]
, the role of gluon-initiated fragmentation to heavy quarks has been considered, and the coupled time-like
evolution of bottom quarks and gluons is considered in detail. This is important as, while at LEP and at Tevatron the

\mathup{{{g}}}\to\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{b}}}}}}}
splitting mechanism was considered subdominant, this is no longer the case at
the LHC. In Ref.
[
924
]
the perturbative component of the fragmentation function of
the
\mathup{{{b}}}
quark to the best of the present theoretical knowledge was presented. The fixed-order calculation
to order
\alpha_{\mathrm{S}}^{2}
of the fragmentation function at the initial scale
[
918
,
919
]
is matched with soft-emission
logarithm resummation to next-to-next-to-leading logarithmic accuracy, so that order-
\alpha_{\mathrm{S}}^{2}

corrections are accounted for exactly, and logarithmically enhanced contributions from
loops of
\mathup{{{b}}}
quarks are included. In Ref.
[
925
]
the perturbative computation of the
\mathup{{{b}}}
-quark fragmentation function at NNLO + NNLL is supplemented
by the fit of the non-perturbative component
\mathup{{{b}}}\to
B hadrons. Similarly, the perturbative component of
\mathup{{{c}}}
-quark fragmentation and the fit of the non-perturbative component
\mathup{{{c}}}\to
D hadrons are discussed in Ref.
[
926
]
. A key question is how can this progress can be implemented in exclusive Monte Carlo simulations.

While perturbative calculations combined with fitted non-perturbative components are adequate for inclusive fragmentation functions, exclusive predictions (e.g. to study the effects of experimental acceptances and cuts) require a different approach:
parton showers are needed
for the perturbative step, and fragmentation
models for the non-perturbative one. These two steps are intertwined and convolved in a complicated space of momenta and colours, so that fragmentation in general cannot be described as a convolution of a
perturbative state and a fragmentation function
f(z)
with
0<z<1
.
In string fragmentation, the colour strings stretched between partons can be attached so as to pull a heavy hadron either to
a lower or to a higher momentum than the mother quark, depending on the string topology at hand
[
927
]
. Thereby
also
z>1
becomes possible, which for some observables can have a significant impact relative to naive expectations. Similar considerations also exist for cluster fragmentation models.

(a)(b)(c)

Figure 68
:
(a)
x
spectra of
\mathup{{{b}}}
quarks and B hadrons.
(b) The average hadron-to-parton
x
ratio as a function of
the parton
x
.
(c) The B hadron spectrum when
0.78<x_{\mathup{{{b}}}}<0.80
.

To illustrate the nontrivial behaviour of String Fragmentation (SF) and
Cluster Fragmentation (CF), in the context
of fragmentation functions, a simple study of
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{Z}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{b}}}}}}}

at the
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{Z}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}
peak, using
Pythia
8.312 is shown here.
Initial-state
QED radiation is switched off, so that the CM frame is well-defined.
The few events where there have been
\mathup{{{g}}}\to\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{b}}}}}}}
branchings
are rejected. In the others, the respective primary daughter B
hadron is identified.

Now study energy fractions
x=x_{E}=2E/E_{\text{CM}}=2E/m_{\mathup{{{Z}}}}
,
or momentum ditto
x=x_{p}=2|\mathbf{p}|/m_{\mathup{{{Z}}}}
.

Figure

68
(a) shows the
x
spectra of the
\mathup{{{b}}}
quarks
and the B hadrons, normalised to unit area. The B hadrons are
softer than the
\mathup{{{b}}}
quarks, as expected. But next consider,
for each
\mathup{{{b}}}
–B pair, the ratio
z=x_{\text{B}}/x_{\mathup{{{b}}}}
, and plot
its average value
\langle z\rangle
as a function of
x_{\mathup{{{b}}}}
,

Figure

68
(b). Already here we see an environment effect,
that hadronisation “slows down” a high-energy
\mathup{{{b}}}
,

\langle z\rangle<1
, but “speeds up” a low-energy one,

\langle z\rangle>1
. In an Independent Fragmentation (IF) approach one would expect the
z

ratio always to be below unity, and
\langle z\rangle
to be constant.

To further zoom in on the role of the environment, now only consider
the
\mathup{{{b}}}
quarks in a narrow bin
0.78<x_{\mathup{{{b}}}}<0.80
,
near the peak of the
x_{\mathup{{{b}}}}
spectrum. Draw a cone of
size
\theta=0.5
(on the unit sphere) around the
\mathup{{{b}}}
quark. Sum up
the background energy
E_{\text{cone}}
, being that of all final
partons inside this cone, except for the
\mathup{{{b}}}
itself, and
scale it to an
x_{\text{cone}}=2E_{\text{cone}}/m_{\mathup{{{Z}}}}
.
Define clean (inside-the-cone) background events as those where

x_{\text{cone}}<0.05
and dirty background ones as those having

x_{\text{cone}}>0.15
. Then compare the
x_{\text{B}}
spectra for the
clean and dirty cases,
Figure

68
(c). As foretold, the dirty
environment offers a larger pool of nearby energy, some of which
can be absorbed back into the B hadron during the hadronisation
process, giving a harder B hadron than in the clean case.

Unfortunately,
Figure

68
(c) is contingent on knowing the
partonic state before hadronisation, both that of the
\mathup{{{b}}}
quark and that
of the surrounding region. It does not directly translate into
observables in the hadronic final state.

5.6.2
Gluon splitting

The splitting of gluons into
\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{b}}}}}}}
or
\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{c}}}}}}}
is only modeled in the perturbative step of the process (not in the string/cluster fragmentation) but still, charm and bottom masses are parameters in the shower. Other relevant differences may be in the treatment of the strong coupling differently for heavy quarks or (massless) gluons in the limit of
p_{\text{T}}=0
. Separation of
h\to
gluons from
h\to\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{b}}}}}}}/\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{c}}}}}}}
(
\sqrt{s}=m_{\mathup{{{Z}}}}
and beyond) is affected.
Details are described in Ref.
[
928
]
.

5.6.3
Improved hadronisation models

Hadronisation, the conversion of an entire partonic ensemble of particles with individual colour charges into an observed ensemble of hadrons is a complex process. Within the string or the cluster model, conversion to hadrons takes place after the parton shower and accounts for the local colour connections. colour reconnection can re-distribute momenta in between colour connected subsystems. For the current status of hadronisation and colour reconnection in multi-purpose event generators we refer to the respective release notes and references therein
[
532
,
48
,
94
]
.

The recent development of hadronisation models highlights the interplay with perturbative evolution, in momentum as well as in colour space
[
529
,
747
,
748
,
533
,
929
]
and can be confronted with full-
N_{c}
parton evolution
[
930
,
931
]
, as well as higher-logarithmic accuracy parton showering
[
170
,
173
,
172
,
171
,
932
,
933
]
in order to reduce uncertainties of the combined description of infrared sensitive observables. Interesting connections also arise in the context of interpreting the parton shower infrared cutoff as a factorization scale
[
749
,
934
]
.

Putting such constraints on hadronisation models raises the question whether they would be flexible enough to describe a wealth of current data, such that these developments should be complemented, and can profit from, machine-learned modeling of the same effect
[
935
,
936
,
937
,
938
,
939
]
, which will not necessarily provide a direct measure of the theoretical uncertainty but can help to constrain building blocks in newly developed models. A number of additional observables able to constrain hadronisation models have also been discussed at earlier ECFA workshops
[
940
]
as well as at the recent Parton Shower and Resummation workshop
[
941
]
. At any rate, hadronisation models predict a richer phenomenology than would be captured by fragmentation functions alone and so should be confronted with existing and novel measurements to further constrain their respective components and the cross talk with modern parton shower algorithms.

5.6.4
Colour reconnection

Colour reconnection (CR) is a common name for mechanisms that lead
to colour flows that are not expected at first sight. For lepton
colliders the main impact is that seemingly separate colour singlet
systems get to be intertwined. The prime example here is
\mathup{{{W}}}
pair
production,
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{W}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{W}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to(\mathup{{{q}}}_{1}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}_{2})(\mathup{{{q}}}_{3}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}_{4})
, where by
CR the fragmenting systems instead are
\mathup{{{q}}}_{1}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}_{4}
and
\mathup{{{q}}}_{3}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}_{2}
.
Such effects were observed at LEP 2, favouring a CR rate of approximately 50%, but unfortunately low statistics did not make for high significance

[
743
]
. Studies for future
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
colliders can be found
e.g. in Ref.
[
942
]
.

Many different CR models have been proposed. Some common physics
components used in the modelling, singly or in combination, include:

•

Reduction of string length, cluster masses or some other
“free energy” measure, whereby also the average hadron multiplicity
is reduced.

•

Physical space–time overlap of the hadronising systems. The further
above threshold a
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{W}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{W}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
pair is, the faster the two move apart, and the
less the likelihood of overlapping. If nevertheless there is a CR,
the effect on that event could be larger, however.

•

Consistent colour assignments in an
N_{C}=3
setup, whereby
only some reconnections become allowed.

Further principles and models may be foreseen in the future, not least
driven by LHC studies.

In addition to primary
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{W}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{W}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
and
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{Z}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{Z}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}
production,
also Higgs decays to
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{W}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{W}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
and
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{Z}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{Z}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}

pairs can be relevant, e.g. to search for any CP-odd admixture in
the Higgs, where CR can affect the angular correlations used to
probe for such effects. The
\mathup{{{t}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{t}}}}}}}
process with hadronic decays
involves three singlets, and thus the possibility of increased effects.
Effects of CR with rapidity gaps in hadronic multi-jet events at the
\mathup{{{Z}}}
pole have been studied
with LEP data
[
943
,
944
,
945
,
946
]
, yielding measurements of CR effects below the predictions of available models.
Future large
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
data samples at the Z pole will be very useful to refine such measurements and constrain CR models.

Bose–Einstein effects among final-state hadrons is another area
where colour singlets could get mixed up. No such interconnection
effects were found at LEP 2, but the issue should be kept open.

5.6.5
Relevance for the physics program of a Higgs/Top/EW Factory

Jets and in particular heavy-flavour jets play an important role in many of the flagship measurements of Higgs/Top/EW Factories. As examples, we highlight here the connection to other ECFA Focus Topics:

Precise study of
\mathup{{{h}}}\rightarrow\mathup{{{g}}}\mathup{{{g}}}/\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{b}}}}}}}/\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{c}}}}}}}
:

Future Higgs Factories will provide sensitivity to these topologies providing capabilities to fully explore the second generation of Yukawa couplings, which is out of reach at the LHC. However, current uncertainties in gluon splitting into heavy quarks would introduce large systematic uncertainties in the measurements. The questions arising are: how to consistently implement gluon splitting in parton shower tools (modeling and free parameters) and how to evaluate the impact of incomplete modeling of the gluon splitting when determining the
\mathup{{{h}}}\rightarrow\mathup{{{g}}}\mathup{{{g}}}/\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{b}}}}}}}/\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{c}}}}}}}
couplings.
This issue is discussed in
Section

4.2
.

Precise determination of W mass and cross section:

\mathup{{{W}}}
mass measurements at future Higgs factories are expected to deliver statistical accuracies at the sub-MeV level exploiting the W-pair threshold cross section lineshape
[
738
,
265
]
.
Alternative measurements from the kinematic reconstructuon of
\mathup{{{W}}}
-pair decay products
also have the potential to achieve MeV-level precision on
m_{\mathup{{{W}}}}
, but for this method
the control of systematic uncertainties will be crucial. At LEP2, the modeling of non-perturbative QCD effects in W boson
hadronic decays was a dominant source of systematic uncertainties. Further theoretical and experimental studies are required to estimate the size of such uncertainties at future colliders.
This issue is discussed in
Section

5.1
.

\mathup{{{Z}}}
– b/c couplings:

What would be the impact of these uncertainties on the extraction of
\mathup{{{Z}}}
–b/c couplings at the
\mathup{{{Z}}}
pole? In Ref.
[
947
]
it is demonstrated that hadronisation uncertainties have a significant impact on determinations of the partial widths normalised to total hadronic width (
R_{\text{b,c}}
), the forward-backward asymmetries (
A_{\text{FB}}^{\text{b,c}}
), or left-right asymmetries at
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
colliders, even after application of cuts to reduce their impact. The size of these uncertainties could be a limiting factor when operating at the
\mathup{{{Z}}}
pole in the high-luminosity scenarios of FCC-ee.
This issue is discussed in
Section

5.3
.

One can try to classify events into most likely history and study the relative composition of (a) two separate hard processes (MPIs, pp only); (b) one hard process and one gluon split; (c) two gluon splits on the same side of the event; and (d) two gluon splits on opposite sides.
