Future
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
facilities, such as CEPC and
FCC-ee, running at the

\mathup{{{Z}}}
pole with an integrated luminosity of
{\cal O}(10-100\penalty\ \text{ab}^{-1})
, are also considered. The sensitivity to Rayleigh focusing on a direct
signal from mono-photon searches in Drell–Yan production leads to the strongest limits on
the scale
\Lambda
for light DM masses.
In the case of a muon collider (
\mu
C) operating at

\sqrt{s}=10
TeV with 10 ab
-1

of integrated luminosity,
both Drell–Yan production and the VBS process
\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\to\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\phi\phi
were considered, requiring the detection of forward muons
with high pseudo-rapidity up
to
\eta
= 7. The sensitivity is maximized by focusing on the invariant mass of the “missing”
four-momentum calculated from the difference between the momentum of the initial state and that of the observables final
states in acceptance.

In addition to collider tests, the role of direct and indirect DM detection experiments in this scenario has been also considered.
Direct detection provides the most stringent limits on elastic spin-independent (SI) WIMP-nucleon cross sections
for dark matter masses ranging from a few GeV to tens of TeV. The LUX-ZEPLIN-2022 (LZ-2022)” experiment is the
leading direct detection experiment, but the Rayleigh DM benchmark remains elusive due to loop-suppressed
interactions with quarks and gluons. Looking at the SI limits and predictions for the Rayleigh differential
cross section bounds are given using data from LZ-2022 and projections from XLZD. Indirect
detection is also promising as DM can annihilate into gauge boson pairs,
which decay into stable SM particles. Focusing on the photon flux from DM annihilation bounds are set using
FERMI-LAT measurements of galactic diffuse emission and future projections for CTA.
More detailed results are presented in Ref.
[
1305
]
.

8.7.5
Leptophilic dark matter

Thermal freeze-out is the only dark matter (DM) production mechanism that is insensitive to unknown high-energy physics above the scale of the DM mass.
Over the past several decades, this mechanism has primarily been associated with the WIMP paradigm within a 10 GeV – 10 TeV mass window.
However, the absence of a verified WIMP signal motivates broadening the search effort outside this mass window and to a wider range of interactions.
In many studies, the most promising DM discovery channel is missing energy in association with a single SM object
X
(typically a single jet or gauge boson).
However, if DM couples preferentially to heavy flavour, there may be additional signals that improve upon the mono-
X
strategy, offering more handles for both signal detection and background rejection.
For example, DM that couples mainly to
\mathup{{{b}}}
-quarks, motivated by the galactic-centre excess, can be probed using
\mathup{{{p}}}\mathup{{{p}}}\to\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{b}}}}}}}\not{E}
production.This strategy can readily be adapted to leptophilic DM that couples primarily to muons and taus.
Production of DM is therefore accompanied by additional charged leptons, whose presence may enhance signal sensitivity.
The future collider discovery potential for models of leptophilic dark matter with mass-proportional
couplings to Standard Model leptons was investigated in Ref.
[
1306
]
.
The representative benchmark scenario consists of a Majorana fermion DM candidate
\mathup{{{\upchi}}}
with mass
m_{\mathup{{{\upchi}}}}

coupled to a
C\!P
-even scalar mediator

\varphi
with mass
m_{\varphi}
via

{\cal L}_{int}=-\frac{g_{\mathup{{{\upchi}}}}}{2}\varphi\mathup{{{\upchi}}}\mathup{{{\upchi}}}-\varphi\!\sum_{\mathup{{{l}}}=\mathup{{{e}}},\mathup{{{\upmu}}},\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}\!g_{\mathup{{{l}}}}\,\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}}}\mathup{{{l}}},\penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ \penalty\ g_{\mathup{{{l}}}}=g_{\mathup{{{e}}}}m_{\mathup{{{l}}}}/m_{\mathup{{{e}}}},

(108)

where
g_{\mathup{{{\upchi}}}}
and
g_{\mathup{{{l}}}}
are respectively the Yukawa couplings to DM and charged leptons
\mathup{{{l}}}
. The mass
proportionality in
g_{\mathup{{{l}}}}
can naturally arise in a Type-III two-Higgs doublet model supplemented with the singlet
scalar
\varphi
if the latter mass-mixes primarily with the heavy
C\!P
-even eigenstate H and has suppressed mixing
with the SM-like 125 GeV eigenstate h.
For thermal freeze-out to be predictive and testable with laboratory measurements, the cross section
for DM annihilation must depend on the
\varphi
coupling to the SM, i.e. annihilation cannot occur strictly in the
dark sector. This requirement is readily achieved by demanding

m_{\varphi}>m_{\mathup{{{\upchi}}}}
, so that the

\varphi\varphi\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
topology
is kinematically allowed for all
\mathup{{{l}}}
satisfying
m_{\mathup{{{\upchi}}}}>m_{\mathup{{{l}}}}
.
During freeze-out, the process

\mathup{{{\upchi}}}\mathup{{{\upchi}}}\to\varphi^{*}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}

directly annihilates DM into SM leptons to yield the observed relic density
\Omega h^{2}=0.120\pm 0.001
.
Since the cross section for this process depends on the coupling between
\varphi
and charged leptons, there is a
minimum value required for viable freeze-out. Thus, a thermal origin through the direct annihilation predicts a minimum signal yield for DM production at
e_{+}e^{-}
colliders via

\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\varphi
.
For
m_{\varphi}>2m_{\mathup{{{\upchi}}}}
the mediator decays predominantly invisibly to dark matter, so the process has
a signature of
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}E^{\text{miss}}
.

Since the
\varphi
coupling to the
\tau
is
enhanced by a factor of
(m_{\tau}/m_{e})^{2}\sim 10^{6}
, the signature

\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\varphi\penalty\ \penalty\ ,\penalty\ \penalty\ (\varphi\to\mathup{{{\upchi}}}\mathup{{{\upchi}}})
,
is considered, where the invisibly decaying mediator is produced as final state radiation and predicts deviations within well-measured SM uncertainties.
From the uncertainty of LEP measurement of the di-tau partial width

\Gamma({Z\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}})=84.08\pm 0.22\,\mathrm{MeV}

the value of
g_{\tau}
at each value of
m_{\varphi}
that satisfies

\Gamma(Z\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\varphi)=2(0.22\,\mathrm{MeV})

is extracted and translated into a constraint on

y\equiv(g_{\mathup{{{e}}}}/\mathup{{{e}}})^{2}\alpha_{\mathup{{{\upchi}}}}(m_{\mathup{{{\upchi}}}}/m_{\varphi})^{4}

for a given choice of
\alpha_{\mathup{{{\upchi}}}}\equiv g_{\mathup{{{\upchi}}}}^{2}/(4\pi)
and
m_{\mathup{{{\upchi}}}}/m_{\varphi}
ratio. The parameter
y
is useful because it has a one-to-one relationship with the total annihilation cross section, independently of the
m_{\phi}/m_{\chi}
or
g_{\chi}/g_{e}
ratios. In Fig.
155
, this constraint bounds the area shaded in grey and labeled as “LEP”.

9
Flavour Physics

9.1
Introduction

Measurements in flavour physics have paved the way to the Standard Model (SM) as we know it to date. The GIM mechanism was inspired by studies in the kaon sector, namely the observation of the rarity of the Flavour Changing Neutral Current (FCNC) process
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{K}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{L}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
; the GIM mechanism yielded in turn to the prediction of the charm quark
[
1307
]
; the observation of
C\!P
violation in 1964
[
1308
]
suggested the existence of a third generation
[
1309
]
; and the first measurements of
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}-\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}
oscillations in 1986 immediately indicated the top quark to be massive (
m_{\mathup{{{t}}}}>50
GeV)
[
1310
]
, well before its discovery.
The discoveries of the top quark and the Higgs boson provided a complete formulation of the SM. Yet, the mass matrices and the mass mixing matrices do not receive a dynamical explanation in the SM and pose questions that are intimately connected to flavour physics and acknowledged as the Flavour puzzles: Why three generations? What explains the observed hierarchy in the fermion masses? What explains the distinctive structure of the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix? Is the SM
C\!P
violation enough to describe the matter-antimatter asymmetry of the universe?

In a bottom-up approach, flavour physics can be seen as a powerful tool of discovery of physics beyond the SM.
The constrained structure dictated by gauge invariance, combined with the peculiar values observed for the Yukawa couplings, endows the SM with a set of accidental properties and approximate symmetries.
A consequence is that some processes are very suppressed or entirely forbidden, such as FCNC transitions and lepton-flavour violating (LFV) decays. Those same accidental properties and symmetries are in general not respected by extensions of the SM and therefore one can expect new physics to induce large contributions to those rare or forbidden processes.
In this context, measuring them indirectly probes the effects of new physics up to very large mass scales, which in some cases exceed by many orders of magnitude any scale that could be reached with present or planned future colliders (e.g. meson mixing, rare kaon or
\mathup{{{B}}}
-meson decays, LFV decays of muons and taus, electric dipole moments, etc.).

The current flagship experiments for quark flavour physics are LHCb at the Large Hadron Collider and Belle II operating in the
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
environment at the
\mathup{{{\Upupsilon}}}(4S)
resonance. These experimental programs are planning upgrades that span over the next two decades, which will keep the field of beauty, charm, and
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
physics vibrant.

We start in
Section

9.2
by setting the context of the experimental study of rare/forbidden processes from the persective of their potential in probing new physics.
In
Section

9.3
we address the anticipated potential of these experimental programmes and compare the attributes of the different experimental environment at
\mathup{{{p}}}\mathup{{{p}}}
and
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
colliders for flavour physics, distinguishing the physics interest of an electroweak factory (
\mathup{{{Z}}}
pole and
\mathup{{{W}}}\mathup{{{W}}}
threshold).
The prospects for improvement in the knowledge of the CKM profile(s) are examined in
Section

9.4
.
The potential to study rare decays of heavy-flavoured particles is considered in
Section

9.5
.
The
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
physics prospects at a future
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
electroweak factory are described in
Section

9.6
.
The detector requirements necessary to achieve the physics objectives will be spelled out when available in these sections. Eventually,
Section

9.7
the possible interplays between a flavour physics programme and the rest of programme of a Higgs, top and electroweak factory, be they related to the experimental tools or the interpretation of the future results.

Some of the studies described here require a high-luminosity run at the
\mathup{{{Z}}}
pole, providing several
10^{12}

\mathup{{{Z}}}
bosons, like proposed at FCC-ee or CEPC. We call such runs “Tera-
\mathup{{{Z}}}
”, unless the studies are specifically done in the context of one accelerator or proposed detector design.

9.2
The new physics perspective and UV models

While the hierarchy problem remains the best motivation for new physics at scales
M_{\text{NP}}\sim 1\penalty\ $\text{\,}\mathrm{TeV}$
, precision flavour measurements push the effective scale of new physics contributing to FCNC and
C\!P
-violating processes to much higher scales.
As mentioned in the Introduction, the reason why rare SM processes are such powerful probes of new physics is their suppression in the SM due to loop, CKM, and other suppression factors.

Let us assume that one is able to measure the Wilson coefficient describing the short-distance SM contribution,
C_{\text{SM}}^{\text{FCNC}}\sim G_{F}\lambda_{\text{SM}}
(here
\lambda_{\text{SM}}
represents the product of all suppression factors while
G_{F}
is the Fermi constant), with a relative precision
\delta
.
Heavy new physics contributing to the same FCNC process can also be parametrised in terms of a Wilson coefficient corresponding to a short-distance operator,
C_{\text{NP}}^{\text{FCNC}}\sim c^{\text{FCNC}}/M_{\text{NP}}^{2}
(where
M_{\text{NP}}
represents the new physics mass scale and
c^{\text{FCNC}}
depends on the dynamics by which it mediates the rare process).
In many cases the reach can be estimated simply as

C_{\text{NP}}^{\text{FCNC}}\lesssim C_{\text{SM}}^{\text{FCNC}}\times\delta\penalty\ ,\quad\rightarrow\quad M_{\text{NP}}/\sqrt{c^{\text{FCNC}}}\gtrsim(\delta\times G_{F}\lambda_{\text{SM}})^{-1/2}\penalty\ .

(109)

From this expression it is clear that, for a given precision
\delta
on the SM contribution, the rarer the SM process is (i.e. the smaller
\lambda_{\text{SM}}
) the larger will be the new physics scale
M_{\text{NP}}
that one is sensitive to.

The tension between the requirements of
(i)
a low new physics scale
M_{\text{NP}}\sim 1\penalty\ $\text{\,}\mathrm{TeV}$
that addresses the Higgs hierarchy problem and
(ii)
strong constraints from flavour physics that push the corresponding scale to large values,
M_{\text{NP}}/\sqrt{c^{\text{FCNC}}}\gg 10\text{--}100\penalty\ $\text{\,}\mathrm{TeV}$
, is known as the new physics flavour problem.
It dictates that any TeV-scale solution to the hierarchy problem has a special flavour structure, i.e. that the new physics affecting FCNC processes should be suppressed, or in other words that
c^{\text{FCNC}}\ll 1
.

“Minimal flavour violation” (MFV) is one such structure, whereby the BSM couples flavour-universally at leading order,
c_{ij}\sim\delta_{ij}
, and the SM Yukawas are the only sources of flavour violation
[
1311
]
. But because MFV new physics couples strongly to valence quarks, such states are now subject to strong LHC bounds, typically
M_{\text{MFV}}\gtrsim$10\text{\,}\mathrm{TeV}$
.
Alternative flavour hypotheses in which the third generation couplings
c_{33}
are disentangled from universal light generation couplings can give just as good flavour suppression
[
1312
]
. This “
U(2)
-like” scenario has two notable differences to MFV:
(i)
if
|c_{11}|,|c_{22}|\ll|c_{33}|=\mathcal{O}(1)
, LHC bounds can be as weak as
M_{U(2)}\gtrsim$1.5\text{\,}\mathrm{TeV}$

[
1047
]
, and
(ii)
the flavour non-universal new physics might simultaneously explain the SM flavour puzzle.

9.2.1
Flavour deconstruction models

In this section we focus on a class of theories that realise the
U(2)
-like hypothesis, wherein part of the SM gauge symmetry is “flavour-deconstructed”. The FCC-ee or CEPC proposals would bring spectacular improvements for precision tests of this scenario, through the complementarity and reach of its electroweak and flavour programs. The present study was done in the context of FCC.

The basic hypothesis is that a SM gauge interaction
G
is resolved into three copies
G_{i}
, one for each generation and with the Higgs coupled only to
G_{3}
. This symmetry, which
arises e.g. from gauge-flavour unification
[
1313
]
, is broken to the SM in two steps, with
G_{1}\times G_{2}\to G_{12}
at

G_{12}\times G_{3}\to G
at
v_{23}\sim 1\text{--}10\penalty\ $\text{\,}\mathrm{TeV}$
; each step delivers a multiplet of heavy gauge bosons in the adjoint of
G
, denoted
X_{12}
and
X_{3}
, with flavour non-universal couplings.
While the third generation Yukawa couplings are unsuppressed, the light Yukawa couplings arise from higher-dimension operators suppressed by heavy mass scales in the model.

Summary.

Flavour deconstructing an electroweak force offers a path to solving the flavour puzzle with a rich phenomenology whose effects cannot be decoupled from electroweak physics. FCC-ee is a powerful machine for probing these theories by achieving comparable sensitivity across diverse measurements traditionally separated into “electroweak” and “flavour” categories, but whose effects in such flavour models are tied together.
Viewing the electroweak and flavour programmes of FCC-ee together, and in combination with high-
p_{\text{T}}
and low-
p_{\text{T}}
HL-LHC data, is therefore crucial to understanding its full power.

9.3
Anticipated theoretical and experimental landscape at the dawn of future colliders

Flavour physics (in particular beauty, charm, and of
\tau
leptons studies) is a vibrant field of study, with the current flagship experiments being LHCb at the Large Hadron Collider, and Belle II at the SuperKEKB collider, featuring
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}
collisions at the
\mathup{{{\Upupsilon}}}(4S)
. Acknowledging the current LHC planning and plans for upgrade, the second part of the 2030 decade will see the operation of the second upgrade of LHCb, which aims at accumulating an integrated luminosity of 300 fb
-1
. This experiment shall collect a dataset 50 times larger than those so far analysed
[
1324
]
. The ATLAS and CMS experiments will continue to contribute strongly to the LHC flavour programme in selected areas, for example the measurement of the weak mixing phase
\phi_{s}
and the studies of
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
and
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{s}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
. The Belle II experiment aims at integrating around 50 ab
-1
, with prospects of further running under discussion. In parallel to the great steps forward in experimental knowledge these projects will bring, one expects corresponding advances in lattice QCD calculations, and the development of other theoretical tools.

Figure

156
shows a possible anticipated status of the Unitarity Triangle after LHCb Upgrade II operation, based on results from that experiment alone and assuming that all results will be in agreement for the sake of an illustrative reference. It should be noted that this analysis assumed in addition plausible lattice QCD improvements
[
1324
]
. High precision will be similarly achieved in the studies of “rare decays”, i.e. suppressed flavour-changing neutral-current (FCNC) processes, featuring either semileptonic or radiative decays.

9.3.1
Expected precision from lattice QCD

The lattice regularisation of QCD allows for
nonperturbative-physics contributions to SM processes to be computed from first principles, i.e., starting from the QCD Lagrangian without any model assumptions.
The lattice-regularised path integral is integrated by means of Monte-Carlo sampling, and the UV and IR regulators given by the lattice spacing and finite volume, respectively, are removed by taking the continuum and infinite-volume limits. Lattice QCD has come a long way since the first numerical simulations in the 1980s within the quenched approximation (only gluonic vacuum-polarisation effects), to simulations of the full QCD path integral including
\mathup{{{u}}},\mathup{{{d}}},\mathup{{{s}}},\mathup{{{c}}}
valence- and sea-quark, as well as
\mathup{{{b}}}
valence-quark effects.
At the level of the effective electroweak theory, nonperturbative QCD effects in flavour physics can be computed as matrix elements of electroweak effective operators between initial and/or final hadronic states.
The summary tables at the beginning of the Flavour Lattice Averaging Group (FLAG) review
[
1327
,
1328
,
1329
,
1330
,
1331
]
provide an overview over results with reliable control over uncertainties, that are of direct relevance for the phenomenology of the SM.
The FLAG review provides results for meson and baryon form factors, for the strong coupling constant and quark masses, which can only be computed with systematically improvable errors within lattice QCD.

Recent developments and opportunities

QCD+QED+strong isospin:
The majority of results in the FLAG review are based on isospin-symmetric QCD, neglecting QED effects — an approximation valid to the level of about 1%. However, as the precision for some quantities within this approximation has now reached below 1%, QED and strong isospin-breaking effects can no longer be ignored. Thanks to recent progress on formal aspects
[
1332
,
1333
,
1334
,
1335
,
1336
,
1337
,
1338
,
1339
,
1340
,
1341
]
, algorithms and computing infrastructure
[
1342
,
1343
]
, we can now make predictions for SM parameters, hadron spectra and leptonic meson decay within QCD+QED. Work is underway to include QED effects also in other observables such as semileptonic decays
[
1344
]
or scattering
[
1345
]
.

2nd-order weak processes:
The past years have seen new developments
[
1346
,
1347
,
1348
,
1349
,
1350
,
1351
,
1352
,
1353
,
1354
,
1355
]
towards computing long-distance contributions to rare decays such as
\mathup{{{K}}}\to\mathup{{{\uppi}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}(\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}})
,
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{K}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{L}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}

[
1356
]
, or
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{s}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}

[
1357
]
. There remain open questions, such as controlling the contributions from multi-particle intermediate states, but we expect these to be tackled in the coming years.

Reconstruction of the spectral density:
Finding ways to reconstruct the spectral density from Euclidean correlation functions has recently become a vibrant research topic
[
1358
,
1359
,
1360
,
1361
,
1362
,
1363
,
1364
]
. For instance, a first prediction of the ratio
R
related to the hadronic vacuum polarisation has been made
[
1365
]
. Spectral reconstruction methods appear particularly attractive for
processes with multi-hadron in or out states, such as hadronic inclusive decays of the tau lepton
[
1366
,
1367
]
and of mesons
[
1361
,
1368
,
1369

1370

. The latter development, for the first time, provides a clear path towards a lattice-computation for inclusive
\mathup{{{B}}}_{(\mathup{{{s}}})}
and
\mathup{{{D}}}_{(\mathup{{{s}}})}
decays on the lattice. This, in turn, allows one to be optimistic that resolving the persistent
V_{\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{b}}}}
and
V_{\mathup{{{u}}}\mathup{{{b}}}}
puzzles can be achieved in the next decade.

C\!P
-violation searches:
A first full computation of the indirect
C\!P
-violation parameter
\epsilon_{\mathup{{{K}}}}
was published last year
[
1348
]
. Entering this result are novel techniques for determining the long-distance contribution to the amplitude of
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{K}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}-\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{K}}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}
mixing, as well as the
\mathup{{{K}}}\to(\mathup{{{\uppi}}}\mathup{{{\uppi}}})_{I}
amplitude in the
I=0
and
I=2

\mathup{{{K}}}\to\mathup{{{\uppi}}}\mathup{{{\uppi}}}

[

,
1372
]
. Initial steps towards computing hadronic
\mathup{{{D}}}
decays have also been reported on
[
1373
,
1374
]
, providing a pathway for lattice QCD to contribute to the search of
C\!P
violation in the charm sector.

Heavy quarks on the lattice:
Simulating both light quarks (which requires a large volume to suppress finite-volume effects) and heavy quarks (which requires a fine lattice spacing to suppress discretization effects) presents significant challenges in lattice QCD. For the heavy
\mathup{{{b}}}
quark in particular, effective actions have to be employed, such as NRQCD
[
1375
]
, RHQ
[
1376
]
or the Fermilab action
[
1377
]
. Alternatively, one must rely on a heavy-quark-mass extrapolation when simulating multiple heavy quark masses relativistically, an often more costly but systematically improvable approach that is starting to be employed by some precision calculations
[
1378
,
1379
,
1380
,
1381
,
1382
,
1383
,
1384
]
. Recent computations
[
1385
,
1386
]
have pioneered an interpolation between relativistic heavy quarks and static quarks to the physical
m_{\mathup{{{b}}}}
mass, showing promising reductions in systematic errors compared to previous methods.

Multi-hadron weak decays:
Multi-hadron final states in weak decay transitions can be addressed in Lattice QCD using a dedicated finite-volume formalism
[
1387
,
1388
,
1389
,
1390
,
1391
]
. Initial applications have focused on the computations of radiative decays
[
1392
,
1393
,
1394
]
, and progress reports have appeared on the
\mathup{{{B}}}\to\mathup{{{\uppi}}}\mathup{{{\uppi}}}\mathup{{{l}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}
decay
[
1395
]
. Advances are also being made in the study of weak decays involving
\mathup{{{N}}}\pi
final states
[
1396
,
1397
]

Computing

For most of the time since the first simulations of lattice QCD in the 1980s, the continued push to ever increasing computing resources has roughly followed Moore’s law. Extreme-scaling is now pushing the boundaries of computing power. Lattice QCD is ideally suited for this development. At the core of the numerical problem is the discretised Dirac operator, which is a sparse matrix, ideally suited for data parallelism. The field is prolific in adapting to new computing paradigms in terms of software and algorithm development
[
1342
,
1343
]
. As a result, the quality of simulations will continue to improve, allowing to further reduce statistical errors and better control systematic uncertainties.
The continuum limit of lattice QCD is defined at a Gaussian fixed point of the theory. As a result, simulation algorithms cease to be ergodic, an effect known as critical slowing down
[
1398
,
1399
,
1400
]
.
Ideas have been developed to mitigate the problem, however critical
slowing down is still limiting fully ergodic simulations well below a
lattice spacing of 0.04 fm.
Novel directions like normalising-flow-based sampling
[
1401
,
1402
]
are attracting attention. Making progress towards finer lattice spacings is particularly important for the study of QCD observables involving the heavier
\mathup{{{c}}}
and
\mathup{{{b}}}
quarks.
Substantial formal and numerical efforts are invested also into quantum computing
[
1403
]
. While current activities mainly concentrate on understanding how QFTs including QCD can be implemented on a quantum computer, this novel computing resource could in the future, when larger systems become available, provide for a step change in lattice-QCD predictions.

Outlook

The last decade has seen enormous progress in the scope and quality of lattice-QCD computations with relevance for testing the SM. The increasingly precise predictions for hadronic matrix elements are crucial input to the interpretation and full exploitation of results from current experiments (e.g. LHCb, CMS, ATLAS, Belle II, BES-III) and ones from future large facilities. The tremendous progress in lattice-QCD computations of the hadronic vacuum-polarisation contribution to the muon
g-2

[
1404
,
1405
,
1406
,
1407
,
1408
,
1409
,
1410
,
1411
,
1412
,
1413
,
1414
,
1415
,
1416
,
1417
,
1418
,
1419
,
1420
,
1421
]
, and the impact this is making on how we look at this decade-old puzzle (and potentially resolve it), and how this is reshaping the field, is an excellent example show-casing the importance and relevance of lattice QCD now, and going forward. The field has reached an impressive maturity, is diverse and vibrant, and continues developing clever new ideas to extend its reach.

9.4
CKM profile prospects

9.4.1
Global analyses: new physics in neutral meson mixings

Experiments at a high-luminosity
\mathup{{{Z}}}
factory can perform sensitive studies of
C\!P
-violating phenomena by making use of the abundant production of boosted
\mathup{{{b}}}
-flavoured hadrons (
{\cal O}(10^{12})
), complemented by a flavour-tagging efficiency close to the one obtained at
\mathup{{{B}}}
-factories. This will allow for improved knowledge of the Unitarity Triangle angles
\alpha
,
\beta
and
\gamma
, as well as the phase
\phi_{\mathup{{{s}}}}
between mixing and decay in the
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{s}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}-\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{s}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}
system. Considerations about the sample sizes suggests that it will be possible to measure the relevant observables with similar or better precision than previous experiments, as reported in Ref.
[
736
]
. This is particularly prominent with the studies of modes containing neutrals, with much larger sample sizes than will be available at Belle II, and better precision and efficiencies than at LHCb. As a case in point, a wide range of charm-meson decay modes in measurements of
C\!P
asymmetries in
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to\mathup{{{D}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{K}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
(where
\mathup{{{D}}}
stands for a superposition of
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{D}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}
and
\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{D}}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}
) and
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{s}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{D}}}_{\mathup{{{s}}}}^{(*)\pm}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{K}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{\mp}}}
are therefore accessible and can provide an enhanced knowledge of the CKM angle
\gamma
. Similar considerations apply to time-dependent measurements, where exciting possibilities include modes relevant for the angle
\alpha
(time-dependent
C\!P
asymmetries in
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uppi}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uppi}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}
).

It is however quite possible that the most significant impact of a future
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
collider in the study of the CKM profile(s) will come from
C\!P
-conserving observable measurements. Let’s consider the results of a model-independent study of possible BSM contributions to the
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}-\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}
and
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{s}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}-\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{s}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}
mixing amplitudes, reported in Ref.
[
1422
]
. This class of phenomena is governed in the SM by box diagrams carrying
C\!P
-violating phases, in which heavy particles (
\mathup{{{W}}}
and
\mathup{{{t}}}
) are contributing. It constitutes therefore a natural entry point for any heavy degrees-of-freedoms from BSM physics and can serve as a figure of merit to assess the potential bottlenecks in precision for future machines. In Ref.
[
1422
]
, the mixing amplitudes are modelled with complex numbers of modulus
h_{\mathup{{{q}}}}
(
\mathup{{{q}}}=\mathup{{{d}}},\mathup{{{s}}}
), each multiplying the SM
\mathup{{{B}}}^{0}_{\mathup{{{q}}}}
mixing Hamiltonian matrix element. Figure
157
shows the constraints on these BSM parameters (assuming the SM value for the sake of an unambiguous interpretation) for four scenarios: current measurements, the anticipated precision from the first LHCb upgrade and Belle II experiments’ measurements, the anticipated precision measurements from the second LHCb Upgrade (together with the more speculative Belle III programme) and finally including those additional measurements from a
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
Higgs/top/electroweak factory including the magnitude of the CKM element
V_{\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{b}}}}
from
\mathup{{{W}}}
decays. The projected performance at Belle II and LHCb are based on the numbers reported in Refs.
[
1324
,
1423
]
, complemented with reasonable assumptions concerning progress in lattice QCD
[
460
]
. Their values are kept the same in the fourth scenario.

{centering}

Figure 157
:

Sensitivity to
h_{\mathup{{{d}}}}-h_{\mathup{{{s}}}}
parameters in
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}
and
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{s}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}
mixing
with (top left) current sensitivity appropriately rescaled to SM values, (top right) the anticipated constraints after LHCb Upgrade I and Belle II operation, (bottom) with the second LHCb Upgrade (together with the more speculative Belle III program), and (bottom right) with improved
V_{\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{b}}}}
precision from
\mathup{{{W}}}

) contours. All plots are made with the SM inputs
h_{\mathup{{{d}}}}=h_{\mathup{{{s}}}}=0.

[

]
.

Despite the expected large sample sizes of LHCb and Belle II and the precision of the
C\!P
-violating observables entering in this global analysis, two factors are limiting the sensitivity to the BSM parameters in Fig.
157
.

•

the precision of the CKM element
V_{\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{b}}}}
, normalising the sides of the Unitarity Triangle, is limiting the sensitivity to the BSM parameters in Fig.
157
. The CKM element
V_{\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{b}}}}
precision comes from measurements of semileptonic
\mathup{{{B}}}
decays, either with inclusive or exclusive decays. In both cases, a hadronic form factor input, e.g. from lattice QCD, is required for
|V_{\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{b}}}}|
to be determined. Another approach that has no such systematic limitation will open up with the several
10^{8}

\mathup{{{W}}}
-boson decays that can be produced at a future
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
collider. This avenue will be explored in greater details in the next section.

•

Lattice QCD computations are required as well (and without an alternate determination in that case) to interpret the oscillation frequencies. These concerns the decay constants and bag factors hadronic mixing parameters. Given the importance of these inputs in order to maximally use the precision of the
C\!P
-violating observables in the global CKM profile test, a section of this report specifically discusses the challenges that lattice QCD precision must meet to match the necessary precision.

9.4.2
\mathup{{{B}}}_{(\mathup{{{u}}},\mathup{{{c}}})}^{+}\to\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}
leptonic decays as probes of
|V_{\mathup{{{u}}}\mathup{{{b}}}}|
,
|V_{\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{b}}}}|
and new physics.

Lepton flavour universality in quark transitions is an important test of the SM. Measurements of tree-dominated observables as the ratio of the semileptonic branching fraction
{\cal R}(\mathup{{{D}}}^{(\ast)})
are reported by experiments at the LHC and
\mathup{{{B}}}
-factories
[
1424
,
1425
,
1426
]
, yielding a longstanding
3\sigma
deviation from SM predictions.
The large
\mathup{{{b}}}
-hadron samples provided by high-luminosity
\mathup{{{Z}}}
runs combined with exquisite vertex resolution gives access to permille-level precision in the determination of
{\cal R}(\mathup{{{X}}})
ratios of
\mathup{{{B}}}\to\mathup{{{X}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}
to
\mathup{{{B}}}\to\mathup{{{X}}}\mathup{{{l}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}
branching fractions
[
1427
]
, improving with respect to the potential of LHCb
[
1428
]
and Belle II
[
1429
]
.

As counterpart of the same
\mathup{{{b}}}\to\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\nu
quark transition, the measurement of the branching fraction BR
(\mathup{{{B}}}_{\mathup{{{q}}}}^{+}\to\mathup{{{\uptau}}}^{+}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}_{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}})
(
\mathup{{{q}}}=\mathup{{{c}}},\mathup{{{u}}}
) can provide an independent way to determine BSM couplings. This has been studied in the context of low-energy EFT
[
1430
]
, providing constraints on the axial and pseudoscalar Wilson coefficients of the transition
\mathup{{{b}}}\to\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}
.
The branching fractions of these leptonic decays BR
(\mathup{{{B}}}_{\mathup{{{q}}}}^{+}\to\mathup{{{\uptau}}}^{+}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}_{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}})
are furthermore sensitive to the magnitude of the CKM elements
|V_{\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{b}}}}|
and
|V_{\mathup{{{u}}}\mathup{{{b}}}}|
. Since these observables are only dependent on the decay constants, which are quite accurately determined by lattice QCD computations, they can contribute to understand and solve the longstanding inclusive vs exclusive puzzle
[
1431
,
1432
]
, with a tension of
3.3\sigma

[
1433
]
.

Prospective studies of these leptonic decays
[
1434
,
1435
]
are conducted at FCC-ee in its
\mathup{{{Z}}}
-pole operation, assuming a total of
6\times 10^{12}

\mathup{{{Z}}}
bosons. The branching fraction precision, from idealistic to pessimistic estimates, are ranging from 1.8% to 3.6% for the
\mathup{{{B}}}^{+}\to\mathup{{{\uptau}}}^{+}\nu_{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}
decay channel and from 1.6% to 2.3% for the
\mathup{{{B}}}_{\mathup{{{c}}}}^{+}\to\mathup{{{\uptau}}}^{+}\nu_{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}
decay channel. A similar sensitivity
is achieved in studies at CEPC
[
1427
]
.

The
|V_{\mathup{{{u}}}\mathup{{{b}}}}|
determination corresponding to the
\mathup{{{B}}}^{+}\to\mathup{{{\uptau}}}^{+}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}_{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}
result is reported in the left plot of
Figure

158
, illustrating the potential for a resolution of the inclusive vs exclusive puzzle. The
|V_{\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{b}}}}|
estimate is not provided as the extraction depends on the production fraction of the
\mathup{{{B}}}_{\mathup{{{c}}}}^{+}
meson, where no measurement is currently available.

As far as the BSM interpretation is concerned, both
\mathup{{{B}}}^{+}\to\mathup{{{\uptau}}}^{+}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}_{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}
and
\mathup{{{B}}}_{c}^{+}\to\mathup{{{\uptau}}}^{+}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}_{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}
are used to set constraints on Wilson coefficients
of the effective Hamiltonian

\displaystyle\mathrm{BR}(B_{q}^{+}\to\tau^{+}\nu_{\tau})=\mathrm{BR}(B_{q}^{+}\to\tau^{+}\nu_{\tau})^{\mathrm{SM}}\times\left|1-\left(C^{q}_{V_{R}}-C^{q}_{V_{L}}\right)+\left(C^{q}_{S_{R}}-C^{q}_{S_{L}}\right)\dfrac{m_{B_{q}}^{2}}{m_{\tau}(m_{b}+m_{q})}\right|^{2}\,,

(110)

which can also be expressed in terms of common combinations
C^{q}_{A}\equiv C^{q}_{V_{R}}-C^{q}_{V_{L}}
and
C^{q}_{P}\equiv C^{q}_{S_{R}}-C^{q}_{S_{L}}
.
The right plot of
Figure

158
shows an example of the constraints on the
C^{c}_{S_{L}}
coefficient from the
\mathup{{{B}}}_{c}^{+}\to\mathup{{{\uptau}}}^{+}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}_{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}
measurement.

9.4.3
Focus Topic:
Measuring
|V_{\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{b}}}}|
and
|V_{\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{s}}}}|
from
\mathup{{{W}}}
decays

Future
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
Higgs factories, such as FCC-ee, CEPC, and ILC, present a unique opportunity to significantly enhance the precision in measuring the absolute values of specific CKM matrix elements, particularly
|V_{\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{b}}}}|
and
|V_{\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{s}}}}|

[
1422
,
1437
,
1438
,
1439
]
. These advancements are possible due to the production of large datasets of
\mathup{{{W}}}\mathup{{{W}}}
boson pairs, expected to reach the order of a few
\times 10^{8}
, combined with state-of-the-art jet-flavour tagging techniques.

The decay of
\mathup{{{W}}}
bosons into quark pairs,
\mathup{{{W}}}\to\mathup{{{u}}}_{i}\mathup{{{d}}}_{j}
, offers a direct method to measure CKM elements from the branching ratios of these processes. The decay width for these channels can be expressed as

\Gamma(\mathup{{{\mathup{{{W}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\to\mathup{{{u}}}_{i}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{d}}}}}}}_{j})=3|V_{ij}|^{2}\Gamma_{0}\equiv\Gamma^{+}_{ij}\,,

(111)

where
\Gamma_{0}\approx\frac{g_{2}^{2}m_{W}}{48\pi}
at leading order, with
g_{2}
being the
\text{SU}(2)_{L}
coupling constant and
m_{\mathup{{{W}}}}=80.4
GeV the mass of the
\mathup{{{W}}}
boson. The factor of 3 accounts for the number of quark colours. This relation holds for both
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{W}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}
and
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{W}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
decays, allowing for a precise extraction of CKM elements by comparing the observed branching ratios to theoretical predictions.
Neglecting small quark-mass effects, the branching ratio of a specific channel can be expressed as
[
954
,
1438
]

\mathcal{B}_{ij}=\frac{\Gamma_{ij}^{\pm}}{\Gamma_{\text{tot}}}=\frac{|V_{ij}|^{2}}{\sum_{l=\mathup{{{u}}},\mathup{{{c}}};\penalty\ m=\mathup{{{d}}},\mathup{{{s}}},\mathup{{{b}}}}|V_{lm}|^{2}}\mathcal{B}_{\text{had}}\,,

(112)

where
\mathcal{B}_{\text{had}}
represents the well-measured total hadronic branching fraction of the
\mathup{{{W}}}
boson. A precise measurement of
|V_{\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{s}}}}|
is particularly important to reduce the parametric uncertainties in the extraction of the QCD coupling
\alpha_{S}
via hadronic
\mathup{{{W}}}
boson decays, and reach a
\mathcal{O}(0.1\%)
uncertainty on this SM parameter
[
954
]
.

Projected Sensitivity at FCC-ee and Systematic Uncertainties

Early studies at FCC-ee suggested that the relative precision on
|V_{\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{b}}}}|
could reach approximately 0.4% using previous BDT-based ILD jet-tagging performances as a reference
[
1422
]
. More recent evaluations have improved these estimates to about 0.15% with optimized GNN-based IDEA performance data
[
1437
]
. However, achieving these precision levels will depend critically on controlling systematic uncertainties, particularly those related to jet-flavour tagging.

A detailed analysis of the impact of systematic uncertainties on the tagging efficiencies, denoted as
\delta_{\epsilon}=\delta\epsilon/\epsilon
, indicates that these uncertainties play a crucial role in limiting the achievable precision on CKM elements
[
1438
]
.
The calibration of the flavour tagging is discussed in more detail in
Section

9.4
. Figure
159
(left) illustrates the sensitivity reach for
|V_{\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{s}}}}|
and
|V_{\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{b}}}}|
, in the
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to\mathup{{{W}}}\mathup{{{W}}}\to 4j
channel at FCC-ee, as a function of the systematic uncertainty in tagging efficiency. It highlights the importance of maintaining systematic uncertainties near the 0.1% level to fully exploit the statistical power of future data. With this level of systematic uncertainties the projected precision could reach 0.15% for
|V_{\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{b}}}}|
and 0.05% for
|V_{\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{s}}}}|
, to be compared with current precisions of 3.4% and 0.6%, respectively.

.

Precision and calibration for the determination of CKM matrix elements from
\mathup{{{W}}}
decays

Flavour tagging is discussed extensively in
Section

3.7.6
.
The understanding of the flavour tagger has been identified as a dominating systematic uncertainty in the determination of CKM matrix elements from
\mathup{{{W}}}
decays, hence precise calibration is key. Both circular and linear machines benefit from dedicated Z-pole running that allows determination of the flavour tagging efficiencies to a sub-permille precision, with the ILC projected to produce some
10^{9}
Z bosons, and FCC-ee and CEPC reaching
10^{12}
Z bosons.
This, however, requires the extrapolation of the calibration results from the Z-pole to the W threshold or the Higgs production energy of 250/240 GeV, whose kinematics are slightly and considerably different, respectively.
It remains subject of further studies to show that this is feasible at the required level of precision.

ILC/ILD Studies and Complementary Approaches

A study utilizing the large ILD 250 GeV full-detector simulation sample and an ILC beam spectrum is currently still ongoing.
The effort focusses on the capabilities of new machine learning-based tagging methods like ParticleNet and Particle Transformer, which enhance flavour identification efficiencies.
While the ILC is expected to produce similar samples of
\mathup{{{W}}}
bosons as FCC-ee and CEPC, the systematic uncertainty from jet-flavour tagging may be slightly larger due to the absence of a Tera-
\mathup{{{Z}}}
run for calibration. Nevertheless, the ILC remains a significant player in the precise measurement of CKM elements and can still provide competitive sensitivity for
|V_{\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{b}}}}|
and
|V_{\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{s}}}}|
.

CEPC Studies and Semileptonic Channels

In a complementary approach, recent studies with the CEPC baseline detector have focused on the semileptonic channel,
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to\mathup{{{W}}}\mathup{{{W}}}\to\mathup{{{l}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{b}}}
, at
\sqrt{s}=240
GeV
[
1439
]
. Using full detector simulations, these studies have projected a relative statistical sensitivity of 0.34% for
|V_{\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{b}}}}|
in an unpolarised scenario with 20 ab
-1
of integrated luminosity.
The study considers a conservative and an optimistic scenario for the combined systematic uncertainties, at 1.5% and 0.2%, respectively. This is summarised in
Figure

159
(right), where results are also extrapolated to different collider running scenarios. While the conservative scenarios would typically not be able to resolve the
|V_{\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{b}}}}|
tension between inclusive and exclusive measurements, the optimistic scenarios would. The comparison also highlights to sensitivity of the WW production to beam polarisation: The polarised scenario with 2 ab
-1
provides about the same statistical precision as the unpolarised one with 5 ab
-1
.

Conclusion

Future
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
colliders hold great promise for advancing our understanding of the CKM matrix, particularly for
|V_{\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{s}}}}|
and
|V_{\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{b}}}}|
, with potential precision improvements by an order of magnitude over current measurements. Achieving these goals will require controlling systematic uncertainties, particularly those related to jet-flavour tagging, and continuing to develop advanced machine learning techniques for event reconstruction.

9.4.4
Measuring
|V_{\mathup{{{t}}}\mathup{{{s}}}}|
from
\mathup{{{t}}}\to\mathup{{{W}}}\mathup{{{s}}}

The current best determination of
|V_{\mathup{{{t}}}\mathup{{{s}}}}|
comes from
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{s}}}
–
\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{s}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}
mixing, which is mediated by box diagrams with top quarks and W bosons.
The PDG
[
1444
]
value is

\displaystyle|V_{\mathup{{{t}}}\mathup{{{s}}}}|=(41.5\pm 0.9)\times 10^{-3},

(113)

which is based on the lattice QCD calculations of the bag parameters and decay constants
[
1445
]
.
The theory uncertainty from lattice QCD is the dominating uncertainty in this measurement, outweighing the experimental uncertainty, from the
\Delta m_{\mathup{{{s}}}}
measurement
[
1444
]
, by about 50 times.
Furthermore, the calculation on the loop-induced process assumes no new physics (NP) in the loop and is therefore model-dependent.

A direct measurement of
|V_{\mathup{{{t}}}\mathup{{{s}}}}|
would therefore be extremely valuable to reduce the model-dependence of the indirect one and to cross-check lattice QCD results.
The proposed
\mathup{{{t}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{t}}}}}}}
operation of FCC-ee at 365 GeV is expected to yield about 2M
\mathup{{{t}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{t}}}}}}}
events, in which the decay chain of top quarks can be fully reconstructed and the final state jet flavour can be identified with excellent efficiency.
Such a dataset presents the opportunity to directly measure
|V_{\mathup{{{t}}}\mathup{{{s}}}}|
via the
\mathup{{{t}}}\to\mathup{{{W}}}\mathup{{{s}}}
decay for the first time.

Jet reconstruction and jet flavour identification is the core of this work.
For jet reconstruction, two clustering algorithms are tested for this analysis: the exclusive jet clustering (
\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{e}}}
-
k_{\text{T}}
, or Durham, algorithm) and the inclusive jet clustering (
\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{e}}}
generalized
k_{\text{T}}
algorithm), both provided by the
FastJet
package
[
1446
]
.
The inclusive jet algorithm with radius parameter
R=0.5
is found to provide a good profiling of jet energy and well-defined true jet flavour, and is consider as the nominal jet definition for this analysis.

The default flavour tagging algorithm at FCC-ee
[
807
]
is based on ParticleNet
[
1447
]
.
The training is performed on 240 GeV
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to\mathup{{{Z}}}\mathup{{{H}}}
,
\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\nu\nu,\mathup{{{H}}}\to\mathup{{{g}}}\mathup{{{g}}}
or
\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{{q}}}
events, where
\mathup{{{q}}}=(\mathup{{{u}}},\mathup{{{d}}}),\mathup{{{s}}},\mathup{{{c}}},\mathup{{{b}}}
, with
\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{e}}}
-gen-
k_{\text{T}}
jets.
As the jets in this analysis feature a different momentum range and potentially a different clustering algorithm from the jets used for the training, the tagging performance
is sub-optimal compared to the reference.
In the current analysis, we apply the sub-optimal tagger as-is.
Retraining the taggers with
365\text{\,}\mathrm{GeV}
samples can potentially improve the tagging performance.

The
\mathup{{{t}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{t}}}}}}}
events can decay to several distinct final states.
This analysis targets 4 event categories: the “dileptonic" category, “semileptonic heavy" category, where the hadronic W decay is
\mathup{{{W}}}\to\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{s}}}
, the “semileptonic light" category, where the hadronic W decay is
\mathup{{{W}}}\to\mathup{{{u}}}\mathup{{{d}}}
, and the fully hadronic category, here also referred to as “dihadronic" category.
The event categories are defined by the number of leptons and jets in the event. Electrons and muons with energy
>

20\text{\,}\mathrm{GeV}
and relative isolation
<
0.25 are considered as (hard) leptons in this analyses.
The inclusive jet algorithm with R5 clustering is chosen for the nominal jets, with additional selections of
m_{j}<

50\text{\,}\mathrm{GeV}
and
E_{j}>

15\text{\,}\mathrm{GeV}
. All electrons and muons with energy
>

10\text{\,}\mathrm{GeV}
are masked from the jet clustering.

In each event category, further selections are applied to refine signal purity. The jet with the highest s-tagging score is chosen as the signal jet candidate. The signal extraction is performed using two approaches: fitting the s-tagging score of the signal jet candidate (in a cut-based approach) and fitting an MVA discriminator trained on the full event kinematics. The MVA approach shows better results in the dileptonic and semileptonic-heavy categories and is chosen as the final fit approach. In the semileptonic-light and fully hadronic categories, no significant improvement is seen for the MVA approach and the cut-based analysis is used for the final result.

The binned maximum-likelihood fit is performed with the CMS
Combine
tool
[
1448
]
. The fit results are summarized in
Table

40
.
As the total
\mathup{{{t}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{t}}}}}}}
cross section can be measured very precisely at FCC-ee, the measurement on the
\mathup{{{t}}}\to\mathup{{{W}}}\mathup{{{s}}}
signal yield can be converted to a measurement on
\mathcal{B}(\mathup{{{t}}}\to\mathup{{{W}}}\mathup{{{s}}})
and therefore a determination of
|V_{\mathup{{{t}}}\mathup{{{s}}}}|
.
With
\sigma(\mathup{{{t}}}\to\mathup{{{W}}}\mathup{{{s}}})\approx 15\%
, the precision on
|V_{\mathup{{{t}}}\mathup{{{s}}}}|
is expected to be about 7.5%.

9.5
Rare decays of
\mathup{{{b}}}
- and
\mathup{{{c}}}
-flavoured particles

As described in
Section

9.2
, rare decays offer unique opportunities to test the SM and probe possible new physics contributions up to effective scales much higher than those explored directly at high-energy colliders.

The experimental study of rare FCNC decays requires a very large sample of meson decays (due to the rarity of the processes), very good detector capabilities to disentangle the small signal from possibly large backgrounds, and good control over both experimental systematics and theoretical uncertainties to minimise the relative uncertainty
\delta
.
The large dataset expected at FCC-
\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{e}}}
or at CEPC (expecting
6\text{\times}{10}^{12}\text{\,}

\mathup{{{Z}}}
bosons), coupled with excellent vertexing and clean experimental conditions, provides a robust setting for probing rare decays with high precision.

In the following we describe some studies of expected sensitivities for a representative sample of rare
\mathup{{{B}}}
-meson decays. A study of semileptonic transitions
\mathup{{{b}}}\to\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
and
\mathup{{{b}}}\to\mathup{{{d}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
with light lepton flavours is provided first to illustrate the typical sensitivity for these modes. This section will then focus on the potential reach of the study of third generation couplings transitions that are unique to these facilities.

9.5.1
Time-dependent precision measurement of the
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{s}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{\upphi}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}}
decay

In this section we investigate the time-dependent
C\!P
violation in the rare decay
{\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{s}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{\upphi}}}(\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{K}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{K}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}})\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}}
at the
\mathup{{{Z}}}
-pole run of the FCC-ee.
Such processes offer a unique opportunity to probe NP, especially through precise
C\!P
violation measurements
[
1449
,
1450
,
1451
,
1452
,
1453
,
1454
]
.
This analysis focuses on measuring the time-dependent
C\!P
asymmetry with key observables such as
D_{\text{f}}
,
S_{\text{f}}
and
C_{\text{f}}
, which are crucial for determining
C\!P
violation. These measurements offer insight into both the SM predictions and possible deviations due to NP contributions, which can be parametrised through Wilson coefficients in the Weak Effective Theory (WET) framework
[
1455
]
. More details can be found in Ref.
[
1456
]
.

Analysis

To model the decay
{\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{s}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{\upphi}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}}
, we use a combination of Monte Carlo event generators and detector simulations. The signal and background events were simulated using the
Pythia8

[
48
]
event generator at the
\mathup{{{Z}}}
pole, and the detector effects were accounted for using
Delphes

[
404
]
with the IDEA detector concept
[
438
,
335
]
. The IDEA detector features a highly precise vertex tracker and an advanced particle identification system, which are crucial for reconstructing the final states and distinguishing signal from background. The signal sample is generated with
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{b}}}}}}}
with focus on
{\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{s}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{\upphi}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}}
decays, while the background includes dominant processes such as
\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{b}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{b}}}}}}}
and
\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{c}}}}}}}
. The generated data was then passed through the cut-based analysis, based on information from reconstructed mass, momentum, etc. The selected
{\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{s}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{\upphi}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}}
signal and total background yields are expected to be around
3.9\text{\times}{10}^{4}\text{\,}

[
1457
]
and
1.6\text{\times}{10}^{3}\text{\,}
, respectively.

At FCC-ee, several measurements can be performed with the
{\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{s}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{\upphi}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}}
decay. The branching ratio measurement and the untagged time-dependent decay rate, described by the observable
D_{\text{f}}
, can be measured without the need of flavour tagging. Furthermore, with flavour tagging one can measure the time-integrated
C\!P
asymmetry,
\langle A_{C\!P}\rangle
and the time-dependent
C\!P
asymmetry, mainly described by the observables
C_{\text{f}}
and
S_{\text{f}}
.

The large dataset collected at FCC-ee enables a significant reduction in statistical uncertainties. Table
41
summarizes the expected precision for the key observables, demonstrating how FCC-ee will vastly improve our understanding of rare decays and
C\!P
violation. Such a level of precision is unattainable at Belle-II due to the limited availability of
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{s}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}
data. Additionally, the tagged measurements are not feasible at LHCb because of insufficient tagging power, making FCC-ee uniquely suited for these studies.

Effective Field Theory Interpretation

The study interprets the estimated precision of the observables within the framework of WET, focusing on the Wilson coefficients (WCs)
C_{7}
,
C_{9}
and
C_{10}
that describe the FCNC transitions responsible for
{\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{s}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{\upphi}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}}
. These WCs play a crucial role in connecting the experimental results to potential NP effects.

In the SM,
C\!P
violation arises from a single complex phase in the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix. However, NP scenarios can introduce additional complex phases, affecting the imaginary components of the WCs. By precisely measuring the BR along with the
C\!P
observables such as
S_{\text{f}}
, we can constrain both the real and imaginary parts of these WCs, offering insights into the possible contributions of NP.

Figure
160
shows the constraints on the real and imaginary parts of
C_{7}
,
C_{9}
and
C_{10}
from the BR and
S_{\text{f}}
measurements at FCC-ee.
22
22

22

Other measurements like
D_{\text{f}}
and
C_{\text{f}}
are not shown here, as they provide relatively weaker constraints.
The diagonal subplots display the 1D likelihood for each individual WC, while the 2D plots illustrate the constraints on a pair of WCs. In the 2D plots, the shaded regions and dashed lines represent the
1\sigma
and
2\sigma
boundaries, respectively. The black lines indicate the combined constraints from the measurements.

{centering}

Figure 160
:
Constraints on the real and imaginary parts of the WCs
C_{7}
,
C_{9}
, and
C_{10}
from the measurements of branching fraction and
C\!P
asymmetry at FCC-ee.

The results show that the BR measurement is more sensitive to the real part of the Wilson coefficients, while
S_{\text{f}}
is particularly sensitive to the imaginary part, making these measurements complementary. By combining them, the flat directions present in individual measurements are reduced, significantly narrowing the allowed parameter space for NP contributions. FCC-ee is expected to achieve unprecedented sensitivity to deviations from SM predictions, probing NP at energy scales up to
{\cal O}($10\text{\,}\mathrm{TeV}$)
.

By constraining both the real and imaginary parts of the WCs, this study uniquely explores potential NP contributions, particularly in the imaginary components, which are less explored. The imaginary parts of the WCs carry critical information about
C\!P
-violating phases introduced by NP, making them essential for a comprehensive understanding of
C\!P
violation. The precise measurements at FCC-ee allow for unprecedented sensitivity, offering a level of precision that is currently unattainable at other facilities. This makes FCC-ee one of the few experiments capable of probing these
C\!P
-violating effects in such detail, reinforcing its importance in the search for new sources of
C\!P
violation and potential deviations from SM predictions.

9.5.2
Focus Topic:

\mathup{{{b}}}\to\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
and
\mathup{{{b}}}\to\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\bar{\mathup{{{\upnu}}}}

Theoretical and phenomenological motivations for
\mathup{{{b}}}\to\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
and
\mathup{{{b}}}\to\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\overline{\mathup{{{\upnu}}}}

The process
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{K}}}^{*}(892)^{0}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
tests the partonic FCNC transition
\mathup{{{b}}}\to\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
. Present limits on this are weak,
\text{BR}(\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\to\mathup{{{K}}}^{*}(892)^{0}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}})<3.1\times 10^{-3}
at 90% CL
[
1458
]
23
23

23

The similar decay
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{K}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
has a slightly more stringent limit,
\text{BR}(\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{K}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}})<2.25\times 10^{-3}
at 90% CL
[
1459
]
.
and
\text{BR}(\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{s}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}})<6.8\times 10^{-3}
at 95% CL
[
1460
]
, while Belle II and LHCb will push these limits to the
10^{-4}
(
10^{-5}
) level for the leptonic (semi-leptonic) mode. These should be compared with the SM prediction, which is at the
\sim 10^{-7}
level for
\text{BR}(\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{K}}}^{*}(892)^{0}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}})

[
1461
]
. The large number of boosted
\mathup{{{B}}}
mesons produced from
\mathup{{{Z}}}
decays at a Tera-Z factory
[
845
]
could allow to improve substantially on the expected Belle-II limits and possibly reach a sensitivity to test the SM prediction.

The theoretical interest in this decay mode is wide, since it would allow to test a FCNC process involving third-generation leptons, complementing the present precise measurements of
\mathup{{{b}}}\to\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{l}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
with light leptons.
The general class of theories based on the
U(2)
-like scenarios discussed in
Section

9.2.1
, for instance, predict the largest New Physics effects to appear in processes with third-generation fermions.
As a specific example, large effects due to New Physics can be expected in connection with the
R(\mathup{{{D}}}^{(*)})
anomalies
[
1436
]
. These involve the
\mathup{{{b}}}\to\mathup{{{c}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{\upnu}}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{\!\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}}
transition, which in turn can be related to
\mathup{{{b}}}\to\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
via
SU(2)_{L}
invariance and flavour symmetries.
The same symmetries put these processes also in relation with
\mathup{{{b}}}\to\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upnu}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{\!\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{\upnu}}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{\!\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}}
transitions, which can be tested, for instance, with
\mathup{{{B}}}\to\mathup{{{K}}}^{(*)}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}}
decays. Such possible correlation motivates including in this focus topic the so-called golden channels
\mathup{{{B}}}\to\mathup{{{K}}}^{(*)}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}}
. These are not affected by long-distance charm loop effects, allowing for lower theoretical uncertainties.

Belle II has recently searched for the
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{K}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}}
decay and determined the branching fraction to be
[2.3\pm 0.5^{+0.5}_{-0.4}]\times 10^{-5}

[
1462
]
. This measurement has a significance of 3.5
\sigma
and is the first evidence for the decay, resulting in a 2.7
\sigma
tension with the SM prediction of
(5.58\pm 0.37)\times 10^{-6}
. A recent study has been performed to give a baseline estimate for the sensitivity achievable at FCC-ee
[
1321
]
, including studies on the particle identification and vertex resolution requirements. This enables in addition measurements of
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{s}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}
and
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\Uplambda}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{b}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}
decays which are impossible at Belle II. Experiments at a high-luminsoity
\mathup{{{Z}}}
-factory will be able to improve substantially upon Belle II measurements of
\mathup{{{b}}}\to\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}}
decays by obtaining branching fraction measurements with
\mathcal{O}(1\%)
sensitivity. This gives potential to make differential branching fraction measurements in these modes and will enable measurements of
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{s}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}
and
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\Uplambda}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{b}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}
decays.

Precision on the branching fraction of the transition
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{K}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{\ast}}}(892)^{0}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}

The experimental search for the transition
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{K}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{\ast}}}(892)^{0}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
is challenging because of the two undetected neutrinos emitted from
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
decays. The knowledge of all the vertices, considering the fully charged
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{K}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{\ast}}}(892)^{0}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{K}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uppi}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
decay and the three-prong hadronic
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uppi}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uppi}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uppi}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}
decays, allows to close the kinematics of the process and opens the possibility to make an exclusive reconstruction of the decay
[
1461
]
. Events simulated with the FCC-ee simulation software featuring the IDEA tracking detector are used to evaluate the physics reach depending on the vertices measurement performances. A large number of physics backgrounds are considered in the study and a selection based on the topology of the decays is performed (see Fig.
161
). The vertexing performances are emulated to provide several working points for which the topological reconstruction is performed and the physics sensitivity is evaluated and reported in Fig.
161
. Several characteristics of vertex detector were then simulated and placed on this curve. The improvements of single hit resolution and various reductions of the budget material of the IDEA vertex detector were considered. A remarkable conclusion of this study is that this physics case is limited by multiple coulombian scattering and therefore by the material budget of the beam pipe, triggering the interest and the thinking about novel vertex detector designs.

Results of the
\mathup{{{b}}}\to\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}}
study

To study the
\mathup{{{b}}}\to\mathup{{{s}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}}
transition, branching fraction measurements of the
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{K}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{S}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}}
,
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{s}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{\upphi}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}}
,
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{K}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{\ast}}}(892)^{0}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}}
and
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\Uplambda}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{b}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{\Uplambda}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}}
decays have been considered.
In Ref.
[
1321
]
the statistical uncertainty on the BFs of
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{K}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{\ast}}}(892)^{0}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}}
,
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{s}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{\upphi}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}}
,
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{K}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{S}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}}
and
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\Uplambda}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{b}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{\Uplambda}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}}
decays are determined to be
0.53\%
,
1.20\%
,
3.37\%
and
9.86\%
. For
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{K}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{\ast}}}(892)^{0}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}}
and
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{s}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{\upphi}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}}
decays this is determined by performing a simple two-stage BDT selection with cuts on the BDT responses optimised simultaneously, as well as a selection of rectangular cuts. The BDTs are trained on signal MC and inclusive background MC to model the various backgrounds originating from
\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}
production, where
\mathup{{{q}}}\in\{\mathup{{{u}}}/\mathup{{{d}}}/\mathup{{{s}}},\mathup{{{c}}},\mathup{{{b}}}\}
. Due to the low number of background events that pass simultaneous cuts on the BDT responses, a bi-cubic spline is used to build a map of the efficiency in signal/background as a function of the BDT responses. For
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{K}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{S}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}}
and
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\Uplambda}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{b}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{\Uplambda}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}}
decay branching fraction, the appropriate reconstruction for the
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{K}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{S}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}
and
\mathup{{{\Uplambda}}}
was not available and their precision was extrapolated assuming similar background as the
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{K}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{\ast}}}(892)^{0}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}}
and
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{s}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{\upphi}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}}
decays and a neutral reconstruction efficiency of
80\%
, suggested by companion studies.
The dependence of the statistical sensitivity to the branching fraction of the
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{B}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{s}}^{\scriptstyle{0}}}\to\mathup{{{\upphi}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}}
decay as a function of its value is shown in Fig.
162
. This initial estimate is obtained assuming perfect particle identification (PID) and vertex seeding. To determine the dependence on PID and vertexing performance naive estimates are obtained. For the PID the signal efficiencies are recomputed after making random mass hypothesis swaps, kaon
\to
pion and pion
\to
kaon over a range of mis-identification rates.
The resulting plots for these studies are shown in Fig.
