9.6
Tau physics

A high-luminosity
\mathup{{{Z}}}
factory with
N_{\mathup{{{Z}}}}=6\times 10^{12}

\mathup{{{Z}}}
decays
[
845
]
such as FCC-ee or CEPC will see an abundant production of
2\times 10^{11}
tau pairs allowing to deepen the studies of
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
physics. In particular, the knowledge of the tau mass and lifetime and that of its leptonic branching fractions
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\to\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}}
,
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\to\mathup{{{e}}}\mathup{{{\upnu}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\upnu}}}}
allows to test lepton universality in
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
decays. This section reports the expected precisions on the tau mass and lifetime yielding a canonical lepton universality test as well as the sensitivity in the search for lepton-flavour violating
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
decays
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\to 3\mathup{{{l}}}
,
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\to\mathup{{{l}}}\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}
.

9.6.1
Tau lepton lifetime measurement at Tera-
\mathup{{{Z}}}

With a sample of
6\times 10^{12}

\mathup{{{Z}}}
decays, it is convenient to measure the tau lifetime on the relatively small sub-sample of tau pairs where both tau leptons decay into a 3-prong topology, like Belle did
[
1463
]
. For these events, the two 3-prong vertices and the constraint of the very small luminous region precisely define the tau leptons’ flight directions, significantly reducing systematics from Monte Carlo simulation of the effects of the undetected neutrinos on the reconstruction of the tau flight directions.

The DELPHI tau lifetime measurement
[
1464
]
, which includes a measurement done on tau pairs both decaying to 3 charged tracks (3–3-prongs topology), is extrapolated to the FCC sample. The DELPHI measurement is performed on the 1991–1995 sample, corresponding to about
4.0\times 10^{6}
hadronic
\mathup{{{Z}}}
decays
[
1465
]
, hence about
N_{\mathup{{{Z}}}}^{\text{DELPHI 2004}}=4.0\times 10^{6}/70\%=5.7\times 10^{6}

\mathup{{{Z}}}
decays.
The relative statistical uncertainty of the measurement restricted to the 3-3 prongs events is

\sigma(\tau_{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}},\text{3--3})/\tau_{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}\times 10^{6}\,\text{ppm}\simeq 18000\,\text{ppm}
,
where
\tau_{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}
is the tau lifetime
[
595
]
.

The statistical and several sources of systematic uncertainties are scaled to the case of a Tera-
\mathup{{{Z}}}
run at FCC-ee as described in Ref.
[
1466
]
.
Scaling the number of
\mathup{{{Z}}}
decays from DELPHI to FCC-ee, we estimate that the relative statistical uncertainty on the tau lifetime will be

\sigma(\tau_{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}},\text{3--3},\text{FCC})/\tau_{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}\simeq 15.0\,\text{ppm}
.

The largest sources of systematic uncertainty in the DELPHI analysis can be optimistically expected to scale down with the square root of the number of events: background subtraction (for which the simulation can be tuned with data control samples), reconstruction bias (which can be studied with data prompt events), and vertex alignment (done with data events).
The tau lifetime measurement also requires the estimation of the average radiated energy in the initial state before the tau pair production. The DELPHI measurement relies on a
\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to\mathup{{{Z}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{+}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}
Monte Carlo simulation, whose estimated uncertainty contributes a 350 ppm systematic uncertainty. We optimistically speculate that an improvement of a factor 30 may be achieved, reducing the related uncertainty on the tau lifetime to 11.5 ppm at FCC.
Additionally the uncertainty on the tau mass contributes 9 ppm, assuming the measurements described in Section
9.6.2
.
In total the systematic uncertainties are expected to sum up to 21.5 ppm.

9.6.2
Prospects for tau mass measurement at Tera-
\mathup{{{Z}}}

Recently, the Belle II collaboration reported the most precise measurement of the tau mass,
$1777.09\text{\,}$\pm$0.08\text{\,}$\pm$0.11\text{\,}\mathrm{MeV}\text{\,}{\mathrm{}}^{-1}$

[
1467
]
. The
systematic uncertainties have been substantially reduced with respect to the previous
\mathup{{{B}}}
-factories’ measurements, and the total uncertainty is smaller than the uncertainties of the measurements performed at the tau pair production threshold
[
1468
,
1469
]
. The Belle II statistical uncertainty of
0.08\text{\,}\mathrm{MeV}\text{\,}{\mathrm{}}^{-1}
(45 ppm) has been obtained with
175\times 10^{6}
tau pairs (
190\text{\,}{\mathrm{fb}}^{-1}
of integrated luminosity), and could be improved to 1.3 ppm with
2.0\times 10^{11}
tau pairs at FCC-ee, without taking into account the larger efficiency that can be expected at FCC-ee from the comparison of LEP versus
\mathup{{{B}}}
-factories tau measurements. Rescaling the statistical uncertainty of the OPAL tau mass measurement
[
1470
]
to number of
\mathup{{{Z}}}
decays expected at FCC-ee gives an estimated statistical precision of 0.9 ppm. The Belle II leading systematic uncertainty of
0.07\text{\,}\mathrm{MeV}\text{\,}{\mathrm{}}^{-1}
(39 ppm) is related to the knowledge of the beam energy, and is expected to be significantly smaller at FCC-ee, where the beam energy can be known with 1 ppm precision. The other Belle II leading systematic uncertainty of
0.06\text{\,}\mathrm{MeV}\text{\,}{\mathrm{}}^{-1}
(34 ppm) is related to the understanding of the charged tracks reconstructed momentum scale, which can probably be calibrated with 2 ppm precision at FCC-ee by matching the measured
\mathup{{{J\mspace{-2mu}/\mspace{-2mu}\uppsi}}}
mass to its world average, presently known to 2 ppm. Belle II reports systematic uncertainties related to the estimator bias (
0.03\text{\,}\mathrm{MeV}\text{\,}{\mathrm{}}^{-1}
), to the choice of the fit function of the pseudo-mass distribution (
0.02\text{\,}\mathrm{MeV}\text{\,}{\mathrm{}}^{-1}
), to the detector material (
0.03\text{\,}\mathrm{MeV}\text{\,}{\mathrm{}}^{-1}
), and to the modeling of ISR, FSR and tau decay (
0.02\text{\,}\mathrm{MeV}\text{\,}{\mathrm{}}^{-1}
), for a total of 29 ppm. We expect that these systematic uncertainties may be reduced by a factor 3 to 10 ppm at FCC-ee, which we take as the estimated precision of the measurement of the tau mass at FCC-ee.

9.6.3
Lepton universality test in
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
decays

The tau leptonic branching fractions were measured by the LEP experiments. As a case in point, ALEPH measured the tau leptonic branching fractions BR
(\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{\upnu}}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{\!\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upnu}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{\!\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}})
and BR
(\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{\upnu}}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{\!\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upnu}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{\!\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}})
with a precision of about 0.44% (0.40% statistical and 0.19% systematic), using
5.9\times 10^{6}

\mathup{{{Z}}}
decays. The extrapolated statistical precision at a high-luminosity
\mathup{{{Z}}}
-factory with
6\times 10^{12}

\mathup{{{Z}}}
decays amounts to 4.0 ppm. The lepton universality test reported in Fig.
163
assumes that the ALEPH systematic uncertainty on the tau leptonic branching fractions can be reduced by a factor 10 to 0.019%, 100% correlated between the muon and the electron tau decay modes. The quantity
B^{\prime}_{e}
denotes the average between the measured branching fraction BR
(\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{e}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{\upnu}}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{\!\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upnu}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{\!\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}})
and its Standard Model prediction inferred from the measured branching fraction BR
(\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\to\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}^{\scriptstyle{-}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{\upnu}}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{\!\mathup{{{\upmu}}}}}}\mathup{{{\mathup{{{\upnu}}}}}{}_{\scriptstyle{\!\mathup{{{\uptau}}}}}})
. This lepton-universality test precision is improved w.r.t. the current knowledge by more than an order of magnitude and would unravel the existence of new amplitudes if the central experimental values remain the same as to date. This breakthrough is mostly brought by the improved

lifetime measurement, unique to a
\mathup{{{Z}}}
-factory.

9.6.4
LFV from
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}
decays

The large samples of
2.0\times 10^{11}
tau pairs produced at a
\mathup{{{Z}}}
-factory allows for high-precision searches for lepton-flavour violation. In particular, the prospects of the search for
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\to\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}
and
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\to\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}}
are examined in the context of FCC-ee and compared to the current and foreseeable prospects at present or envisaged facilities.

Search for
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\to\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}

A simulation corresponding to
7\times 10^{10}
visible
\mathup{{{Z}}}
decays has been used to estimate how many
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\to\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}
decay candidates from background sources are to be expected for
3\times 10^{12}

\mathup{{{Z}}}
decays at an FCC-ee experiment
[
844
,
1466
]
. By assuming a reasonable reconstruction and selection efficiency, a sensitivity of
2\times 10^{-9}
has been estimated, corresponding to a signal equal to a double-sided
2\sigma
fluctuation of the large number of expected background events, in the Gaussian approximation
[
844
]
. The sensitivity in terms of the expected upper limit at 90% confidence level (CL) for a search of
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\to\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}
on a sample of
6\times 10^{12}

\mathup{{{Z}}}
decays at FCC-ee is extrapolated to be
BR
(\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\to\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\upgamma}}})\lessapprox 1.2\times 10^{-9}\ \text{at 90\%\,CL}
.

reports the present upper limits and the expected upper limits for BR
(\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\to\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\upgamma}}})

Search for
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\to\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}}

The Belle II collaboration reported a 90% CL upper limit of
1.9\times 10^{-8}
for the lepton-flavour-violating branching fraction BR
(\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\to\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}})

[
1471
]
, using

390{\times}10^{6}
tau pairs (corresponding to
424\text{\,}{\mathrm{fb}}^{-1}
of integrated luminosity). The estimated selection efficiency is about 20.4%, significantly larger than the one attained by the previous Belle search
[
1472
]
, 7.6%, and is now comparable to the efficiency that has been reported at LEP 1 for the DELPHI
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\to\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}
search
[
1473
]
, 24.5%, which is about 4 times the efficiency reported by the same
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\to\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\upgamma}}}
search by BaBar
[
1474
]
. When assuming that for the
\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\to\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}}
search an efficiency of 35.0% may be obtained at FCC-ee, exploiting the highly efficient and pure muon selection at the
\mathup{{{Z}}}
peak energies, the expected upper limit at a high-luminosity
\mathup{{{Z}}}
-factory featuring
2.0\times 10^{11}
tau pairs reads as BR
(\mathup{{{\uptau}}}\to\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}}\mathup{{{\upmu}}})\lessapprox 2.\times 10^{-11}\ \text{at 90\%\,CL}
.

9.7
Outlook on other avenues

There was a surge of new hadrons observed at the LHC and the Belle II and BESIII experiments. Many of those are exotic in nature, not fitting expectations from
\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{{q}}}
or
\mathup{{{q}}}\mathup{{\overline{{\mathup{{{q}}}}}}}
quark contents. So far 23 exotic particles containing at least one charm quark have been observed at the LHC, many in amplitude analyses of
\mathup{{{b}}}
hadrons
[
1475
,
1476
]
. It is not clear whether they are compact objects of four or five quarks, or rather molecule-like bounds states of conventional hadrons, or even both. Many more such states are expected to be found LHCb and Belle II. A Tera-
\mathup{{{Z}}}
run will add valuable information. As LHCb has reduced precision for neutral final states, and Belle II lower data yields. The high precision of a
\mathup{{{Z}}}
run permits amplitude analyses involving neutral pions and kaons with similar precision as the corresponding mainly charged-only LHCb analyses. Such studies are essential to find isospin partners of known states, and find new states, thereby shedding light on their nature.
